articles.title: Ukraine's interceptor tech outpaced by Russia’s jet-powered Geran-5 drones
articles.body:
Ukraine's interceptor tech outpaced by Russia’s jet-powered Geran-5 drones
Rescuers work at a school damaged by a Russian drone strike in Kyiv, Ukraine, on Oct. 1, 2026. (Tetiana Dzhafarova / AFP via Getty Images)
The jet-black Russian munition slammed into the Presidium building of Ukraine's National Academy of Sciences, an iconic Tsarist-era structure right in the center of Kyiv, setting the building on fire. Survivors climbed out of the windows and clambered onto the building's ledges, fleeing the flames and choking black smoke. Two people were killed in the attack. Around an hour later, an identical munition struck a private medical clinic a few blocks away.
The Geran-5 jet-powered drone is Russia's latest attempt to destroy civilian life in Kyiv and force Ukraine to capitulate, as Russian offensives stall and Moscow's forces lose ground on the battlefield. Small, and with a tubular fuselage reminiscent of a missile rather than a drone, the Geran-5 flies higher, faster, and is significantly more difficult to shoot down.
"The Geran-5 is a significantly more difficult target to intercept than the Geran-4, or any of the previous generation of Russian drones," a senior engineer working for a defense contractor told the Kyiv Independent, speaking on condition of anonymity due to the work's sensitive nature. "We have multiple teams attacking the problem from 4-5 different angles at the same time," he said.
"The Geran-5 flies 150km/h faster than the Geran-4, so the goal is to intercept from the front rather than the rear - a much harder problem to solve," the engineer said.
Launched at the city in waves, Russia's jet drones target civilian infrastructure such as supermarkets, schools, shopping malls, telecommunications infrastructure, data centers, gas stations, and medical facilities.
Planning everyday activities with any degree of certainty has become increasingly difficult through the disruptive effect of constant air raids. When an air alert is sounded, shopping malls, bridges, gas stations, restaurants, and government buildings close. Constant explosions wrack the nerves of Kyiv's residents as the sense of danger in districts once considered safe becomes nearly palpable.
Russia is attempting to “destroy pretty much the entire economy," economy minister Oleksandr Kravchenko told the Guardian, claiming that air raid alerts cost the Ukrainian economy $45 million for each hour businesses stop their operations. The past week saw air raids of over 20 combined hours in a single day.
"What we had not fully anticipated was how quickly Russia would develop these jet-powered drones and use them to target everything," Kravchenko said.
Russia is rapidly scaling the number of jet-powered drones it uses in raids on Kyiv. "Sometimes, two-thirds of all drones launched during the day are jet-powered," Colonel Yurii Ihnat, head of the Air Force Command's Communications Department, told the Kyiv Independent.
Ukrainian intelligence estimates that Russia can currently produce 3,000 jet-powered Geran-4 and Geran-5 models per month, a figure Moscow seeks to rapidly increase. Like many of Russia's other high-end munitions, both the Geran-4 and Geran-5 include many Western components, according to the Ukrainian government and independent analysis of crashed models.
Only 57% of jet-powered drones are currently shot down by Ukraine, President Zelensky acknowledged in his evening address on Sept. 28, a figure he described as "much less than necessary."
The methods Ukraine pioneered and perfected for dealing with Russia's older, piston-powered drones, such as mobile anti-aircraft teams and interceptor drones, are no longer sufficient.
read also
A new generation of Russian drones
The older jet-powered Geran-3 and Geran-4 have a delta-winged aerodynamic form similar to Russia's older, Iranian-derived, piston-engined Geran-1 and Geran-2 drones. The Geran-5's form is far closer to a traditional cruise missile, giving it a significantly higher maximum speed.
"The Geran-5 much more resembles a low-cost cruise missile than a long-range drone like the original Shahed derivatives," Fabian Hoffmann, a senior research fellow at the Norwegian Institute for Defence Studies, told the Kyiv Independent.
A low-cost cruise missile is a type of munition that occupies a middle ground between Russia's cheap piston-engined long-range drones, and its expensive, highly sophisticated cruise and ballistic missiles, Hoffmann explained.
As such, Russia's Geran-5 drones are more expensive than older piston-engined models, with the Chinese-imported turbojet engine alone costing $40,000. The drone's overall price is estimated at around $115,000, compared to older piston-engined models, estimated at as little as $30,000.
"The biggest weakness probably is that Russia is not yet able to mass produce the engine on its own and relies on Chinese imports," Hoffmann told the Kyiv Independent.
Yet, the cost of the Geran-5 is just a fraction of a traditional cruise missile’s cost, allowing Russia to produce and launch them en masse. At the same time, the Geran-5 is less destructive than a traditional cruise missile.
The drone carries a warhead of about 90 kg, Ukrainian military intelligence estimates, compared to the 480 kg warhead carried by the ground-launched 9M728 Iskander-K, which costs around $1.5 million per missile, or the air-launched Kh-101 cruise missile, which can carry a warhead of up to 800 kg, and costs around $2 million per missile.
read also
An airborne arms race
Commenting on the recent waves of Russian jet-powered drone strikes, Serhiy Sternenko, drone warfare adviser to former Ukrainian Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov, said "there is currently no mass produced effective product among interceptors."
"There are prototypes that showed different results, but to bring the prototype to a large series requires a lot of effort, and sometimes it is even impossible due to limited access to certain components," Sternenko said.
Successfully demonstrated prototypes include the STING S interceptor, manufactured by Wild Hornets and the P1-SUN Jetkiller, manufactured by SkyFall, which are confirmed to have shot down a small number of Geran-5 drones.
Another promising prototype is manufactured by Quantum WIY Industries, the Ukrainian subsidiary of German defense concern Quantum Systems. Video released by Quantum Systems shows one of the company's "SPYS" drones successfully intercept a Geran-5 over Ukraine.
The "SPYS" drone is a propeller-powered interceptor, whose special motors allow the drone to 'sprint' to 600kph for short periods of time, a company representative told Ukrainian outlet Militarnyi. It trades this increased speed for decreased flight endurance to intercept the much faster Geran-5.
"It's not only us who are working on such solutions," Sven Kruck, co-CEO of Quantum Systems, told the Kyiv Independent, explaining that many other companies also work on improved interceptor drones.
"I think that in the next upcoming weeks, we can hopefully see the results from these companies," Kruck added. "So I would say that maybe in four to eight weeks, we should see we are more controlling the air again".
Besides the upgraded propeller-powered interceptors, Ukraine is also developing a new generation of jet-powered interceptor drones. The first model, the Alexa Spatium, entered service on Aug. 21, according to the Ukrainian Defense Ministry.
Ukraine's internal security service, the SBU, has been developing a different, delta-winged jet-powered interceptor, Zelensky announced on Sept. 19, sharing video of the interceptor successfully downing a Geran-5.
Quantum Systems is also developing a jet-powered interceptor. "We have invented a jet, a counter-UAS element, which we call SPICE, which is able to counter these jet Shahed drones," Kruck told the Kyiv Independent.
"The jet-powered interceptor design is still maturing, but Ukraine will get there," Hoffmann said. "The main problem is that Ukraine will be much more reliant on American and European partners, Taiwan, and China for jet engine imports, as it is not producing these engines itself. So scaling production will require steady and growing supply from abroad, or establishing licensed production facilities to mass produce engines in Ukraine."

articles.title: CENTEF report reveals Hezbollah acquired $157m of weapons in 2024, majority provided freely by Iran
articles.body:
Hezbollah acquired an estimated $157 million worth of weaponry in 2024, despite its war with Israel, with the vast majority of it donated by the Islamic Republic of Iran at no cost to the terror group, according to the Israeli Center for Research of Terror Financing’s new research published on Thursday.
The report, “Hezbollah Financial Statements,” is the first installment in a series set to expose Hezbollah’s media spending, payments to wounded fighters and spending on its military infrastructure.
Based on open-source information and valuations of known Hezbollah military assets, CENTEF estimates that Iran provided roughly $129 million worth of weapons and military equipment as an in-kind grant while Hezbollah itself spent approximately $28 million in cash on its acquisitions.
Seeking to understand Hezbollah’s expenses as a business entity, to better assess the terror group’s financial health and identify ways to weaken it, while avoiding the costly airstrikes that can have significant consequences for Lebanese civilians, the researchers examined the group’s weapons procurement and manufacturing costs, as well as its ability to sustain its arsenal if the Islamic Republic’s capacity to supply it were reduced.
Explaining the rationale behind the analysis, CENTEF CEO Sharon Gal told The Jerusalem Post that breaking down Hezbollah’s finances could help legislators and operators efficiently identify and prioritize key supply chains to disrupt, creating pressure points for the Iranian-backed terror group.
Researchers aim for interactive tool on Hezbollah finances
Expanding those efforts, researcher Marc Cohen told the Post that they plan to release an interactive tool to help civilians understand Hezbollah’s financial statements, with the hope that it can raise awareness of Hezbollah’s negative impact on the Lebanese economy and the scale of its operations.
The researchers looked at the different types of military equipment Hezbollah is estimated to have acquired in 2024, including rockets, missiles, drones, ATGMs, air-defense systems, ammunition, launchers, naval equipment, and IED-related assets.
Hezbollah’s own investment in its weapons is limited to small arms, ammunition, drone components, dual-use equipment, and equipment obtained through its international procurement networks.
Because Hezbollah’s weapons acquisitions are clandestine, the researchers had to estimate how many weapons the group acquired in 2024 rather than rely on procurement records. They used three methods: Analyzing Hezbollah’s historical rate of replenishing its arsenal, assessing Iran’s capacity to manufacture and deliver weapons, and comparing global benchmarks for the costs of equipping, training, and mobilizing military forces.
The first method was based on Hezbollah’s growth over the past two decades. According to estimates from the Center for Strategic and International Studies, Hezbollah had approximately 15,000 rockets in 2006 and had expanded its arsenal to roughly 150,000 by 2024, amounting to an average increase of about 7,500 rockets per year over 18 years of Iranian resupply.
Acknowledging that Hezbollah’s replenishment likely varied year-to-year, it estimated that the disruption to Hezbollah’s supply chain and manufacturing abilities during the 2024 fighting resulted in them acquiring approximately 4,500 to 6,500 rockets and missiles during the year.
The second method considered was Iran’s ability to directly supply Hezbollah. The researchers noted that Iran can only manufacture and physically deliver a limited number of sophisticated weapons, and those weapons must be distributed among Iran’s own forces and multiple proxies.
Iran is estimated to produce approximately 50 to 240 ballistic missiles per month and 1,800 to 3,000 attack drones per year total. This places a ceiling on how many guided missiles and drones Hezbollah could realistically have acquired in 2024. With that in mind, researchers analyzed the value of weapons in Hezbollah’s arsenal to understand exactly what Iranian support was worth and confirm that Hezbollah would be unable to afford such advanced weaponry without Tehran’s patronage.
Hezbollah arsenal includes heavy Iranian Falaq rockets, Katyushas
A staple of Hezbollah’s arsenal is the Katyusha rocket, alongside Iran’s heavier Falaq-1 and Falaq-2 rockets, which have 240mm and 333mm warheads respectively, and the crude, large-warhead Burkan rocket. The 122mm Katyusha is one of the few systems for which there is a publicly available price, at approximately $300 per round, while the Burkan is estimated to cost around $400 per rocket. Based on OSINT, the researchers estimate that Hezbollah acquired approximately 4,000 of the short-range rockets, 400 Falaq rockets, and 120 Burkan rockets in 2024.
Hezbollah’s inventory also includes Iran’s Fajr series and Syrian-origin heavy rockets. The Fajr-3 is a 240mm artillery rocket armed with a 45-kilogram warhead, while the Fajr-5 is a 333 mm rocket with a GPS-guided Fajr-5C variant. CENTEF estimates that Hezbollah acquired approximately 600 rockets across this class in 2024, at an estimated cost of $2,000 to $10,000 per unit.
The inventory also includes the unguided Zelzal-2, which costs an estimated $25,000 per rocket, and the GPS-guided Fateh-110/M-600, a high-priority transfer estimated by JINSA to cost $110,000. The transfer can also be fitted with a $5,000 to $10,000 GPS guidance kit to turn them into a guided weapon.
With Iran’s missile production shared among several recipients and the supply corridor repeatedly disrupted during 2024, Hezbollah’s acquisition of these systems was thought to have been tightly constrained, and it is understood the group acquired only 60 Zelzal rockets, 40 Fateh-110/M-600 missiles, and 150 guidance kits.
The inventory also includes Iran’s Paveh land-attack cruise missile, which has a range of approximately 700 to 2,000 kilometers. Given its high unit value, CENTEF estimates that only about 12 were acquired in 2024.
Anti-tank guided missiles (ATGMs) accounted for about 20% of Hezbollah’s attacks on Israel during its attacks after October 8, 2023, and were likely its largest-value weapons category, according to the researchers.
The Russian-made Kornet, supplied via Syria, costs approximately $26,000 per round, while Iran’s reverse-engineered Dehlavieh costs an estimated $12,000 to $15,000. Hezbollah also uses the Iranian Almas, older Konkurs and Metis systems, and the RPG-29. CENTEF estimates that Hezbollah received approximately 700 Kornet and 500 Dehlavieh rounds, 500 Almas missiles and 400 Konkurs/Metis missiles, along with 30 launchers in 2024.
The RPG-7, a standard squad-level anti-armor weapon with reusable launchers, costs about $350, and rounds cost $100 to $500; CENTEF estimated that Hezbollah acquired approximately 800 RPG launchers and 15,000 rounds in 2024, with some rounds procured on the black market.
Hezbollah also acquired drones and unmanned aerial vehicles, including the Iranian Mirsad-1 and Ababil-T and small Shahed-101-class loitering munitions. Loitering munitions cost an estimated $20,000 to $40,000, while commercial and FPV quadcopters range from $1,000 to $15,000. CENTEF estimates that Hezbollah acquired approximately 300 Mirsad and Ababil drones combined, 200 loitering munitions, 400 commercial and FPV drones, and several reconnaissance UAVs in 2024.
Hezbollah’s air-defense inventory includes MANPADS costing roughly $5,000 to $100,000 each depending on the model, and it is thought to have also received 358 of Iran’s loitering surface-to-air missiles.
Small arms, IEDs relatively cheap for Hezbollah
Small arms are comparatively inexpensive. Hezbollah uses AKM and AK-103 assault rifles, along with PKM and DShK machine guns and SVD sniper rifles. CENTEF estimates that it acquired about 5,000 rifles, 900 crew-served weapons, 80 mortar tubes, 15,000 mortar rounds, and 8 million rounds of ammunition in 2024.
Given that IEDs are relatively cheap to manufacture and can be produced in Lebanon, the researchers estimated the group invested in 2,000.
CENTEF is also gathering data on how Hezbollah spends money on its civilian arm, including through charities that assist residents of Lebanon’s south displaced through the group’s wars. While still analyzing the cost of Hezbollah’s media landscape, it has already estimated that Hezbollah spent $26 million to $28 million on media in 2024, with Al-Manar alone accounting for $16.5 million to $17.2 million.
The researchers said understanding these expenses, alongside Hezbollah’s military spending and Iran’s support, could provide a fuller picture of the group’s financial dependencies and generate more choke points to pressure it.

articles.title: Putin Raises Nuclear Threat Over Kaliningrad, Says Russia Monitors Arms Factories in Europe
articles.body:
Russian President Vladimir Putin warned that a direct attack on Russia or Kaliningrad exclave would immediately raise the question of using all of Moscow’s weapons, including nuclear, days after Russia previously threatened NATO over the exclave.
Speaking during the annual Valdai Discussion Club forum, Putin also said Russia was monitoring European factories that are producing weapons for Ukraine.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“If it comes to a direct attack on Russia, on Kaliningrad, the question of using all the weapons we have will immediately arise,” Putin said, according to translated excerpts published by Clash Report.
“No one currently has weapons like those possessed by Russia,” he claimed.
Insisting that Moscow will not attack Europe
Putin reiterated that Moscow has no initiative to attack Europe, even as Russian drone incursions, airspace violations and sabotage campaigns increase across the EU.
His claims came a week after a Russian military helicopter violated Polish airspace and two days after Estonia concluded that Russian intelligence ordered an arson attack on a defense company supplying Ukraine.
“We don’t intend to attack anyone in 2029, in 2030, or 2050, but if we are attacked, we will have to respond,” he said, adding that “citizens of European countries should be fully aware of that.”
Yet, the First Deputy Chairman of the State Duma Committee on CIS Affairs, Viktor Vodolatsky, called for mandatory military training to begin in fifth grade, arguing that Russia must prepare its youth for a possible war with NATO and the EU by 2030.
UK Announces Package of 31 Sanctions Against Russia
From Sept. 1, Russia has already expanded military training for children, including in occupied Ukrainian territories, and raised the share of mandatory instruction to 50% of school time.
During the same address, he said that arms production for Ukraine remains a threat to Moscow and that the Kremlin is monitoring them closely.
“I am not saying that we are going to strike enterprises in the countries supplying weapons to Ukraine, but this is a threat,” Putin said.
In August, Bloomberg reported that the Kremlin increasingly views Ukrainian strikes as an attack from NATO itself, particularly because alliance members supply Kyiv with weapons and intelligence.
Speaking about nuclear weapons, Putin cited a principle associated with Russian writer Anton Chekhov; “If a gun is hanging on the stage, sooner or later it must go off,” he said, repeating the Kremlin’s long-standing claims that the war “was started against us.”
Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022 and has so far rejected every proposal for a direct meeting or a possible ceasefire.
Why Kaliningrad matters
Putin’s assurances contrast with a series of direct threats from Moscow against NATO and its members in recent weeks.
On Monday, Sept. 28, Russia’s embassy in Belgium said it had delivered a position to NATO’s International Secretariat and Belgium’s Foreign Ministry warning that Moscow was ready to deploy its entire arsenal if alliance members tried to isolate Kaliningrad.
The embassy accused NATO of an “aggressive policy” without specifying which actions prompted the warning.
NATO spokesperson Allison Hart said that the alliance had responded to Moscow’s informal diplomatic document by reiterating that NATO is an exclusively defensive alliance, simultaneously condemning Moscow’s “irresponsible nuclear rhetoric.”
The exclave Russia seeks to “protect” is wedged between Lithuania and Poland, both NATO members, and is connected to Russia only by sea. However, it is Russia’s only ice-free Baltic port, which may be particularly important due to Western sanctions imposed on Russia and its shadow fleet vessels.
Kaliningrad also hosts the headquarters of the Baltic Fleet and has Iskander missiles with a range of about 500 kilometers (about 311 miles).
The Suwałki Gap, a roughly 65-kilometer (40 miles) stretch of the Polish-Lithuanian border separating Kaliningrad from Belarus remains a big concern for NATO. Should a conflict emerge, Russian forces could try to seize the corridor and cut the Baltic states off from allied reinforcements.
Further threats aimed at NATO and the Baltics
Earlier on Thursday, Russia has also accused the alliance of a reckless course carrying a high risk of direct armed conflict and threatened to strike “decision-making centers” in member countries.
On Sept. 11, former Russian President Dmitry Medvedev threatened that Lithuania would “disappear from the map” if it lifted its ban on nuclear weapons, claiming NATO would not invoke Article 5 to defend the country as that would mean a “global catastrophe.”
Two weeks later, Putin repeated unfounded claims about the mistreatment of Russian-speaking minorities in the Baltic states, the same grievance the Kremlin used to justify its full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
The string of latest threats has raised fears that the Kremlin may be seeking a justification for a direct attack on the Baltic states.
Separately, President Volodymyr Zelensky has warned that Russia could directly attack another European country, including through a limited ground incursion.
Speaking during a summit in Brussels on Wednesday, Sept. 30, NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte condemned Moscow’s rhetoric. NATO’s combined strength exceeds Russia’s, he said, adding that he does not take the nuclear threats seriously.

articles.title: Hegseth Unveils New Autonomous Warfare Command in ‘State of the Force’ Address
articles.body:
MARINE CORPS BASE QUANTICO, Va.—Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth announced plans for a new four-star command to lead the military-wide drive to field autonomous systems, as the Pentagon’s takes a bullish approach towards artificial intelligence and drone warfare. He also unveiled five other initiatives during what he promised will become an annual “State of the Force” address here Sept. 30.
Hegseth plans to launch the Autonomous Warfare Command within a year as a combatant command endowed with “service-like authorities, built to scale autonomous and robotic capabilities across the joint force,” he said. Its portfolio will include drones, artificial intelligence, and command and control systems.
Hegseth also announced the creation of a new program office, led by a two-star officer, to ensure military installations can generate their own power to isolate themselves from attacks on public grids. Bases in the homeland are increasingly seen as possibly contested environments where the U.S. military must be able to operate while under threat in a age of increasingly sophisticated cyberattacks and so-called hybrid warfare activities by America’s adversaries.
And he confirmed plans to slash the total number of generals and admirals across the military by 20 percent, a move Air & Space Forces Magazine and other outlets had reported would be part of Hegseth’s speech.
Other initiatives include:
- A new group, dubbed “Project Meridian,” to study the future of warfare led by tech leaders Palmer Luckey and Elon Musk and former Speaker of the House Newt Gingrich, who were in attendance.
- An initiative, called the “Next Great American Base,” to build a new military installation to host 15,000-25,000 service members. Hegseth said governors and adjutant generals from every state will be invited to the Pentagon to pitch locations.
- The creation of five new corps of cadets at Hillsdale College, Louisiana State University, Liberty University, Mississippi State University, and Tuskegee University, which will all be given priority in officer commissioning.
- A new “Office of Religious Affairs” reporting directly to the Secretary of Defense to give chaplains better access to senior leadership.
Exactly one year after Hegseth summoned hundreds of senior officers and enlisted from commands across the globe to Quantico for an address outlining his vision for the U.S. military, he spoke this time to an audience of around 600 E-6 enlisted members and O-3 officers, who the Pentagon said were selected by their units for their performance and leadership potential.
Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff Air Force Gen. Dan Caine briefly addressed the crowd and introduced Hegseth.
Autonomy
The new Autonomous Warfare Command will drive the design, development, and fielding of autonomous and semi-autonomous capabilities and systems.
“The autonomous and robotic revolution has enormous implications for equipment, doctrine, organization, and the assumptions that have governed warfare for decades,” Hegseth said. “Civilian leaders can provide direction and urgency, but lasting change must be anchored in military command structures and operationalized by leaders across our joint force.”
The Pentagon is already leaning heavily into autonomy, and the new command is designed to significantly accelerate that effort. Lawmakers in the Senate had proposed the creation of such a combatant command during deliberations for the 2027 defense policy bill. The measure cleared the committee, but the bill is still pending. To be authorized, the House would also have to approve the measure.
It is not yet clear how the new four-star command will be structured, who will lead it, or how it will work with the autonomy efforts already underway within the different services. In a memo, Hegseth wrote the Pentagon plans to work with Congress to stand up the command by October 1, 2027, a year on from the announcement.
Hegseth said it will start with an interim step, dubbed “Project Agincourt,” named for the Battle of Agincourt in 1415. Project Agincourt will draw from existing efforts like the Defense Innovation Unit and the Drone Dominance program, Hegseth said, and pair “operators with entrepreneurs in rapid adaptation cycles while distributing decisions and dollars closer to frontline units.”
Project Agincourt will be guided by DIU director Owen West and Navy SEAL Senior Chief Max Strasiser, the first enlisted SEAL to graduate from Navy Test Pilot School. Creating Autonomous Warfare Command will take place “over the course of several months,” Hegseth said.
The Air Force and Navy are already developing Collaborative Combat Aircraft: semi-autonomous drones designed to work alongside crewed fighters. The Air Force is also pursuing a lower-cost intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance drone with autonomous capabilities under its Massed Modular Aircraft program, and the Navy is working to field an unmanned tanker drone, the MQ-25.
The growth of autonomomy and the Penatagon’s future plans to harvest technology with its new command represent the “fastest peacetime shift in modern military history,” Hegseth said.
“Drone warfare supercharged by SI-enabled targeting is the biggest battlefield revolution in generations,” he added, using an acronym for so-called super intelligence, President Donald Trump’s favored term for AI.
At AFA’s Air, Space & Cyber conference earlier this month, Air Force leadership made it clear they see autonomous systems as central to the service’s future. Air Force Chief of Staff Gen. Ken Wilsbach told Air & Space Forces Magazine at the conference that while true autonomous aircraft are a “few years off,” the service is leaning heavily into autonomy in its current future Force Design model.
“The FQ-42 and the FQ-44 [Collaborative Combat Aircraft] are autonomous fighters, and then we’re going to have perhaps other platforms that are autonomous, where you don’t actually need a crew to do a fighter mission,” Wilsbach said during a session with reporters. “You just send the aircraft off, and it does its mission because it’s automated.”
The Pentagon has deployed uncrewed surface vessels operationally in the Middle East for a few years for maritime surveillance. This summer, a U.S. Navy drone boat was even able to rescue two downed Army Apache pilots near the Strait of Hormuz. U.S. Southern Command, which has been conducting strikes on boats suspected of smuggling drugs for over a year, recently established an autonomous warfare branch that will employ its own uncrewed vessels and aerial intelligence-gathering platforms. On the southern border, the U.S. military is now using 10 uncrewed surface vessels to patrol the Rio Grande River, Assistant Secretary of Defense for Homeland Defense and Americas Security Affairs M. Roosevelt Ditlevson told Air & Space Forces Magazine in a recent interview.
“We’re moving into next-generation tools here that we’re going to employ to make sure that we hold these narcoterrorists at bay,” Ditlevson said, referring to drug smugglers. “I’m very excited about what is going to happen in the autonomy space and how we’re going to employ these different systems.”
But the Pentagon is automating more than aircraft, ships, and vehicles.
The Pentagon’s Maven Smart System has become a key tool for the U.S. military, a system aggregating sensors, intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance, and command and control as part of the targeting process. Maven is used for operations ranging from targeting assistance in the Middle East to, more recently, counter-drone and anti-smuggling efforts on the southern border.
Ditlevson said AI, through Maven, will also feed into the Pentagon’s sweeping Golden Dome missile defense shield. “Maven Smart System is going to feed into the Golden Dome picture,” he said.
At the border, the Defense Department also uses autonomy software called Fortress, an adaptation of Anduril’s Lattice, which integrates data and sensors using AI. “All of our systems must be compatible with Maven Smart System,” Ditlevson said. “Everything that we have, that data needs to be integrated into Maven and into Lattice.”
To support all these new autonomous systems, Hegseth said, each military service will phase in new military occupational specialties for autonomy.
“We need institutional knowledge and career paths for a new generation of autonomous warfighters,” he said.
Fortress America
Hegseth also said the Pentagon is creating a new initiative called “Fortress America” to ensure military installations are able to generate their own power. The Pentagon has been working on building nuclear microreactors at key U.S. bases in the homeland and has previously said it plans to field a nuclear reactor at a military base by September 2028.
The Air Force in particular is working on a microreactor at Eielson Air Force Base, Alaska, with plans to build more at other bases in the coming years. The service has also explored using alternate power sources like solar panels, geothermal plants, and more to create so-called “microgirds” for bases so they’re not entirely reliant on local civilian power grids.
The drive to give bases their own energy sources is driven by concerns that adversaries may target critical infrastructure, around 80 percent of which is currently in the commercial sector, to kneecap the military’s ability to generate forces. The Pentagon chief referred to the program as “nation’s insurance policy” in a memo directing the establishment of Fortress America.
“If an adversary takes down the grid by cyber attack, by sabotage, or by any means, our bases stay lit, our aircraft keep flying, our command centers never go dark,” Hegseth said.
Hegseth is also slashing the number of general and flag officers, cutting billets by 20 percent. That doubles down on the 10 percent cut to general and flag officers he ordered last year, which he dubbed the “less generals, more GIs” policy.
“The number-crunchers say we fired 10 percent of the generals and admirals across the force, and that number sounds about right,” Hegseth said. “And I know because I directed it that we’ve also reduced the overall number of general officer slots by an additional 10 percent. So yes, 20 percent reduction across the board.”
Generals and admirals make up less than 1 percent of the military. According to the Congressional Research Service data, there were about 850 general officer positions in 2023. Some of those positions were unfilled at the time, as is the case today.
The maximum number of general officers allowed per service is set by law, though those caps do not apply to joint positions. The law also sets a minimum number of general officers in joint jobs.
The Air Force has roughly 250 generals. The Space Force has roughly 30 generals, and has plans to continue to grow that number.
A year ago, most senior military leaders gave stoic reactions during politically charged speeches from Hegseth and Trump, keeping with the military’s apolitical tradition. The troops at this year’s addres gave Hegseth a more vocal reception, particularly during his reference to Musk, Luckey, and Gingrich, and Hegseth exited to applause from the troops, though service members appeared to avoid visual reactions to Hegseth’s more ideological comments. Attendees were separated by branch, and were given a “War Department Field Manual,” a collection speeches by Hegseth with a forward written by Trump. Earlier in the day, the service members in attendance participated in a physical training session with Hegseth on the grounds of the Pentagon.

articles.title: Ukraine war latest: Russian losses soar by 46% during 2026
articles.body:
Key developments on Oct. 1:
- Russian losses soar by 46% during 2026
- Russian drones strike Kyiv school, key bridge linking eastern, western banks of city
- Russian drone strikes Kyiv nuclear institute housing research reactor
- Ukrainian pilot dies after MiG-29 fighter shot down by Russian missile
- 'Returning Russia's sick war to where it came from' — Ukraine marks Defenders Day
Russian forces suffered an estimated 46,230 personnel losses in September, the highest monthly figure recorded by Ukraine so far in 2026, Ukraine's General Staff said on Oct. 1.
The September figure surpassed previous summer highs of 42,860 in July and 42,020 in August. According to the General Staff, Russian personnel losses have risen from 31,710 in January to 46,230 in September — an increase of nearly 46%.
"This dynamic demonstrates the complete inability of the occupying forces' military leadership to achieve its objectives, as well as the growing accuracy and effectiveness of Ukrainian units' strikes," the General Staff said on Telegram.
Inflicting heavy personnel losses has become a stated strategic objective of Ukraine. In January, then-Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov said Ukraine aimed to "kill 50,000 Russians per month," arguing that losses on that scale could undermine Moscow's ability to sustain the war.
The September figure brings Russia's estimated monthly losses closer to that target than at any previous point this year.
The increase also comes as Russia faces growing pressure to replace troops while sustaining offensive operations along the front.
December 2025 marked the first month in which Russian personnel losses exceeded the number of troops Moscow managed to recruit, according to the General Staff. Since then, the manpower balance has remained an increasingly important issue as the Kremlin seeks to sustain the war without announcing a new wave of mobilization.

Russia strikes Kyiv bridge for first time
Two Russian drones struck near the supports of Kyiv's Southern Bridge on Oct. 1, disrupting a key metro link between the city's eastern and western banks, Mayor Vitali Klitschko said.
This is the first time Russian drones have struck one of the capital's bridges.
The attack took place at around 11:30 a.m. local time, as cars and a metro train continued to cross the bridge. Videos began appearing on social media around the same time, showing a fire on the bridge and a column of smoke rising above it.
Following the strikes, traffic across the bridge was halted as emergency services inspected the site and assessed the damage, the mayor said.
As the train was passing through the area, dust entered the carriage through the ventilation system following the blast wave. Neither passengers nor the driver were injured, and the train's windows and carriage were undamaged. The train was sent to a depot for further inspection, the Kyiv City State Administration said.
Russian drone strikes Kyiv nuclear institute housing research reactor
A Russian drone struck the grounds of the Institute for Nuclear Research in Kyiv on Sept. 30, where a research nuclear reactor is located, Ukraine's State Nuclear Regulatory Inspectorate said on Telegram on Oct. 1.
The strike, which occurred at around 6:18 p.m. local time, sparked a fire that was quickly extinguished. No one was injured in the attack, according to the statement.
The VVR-M research reactor itself and systems important for its safety were not damaged, according to the regulator. Radiation levels remained within the normal background range of 0.16-0.20 microsieverts per hour.
The reactor has been shut down since February 2022, when its core was fully unloaded to reduce radiation risks following the start of Russia's full-scale invasion. It is currently used only for maintenance of safety-related systems.
The institute is part of Ukraine's National Academy of Sciences and conducts research in nuclear physics, atomic energy, and radioecology.
"The drone strike on the territory of the Institute for Nuclear Research was an attack on a peaceful nuclear facility used exclusively for scientific and research purposes," the regulator said.

Ukrainian pilot dies after MiG-29 fighter shot down by Russian missile
A Ukrainian pilot has died after his MiG-29 fighter jet was shot down by a Russian missile whilst performing a combat mission in eastern Ukraine, the country's Air Force said on Oct. 1.
The pilot, Captain Marat Redvanovych Mambetov, ejected but did not survive, the Air Force said in a statement on social media.
Mambetov, who was 25 years old, served as a flight commander in the "Ghost of Kyiv" 40th Tactical Aviation Brigade.
The brigade, based at Vasylkiv Air Base in Kyiv Oblast, flies part of Ukraine's ageing fleet of Soviet-era Mikoyan MiG-29 fighter jets.
"We express our sincere condolences to Marat’s family and friends, he defended Ukraine until his last breath," the Air Force said.

'Returning Russia's sick war to where it came from' — Ukraine marks Defenders Day
Ukraine marked the Day of Defenders on Oct. 1, honoring those serving in the country's military as Russia's full-scale invasion continues.
"Thank you to all our defenders who are working to return Russia's sick war to where it came from," President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Telegram.
The president also said Ukrainian forces had struck a target in the Black Sea, a site in Russia's Oryol Oblast used to launch and store attack drones, an oil facility in Samara Oblast, and a supply depot supporting Russian forces in Bryansk Oblast.
"These are exactly the kind of just responses that are needed now. We will continue depriving Russia of the ability to continue this war," Zelensky said.
Commander-in-Chief Mykhailo Drapatyi highlighted a defining feature of Ukraine's fight in a message marking Defenders Day: relying on innovation, unmanned systems, precision and unconventional solutions rather than sheer numbers.
"While the aggressor tries to overwhelm us with quantities of scrap metal and 'meat grinder assaults,' we are betting on innovation and unmanned systems, precise calculations and unconventional solutions, while preserving and developing our human capital as much as possible," Drapatyi said.

articles.title: ‘A Deliberate Tactic’: Zelensky Condemns Russian Drone Strike on Kyiv School
articles.body:
President Volodymyr Zelensky called Russia’s strikes on schools “a deliberate tactic” after a Russian Geran-4 drone hit a school in Kyiv with more than 100 children and 60 teachers sheltering inside.
In a statement posted to Telegram on Thursday, Oct. 1, Zelensky confirmed that he had spoken with the principal and teachers of the school, which was hit earlier in the morning.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“The most important thing is that everyone is alive,” Zelensky said, adding that “striking schools and kindergartens is a deliberate tactic used by Russians, who target ordinary life.”
Warhead failed to detonate
Citing Kyiv police, Ukrinform reported that a Geran-4 drone struck the wall of a stairwell between the school’s second and third floors.
The warhead, weighing about 50 kilograms (110 lbs), pierced the floor between levels and fell onto the stairs. Had it detonated, the explosion could have collapsed all four floors of the building, according to specialists.
Bomb disposal experts removed the munition and took it to a training ground to be destroyed.
The drone hit the school in Kyiv’s Solomianskyi district during an air raid alert that lasted from 8:48 a.m. to 9:31 a.m., starting a fire. At the time, Ukraine’s State Emergency Service said the third floor of the four-story building was damaged and that firefighters had extinguished the blaze.
Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said that Russian forces also struck warehouse facilities in the same district.
UK Announces Package of 31 Sanctions Against Russia
The school strike followed an overnight Russian attack on Kyiv that injured one man and sparked fires in several districts, including at a café on the ground floor of a 16-story residential building in the Solomianskyi district.
On Wednesday, Sept. 30, Russian strikes on the capital with ballistic missiles and jet-powered drones killed three people, including two women aged 46 and 95, and wounded seven.
In the Obolonskyi district, a jet-powered drone clipped the roof of a nine-story apartment building before crashing near a children’s playground without detonating.
Zelensky said air raid alerts had lasted almost the entire day in Kyiv and other Ukrainian cities, calling the strikes a “new escalation of terror.”
Zelensky orders restoration
Zelensky instructed the Presidential Office, local authorities and the Ministry of Education and Science to ensure the school is quickly restored and energy made independent.
“We are continuously working to strengthen air defense and scaling up production of Ukrainian interceptors against jet-powered Shaheds to protect our cities and communities from such strikes,” he said.
Earlier on Thursday, Ukraine had used its domestically produced FP-7 tactical ballistic missile in combat for the first time, marking a milestone in Kyiv’s push to build its own strike weapons as Russia intensifies its campaign on civilian infrastructure nationwide.

articles.title: What Trump Has Built
articles.body:
Donald Trump struts onto the new White House helipad, an 80,000-sq.-ft. expanse of carved granite on the South Lawn. “Can you believe this?” he says, taking in the scene, the Washington Monument rising in the distance. The President lingers over the details of the project with obvious pleasure, pointing out the gray stone imported from Italy and describing how five separate sections were fitted together, with measurements he says are precise to an eighth of an inch.
Behind him rises a bigger renovation project: the new White House ballroom, its concrete skeleton consuming the former East Wing. Lawsuits have followed the endeavor, alleging that Trump demolished the historic structure and began building its replacement without congressional authorization or the required federal reviews. He kept building anyway. Trump points to the walls, calling them “nuclear concrete” (the sort, he says, used in nuclear facilities), and describes a military complex beneath the ballroom that will plunge six stories underground. There will be five separate floors, he says, with one side made entirely of glass, 6 or 8 in. thick. He holds his hands apart to demonstrate. “The steel goes up next week.” 
As we walk toward the Oval Office, Trump stops several times to inspect his handiwork. There are freshly painted doors, new gold doorknobs, the Rose Garden lawn ripped out and replaced with a Mar-a-Lago-style patio, where he now presides over dinners at what he calls the Rose Garden Club. “People say, why do you spend so much time on this?” he says. “But I find it relaxing.” Later, he returns to the subject again. “It’s what I do best,” he muses aloud. “I say, am I a better builder or a politician?”
One can understand Trump’s fixation on his construction projects. At one of the lowest points of his presidency, he is absorbed with the physical details of a world he can remake to his liking. There is something revealing in the contrast. Here, he can still point to a wall and say how thick it should be, decide where the grass ends and the stone begins, make demands and have them fulfilled. With his presidency seemingly spinning off course, Trump has busied himself with things he can control.
Outside these gates, events have become increasingly resistant to Trump’s will. The war in Iran, launched without congressional authorization and initially described by Trump as a four-to-six-week undertaking, is seven months old when we meet, with no end in sight. It has sent oil and gasoline prices soaring and convulsed the global economy. Inflationary pressures compounded by Trump’s tariffs have pushed the Federal Reserve—now led by his handpicked chairman—to raise interest rates over his objections, with another hike possible before year’s end. Mortgage rates have climbed to 7.5%, worsening an already punishing housing market.
The political coalition that returned Trump to power has frayed, with signs of discontent among independents, rural voters, and parts of the Latino electorate, even as his GOP base remains substantially loyal. A Reuters/Ipsos poll in September put his approval at 32%, the lowest of his political career; a recent Wall Street Journal survey recorded the lowest ratings of any President heading into midterm elections since 1990. Republican candidates have distanced themselves from his military actions and his deportation campaign. Voters have recoiled at his laissez-faire approach to the artificial intelligence industry and his accumulation of wealth while in office through crypto deals, thousands of disclosed stock trades, and an expanding empire of Trump-branded developments stretching from Saudi Arabia and Qatar to India and Vietnam.
Inside the Administration, senior advisers increasingly recognize that he has passed the apogee of his second-term power. Across the Republican Party, officials are preparing for the likelihood of losing the House—and perhaps the Senate—in the midterms. After two years spent almost entirely on offense, Trump may soon be forced onto defense. Democratic control of Congress would bring investigations and subpoenas, hearings, and potentially a third round of impeachment proceedings. Cabinet officials could be hauled before Congress. Trump describes the prospect in characteristic terms. “They’ll probably go after me,” he says, “and I’ll go after them.”
Yet with so much at stake—for the country and the world, for his party and his own power—Trump can seem curiously preoccupied. During a 75-minute Oval Office interview with TIME, he was discursive and grievance-fueled, veering from the crises of his presidency to resentments old and emerging. He said he regretted appointing Neil Gorsuch, Brett Kavanaugh, and Amy Coney Barrett to the Supreme Court, after they ruled against him on tariffs, mail ballots, and birthright citizenship. “I gave them the position of a lifetime,” he said, “and they voted against me often.” On his expectation of fealty, he was unapologetic: “I do like loyalty, yeah.” Again and again, he returned to the condition of the White House itself, complaining that his predecessors had left the building in disrepair and deriding Barack Obama as someone who “doesn’t know if something’s dirty or clean.”
Trump dismissed widespread opposition to the rapid build-out of data centers, including among his own base, as a prescription for a poorer America. When pressed on the limits of his power, Trump left himself ample room: He would not rule out declaring a national emergency or invoking the Insurrection Act around the midterms, nor promise to refrain from bringing wrecking balls to the Kennedy Center without congressional approval. “I’m not committing to anything,” he says. “We’re going to see how it plays out in court.”
In Trump’s telling, he is simply doing what has to be done, even when that means breaking foundational promises to his voters. He campaigned as a president of peace, but is now waging a war he says was necessary to prevent Iran from obtaining a nuclear weapon. He points to Venezuela, where his removal of Nicolás Maduro and the elevation of Delcy Rodríguez have brought the country into Washington’s orbit, as proof that his projection of U.S. power can produce results. He touts most-favored-nation drug pricing and restricting institutional investors from buying single-family homes as measures that will lower costs for Americans. New GDP and inflation figures suggest the economy remains strong.
When asked why he remains consumed with construction projects so removed from the country’s concerns, Trump offers a rationale: “The White House is a very special symbol. It’s a symbol of America. It’s a symbol of our greatness.” He speaks of his building projects in the language of legacy—monuments meant to endure long after he is gone. But while Trump obsesses over stonework and fixtures, gold and glass, the more important parts of his legacy are being built too—in the decisions he makes from inside these walls, and the consequences unfolding far beyond them. 
In late April, the President summoned Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and a retinue of military and national security officials to the Oval Office. By Trump’s own timeline, the war with Iran was supposed to be over already, with a new regime in place and a nuclear program throttled. But the Islamic Republic had proved resilient and resourceful, choking off oil through the Strait of Hormuz and sending tremors through the global economy.
Now there was another problem. Trump had learned from a New York Times report that the U.S. military was running low on certain munitions after firing more than 1,200 Patriot missile interceptors. To replenish the losses, the Pentagon was drawing on assets stationed in Asia and Europe, potentially weakening American defenses in other theaters. “What the f-ck is this?” Trump said to Hegseth, according to two officials familiar with the exchange, handing him a printout of the story.
According to those officials, Hegseth borrowed one of Trump’s favorite terms of derision, telling the President it was “fake news.” The Secretary of Defense insisted that the reporters had taken the facts out of context and exaggerated them to make the Administration look bad. But the reporting emerged from an official DOD inspector general’s assessment. (A spokesperson for Hegseth denied the exchange.)
Trump’s frustration went beyond munition stores. The war was polling miserably. At the time, 13 U.S. service members had been killed and nearly 400 wounded. (Those numbers would increase to 19 killed and more than 800 wounded by the end of September.) Gasoline prices had risen more than 40% since the opening attacks on Feb. 28. The conflict had already cost more than $25 billion, and the consequences were beginning to bleed into the midterm campaign. The President found himself without an exit ramp. That dynamic appears to hold true: Instead of concluding the war, Trump tells TIME, he may ramp up the bombing after the midterms if they can’t reach a satisfactory deal. “Because by annihilating Iran, we’ve created peace in the world,” he says. “With Iran, I don’t think you could ever have peace.”
In recent months, Trump’s relationship with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has grown more acrimonious, according to a senior Administration official. Netanyahu urged Trump toward war with Tehran but has since complicated Trump’s efforts to end it, including by striking Hezbollah targets in Lebanon after Trump told him not to, multiple U.S. officials tell TIME. Trump says he does not believe reports that Netanyahu was warned by Egypt and the UAE ahead of the Oct. 7 attacks, but stops short of endorsing him for re-election as Israelis prepare to vote in late October for the first time since the worst security failure in the country’s history. Asked whether he might work better with Netanyahu’s leading challenger, former military chief Gadi Eisenkot, Trump leaves the possibility open. “Well, I don’t know,” he says. “I don’t hear bad things about him.”
The decision to attack Iran was a hinge point in Trump’s second term. His first year back in power had unfolded as a frenetic exercise in presidential will, a barrage of executive actions and dismantled guardrails that had largely gone according to plan. Then his second year opened with the raid on Caracas and capture of Maduro, a daring operation that reinforced Trump’s conviction that audacity could succeed where caution had failed. The subsequent attack on Tehran would test the limits of that conviction—and reveal how quickly confidence born of success could lead to overreach.
A cascade of crises followed. Though Trump has dismissed the pain of rising gas prices, he concedes the war has depleted a subset of U.S. munitions. “Some forms of ammunition are a little bit lower than other forms,” he says. Trump says he has struck deals with leading defense manufacturers, including Raytheon and Lockheed Martin, to replenish the arsenal and expand production. “They’re building four, five, six plants,” he says, citing Patriot and THAAD anti-ballistic-missile facilities. “They’re building tremendous amounts of capability.”
When asked what this will cost American taxpayers, Trump offers a curious metric: less, he says, than America makes in a single month from Venezuelan oil. Yet Americans have so far felt little benefit from that arrangement. Major U.S. oil companies have returned to Venezuela and begun extracting from the world’s largest proven crude reserves, but gas prices remain at record highs for September. Meanwhile, Trump’s tariff regime strained America’s global relationships and reverberated through the economy. 
Trump points to low unemployment, robust consumer spending, and a stock market at record highs as evidence that his economic program is working. By those measures, the economy has remained strong. But they coexist with a harsher reality: the cost of everyday life remains painfully high.
By summer, Trump was growing angrier with U.S. allies that had refused to come to America’s aid against Iran—from the European powers and South Korea to Canada. Trump has directed much of his ire over the issue at America’s neighbor to the north, according to a close aide. “He doesn’t like the fact that we essentially protect them because of their proximity to our military might, and doesn’t think they give us enough in return,” says a Trump senior adviser. On July 20, Trump invoked a 1930 statute to impose a 50% tariff on Canadian goods. The trade war with America’s second largest trading partner hit steel, aluminum, and lumber especially hard, disrupting supply chains and raising the cost of materials that went into everything from factories to new homes. 
Borrowing costs were becoming their own problem. For Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, preventing a sell-off in the bond market from becoming a broader crisis was an increasingly urgent task. By late September, only 25% of Americans believed Trump’s policies had improved the economy, according to a Wall Street Journal poll, while 60% said they had worsened it. Trump had returned to office promising cheaper energy, lower prices, and an economic boom. Instead, voters were finding the opposite. “It’s not lost on any of us,” a Trump adviser tells TIME. “When voters aren’t happy with the economy, they tend to vote against the party in charge.”
Since returning to office, Trump has marveled at AI’s capabilities. He is increasingly in thrall to the tech executives courting him. In December 2025, Elon Musk returned to the Oval Office for a clandestine meeting. Trump spent hours asking Grok, Musk’s AI chatbot, questions about his presidency and legacy, according to an official present. At the time, Trump was ordering missile strikes against Venezuelan boats he alleged were smuggling drugs into the U.S. He asked Grok how Venezuelans would react if the U.S. captured Maduro. According to the official present, the chatbot responded that Maduro was a repressive and deeply unpopular dictator and that many Venezuelans would likely celebrate his downfall. After Trump ordered the mission to seize Maduro, the following month, celebrations broke out in the streets. Trump, according to officials, came away thinking Grok was ingenious.
Along with his fascination with the technology came two related concerns. One was economic: that enthusiasm for AI’s potential was propping up the stock market. The other was geopolitical, reinforced in conversations with industry titans such as Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang: that China could gain a decisive advantage over the U.S. if it developed more powerful AI first. Trump was committed to giving American companies the freedom to build faster than their foreign competitors. That meant embracing the unprecedented infrastructure build-out required to support the industry’s computing needs. After watching a cable news segment about the backlash, Trump fired off a Truth Social post. “The only reason that communities throughout the U.S.A. should not want Data Centers is if they want to end up being backwards and poor,” he wrote Aug. 31. “If they want to be successful and rich, with far lower taxes and jobs all over the place, let Data Reign.” 
Days later, aides showed Trump surveys from his longtime pollster, Tony Fabrizio, showing pervasive anxiety about AI: fears of lost jobs, rising costs, and technology eventually escaping human control. Fellow Republicans facing voters in November were increasingly eager to put distance between themselves and the issue. Trump “really just didn’t seem to care,” one aide says. “He wants to do what he wants to do. He’s used to generating outrage and then watching everyone eventually crawl back to him. It’s hard to convince him to do anything at this point.”
Trump was unfazed by the burgeoning bipartisan calls for new AI regulations. “I don’t have to destroy the industry,” he says. “We’re making a lot of money with that industry. That industry is the Industrial Revolution, but bigger. It’s the internet, but much bigger.” The details don’t appear to concern him. When TIME asks about OpenAI agents’ meddling with federal government websites, Trump responds: “Who breached it? They’re not allowed to do that.”
Trump’s contribution to the debate about AI safeguards has been to announce the formation of an “AI Force,” which he now wants to rename the “SI Force”—part of his effort to rebrand artificial intelligence as “super intelligence.” Asked what the group will do, Trump responds: “It’s going to be super intelligent.” Pressed further, he explains that it will consist of industry leaders advising him on government policy. On Sept. 29, he met with AI leaders at the White House, where the President and top executives from six leading tech companies signed a “constitution” to police themselves—a covenant of self-regulation in lieu of government oversight. An Administration official present said they left with a “no surprises if something happens” understanding between the White House and the industry. 
It was an example of how Trump has surrounded himself with industry leaders, seeking their advice, favor, and political donations. A recent CNN poll found 75% of Americans viewed artificial intelligence with more fear and concern than excitement, with broad bipartisan support for greater federal oversight. But Trump waves away AI fears, placing them in a familiar catalogue of what he considers manufactured panics. “They said that our country was going to burn down because of global warming,” he says. “Then they changed the name to climate change because global warming turned out to be a hoax. Russia, Russia, Russia was a hoax.” Asked who, exactly, is perpetrating the supposed hoax of AI concern, Trump throws his hands in the air. “The whole country is based on fake stuff,” he says, “because these people have Trump derangement syndrome.”
Inside the Oval Office, Trump’s redesign is impossible to miss. There is gold everywhere, from the decorative plasterwork to the inscriptions on the ceiling and the gilded frames crowding the walls. The room is so dazzling you practically need sunglasses. Trumpian tchotchkes are scattered about: a FIFA “World Peace Prize” sits next to the Resolute Desk, where the President keeps a commendation given to his uncle during his years as an MIT professor. 
At times, Trump’s train of thought was difficult to keep up with, his conversation moving in streams and eddies before circling back to familiar obsessions. He recounted conversations that sometimes sounded improbable. At one point, Trump claimed the Secret Service had wanted to tear down the Oval Office and rebuild it, only for him to intervene. “I said, ‘My ass, you can’t build a new one. This is a special place.’”
Whatever happens in November, people close to Trump expect him to devote more of his remaining presidency to foreign affairs, as second-term Presidents often do, with particular attention to the western hemisphere, where ideologically sympathetic governments have given him opportunities to expand American influence. At home, they expect another emphasis altogether: Trump’s campaign against what he calls “lawfare” and his effort to reshape cultural institutions, including the nation’s museums, in his battle against what he calls “woke” ideology.
Looking ahead to the midterms, Trump dismisses unfavorable polls as fake and insists Republicans can prevail. “I think we’ll do OK if I campaign, and I intend to,” he says. So far, he has done little beyond a two-day midterm convention and a few fundraisers, but top advisers say the President is preparing a campaign sprint to help Republicans stave off disaster in the midterms: visiting 32 competitive districts in the next month, with the MAGA-style rallies that powered his political rise.
Inside the White House, advisers are already contemplating what a divided Washington would mean. “I think if the worst happens in the midterms, we’ll be forced to think more bipartisan,” one top official says. “I would hope that if we win, we can still do that, because for two years we’ve run a completely partisan play. When you’re looking back on your time, I don’t think that’s what you should be proud of, even if it was successful.”
Trump’s political operation boasts a $400 million war chest, but he has only recently begun opening his checkbook. Aides say he has been reluctant to spend because he wants to preserve cash for future elections as a means of keeping his grip on his party. “He wants to have as much money in his account as possible when he’s no longer able to raise the kind of money he can now,” a Trump aide told TIME this fall. “He doesn’t seem to care that much about the midterms, thinks they’re a lost cause anyway, and wants to preserve future possibilities.”
Aides are bracing for turnover after the midterms as Trump sheds officials who have frustrated him. A source close to the President says he has openly mused about firing the FBI Director Kash Patel and has expressed frustration with Hegseth. Trump says he intends to protect those who remain. When TIME asks whether he plans to issue pre-emptive pardons to aides and associates before Democrats—or a future Administration—can pursue them, he suggests he will, offering a familiar justification: “Sleepy Joe gave pardons to everybody.”
As the conversation moves between war and peace, his own grip on power, and the possibility of impeachment, Trump keeps returning to the trappings of the office. He asks Natalie Harp, his ever present aide, to bring in photographs of earlier White House construction projects, including renovations from the 1930s and the Truman-era reconstruction. He studies the pictures as evidence for his case, lamenting the judges and injunctions now complicating his own efforts. Holding up a photograph of work being performed on the State Dining Room in 1950, Trump complains about a judge he says accused him of destroying the White House. “It’s the sh-t I have to go through,” he says. 
Toward the end of our interview, I ask what he will miss most when his presidency is over. This time there is no digression, no grievance, no story. Trump does not need a moment to think: “This beautiful room.” 
—With reporting by Leslie Dickstein, Simmone Shah, and Olivia B. Waxman

articles.title: World living through a dangerous moment, says Putin, warns West not to escalate
articles.body:
World living through a dangerous moment, says Putin, warns West not to escalate
- Putin warns the world is in a dangerous moment and threatens to use all weapons, including nuclear, to defend Russia's Kaliningrad exclave if attacked by NATO.
- He insists Russia has no plans to attack European countries and seeks peaceful coexistence but highlights the risks of escalating conflicts leading to catastrophic consequences.
- Putin rejects halting strikes on Ukraine, acknowledges economic impacts of Ukrainian attacks, and is open to talks involving China and the US if a proper agenda is set.
AI generated
MOSCOW - President Vladimir Putin said on Oct 1 the world was living through a dangerous moment and warned the West not to escalate a standoff over Ukraine by threatening the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad, which Moscow has said it will defend with nuclear weapons if necessary.
Locked in a war in Ukraine which he said Russia had no choice but to launch in order to safeguard its own security, Putin said Russia had no plans to attack any European country and wanted to coexist peacefully.
But he reiterated that Moscow would resort to all weapons in its arsenal, including nuclear ones, if its most westerly territory - Kaliningrad, which is wedged between Poland and Lithuania - was threatened.
“If it comes to a direct attack on the Russian Federation – in this case, we are referring to Kaliningrad, and perhaps other territories as well – the question of the Russian Federation deploying all the weapons at our country’s disposal will, of course, inevitably and immediately be on the agenda,” Putin told the Valdai Forum of international Russia experts in Moscow.
“This is inevitable,” he said.
Putin said Russia realised it would be facing “an enemy (NATO) twice our size.”
“And we will have to make use of our competitive advantages in this struggle. Yes, of course, France and Britain are nuclear powers – we understand that perfectly well and are fully aware of it,” he said.
“But no one else possesses the kind of weapons that Russia has today. That is our competitive advantage.”
Nuclear warning
Putin’s comments followed a diplomatic note which NATO said this week it had received from Russia, warning the Western military alliance it would be ready to resort to nuclear weapons if NATO attempted to cut off Russia’s Baltic exclave.
Russia’s warning highlighted Moscow’s urgent concern at what it has presented as a growing NATO threat to Kaliningrad, a heavily militarised Russian territory that is slightly bigger than the US state of Connecticut.
NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte said the alliance had responded by emphasising that it was a defensive alliance and that nuclear threats were not helpful.
Relations, already dire since Putin’s decision to send troops into Ukraine in 2022, have worsened this year, with European governments accusing Moscow of stepping up a “hybrid war” on the continent through acts including sabotage and arson.
Russia denies that, and rejects repeated statements by Western politicians that it is gearing up for a possible military attack on a NATO country.
Putin warned that cycles of escalation in international conflict could quickly lead to dangerous scenarios.
“We must realise that the moment when nothing can be changed any longer may come very quickly and unexpectedly for everyone. The logic of escalating, increasingly harsh retaliatory measures leads to a fatal point of no return,” he said.
“At the heart of this escalation lie arrogance and overconfidence. This is a path to the brink of the abyss. All the more so today, when the arsenals of the world’s leading powers contain weapons capable of destroying all life or, at the very least, reducing the Earth to a catastrophic state,” Putin said.
“Can we be certain that these weapons will never be used? Well, of course not. We must bear this in mind and avoid such an outcome,” he added.
Putin, who said he was ready for a trilateral meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping and US President Donald Trump if a proper agenda was worked out first, ruled out the idea of stopping Russian strikes on Ukrainian targets in the Black Sea area, while conceding that Ukrainian strikes on oil refineries across Russia had cost Russia 1% of its gross domestic product (GDP).
He said Russia was now responding to Ukraine in kind.
But while he cast Western help to Kyiv when it came to launching deep strikes inside Russia as a future threat, he said Moscow was not planning to attack arms factories in Europe which supplied Ukraine “tomorrow.” REUTERS

articles.title: Ukraine confirms first combat use of new ballistic missile
articles.body:
- President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Ukraine's FP-7 tactical ballistic missile, developed by Fire Point, has been used in combat for the first time.
- Fire Point lists the FP-7's range at up to 250 km, with a 200-kg payload and 14-meter accuracy.
Ukraine has used its homegrown FP-7 tactical ballistic missile in combat for the first time, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Oct. 1, adding that the next step is production.
“Ukrainian tactical ballistics. FP-7. First combat use. Thank you for the result. Next, production. Glory to Ukraine!” Zelenskyy said.
He did not say when or where the missile was fired, what it hit, or which unit launched it.
The FP-7 is built by Fire Point, the Ukrainian company behind the FP-1 long-range attack drone and the FP-5 Flamingo cruise missile. Fire Point describes the FP-7 as the compact ballistic missile in its family of weapons and lists a range of up to 250 km (155 miles), a payload of up to 200 kg (440 pounds), a top speed of 1,500 meters per second, or about 5,400 km/h (3,360 mph), and a maximum altitude of 60 km (37 miles). The company puts its accuracy at 14 meters (46 feet), though it does not say how that figure was measured, and none of the specifications can be independently verified.
A ballistic missile climbs steeply on rocket power and then falls toward its target at very high speed, giving air defenses far less time to react than they have against the drones and cruise missiles Ukraine has mostly used for long-range strikes so far. Russia has fired large numbers of Iskander and other ballistic missiles at Ukraine throughout the war, while Ukraine has relied mainly on U.S.-supplied ATACMS for ballistic strikes, which flies up to about 300 km.
With a range of 250 km, the FP-7 falls in the tactical class, able to reach Russian command posts, air defense sites, ammunition depots and airfields behind the front line and in occupied territory, but not deep into Russia. Fire Point has also announced a larger ballistic missile, the FP-9, intended for longer ranges.

articles.title: Putin Says World Is Living Through Dangerous Moment and Warns of Risk of Nuclear Weapons Use
articles.body:
President Vladimir Putin said on Thursday the world was living through a dangerous moment and warned the West not to escalate a standoff over Ukraine by threatening the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad, which Moscow has made clear it would defend with nuclear weapons if necessary.
Locked in a war in Ukraine which he said Russia had no choice but to launch in order to safeguard its own security, Putin said Russia had no plans to attack any European country and wanted to coexist peacefully.
But he reiterated that Moscow would resort to all weapons in its arsenal, including nuclear ones, if its most westerly territory — Kaliningrad, which is wedged between Poland and Lithuania — was threatened.
"If it comes to a direct attack on the Russian Federation – in this case, we are referring to Kaliningrad, and perhaps other territories as well — the question of the Russian Federation deploying all the weapons at our country’s disposal will, of course, inevitably and immediately be on the agenda," Putin told the Valdai Forum of international Russia experts in Moscow.
"This is inevitable," he said.
Putin said Russia realized it would be facing "an enemy [NATO] twice our size."
"And we will have to make use of our competitive advantages in this struggle. Yes, of course, France and Britain are nuclear powers — we understand that perfectly well and are fully aware of it," he said. "But no one else possesses the kind of weapons that Russia has today. That is our competitive advantage."
Nuclear warning
Putin's comments followed a diplomatic note which NATO said this week it had received from Russia, warning the Western military alliance it would be ready to resort to nuclear weapons if NATO attempted to cut off Russia's Baltic exclave.
Russia's warning highlighted Moscow's urgent concern at what it has presented as a growing NATO threat to Kaliningrad, a heavily militarized Russian territory that is slightly bigger than the U.S. state of Connecticut. NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte said the alliance had responded by emphasising that it was a defensive alliance and that nuclear threats were not helpful.
Relations, already dire since Putin's decision to send troops into Ukraine in 2022, have worsened this year, with European governments accusing Moscow of stepping up a "hybrid war" on the continent through acts including sabotage and arson.
Russia denies that, and rejects repeated statements by Western politicians that it is gearing up for a possible military attack on a NATO country.
Putin warned that cycles of escalation in international conflict could quickly lead to dangerous scenarios.
"We must realize that the moment when nothing can be changed any longer may come very quickly and unexpectedly for everyone. The logic of escalating, increasingly harsh retaliatory measures leads to a fatal point of no return," he said.
"At the heart of this escalation lie arrogance and overconfidence. This is a path to the brink of the abyss. All the more so today, when the arsenals of the world’s leading powers contain weapons capable of destroying all life or, at the very least, reducing the Earth to a catastrophic state," Putin said.
"Can we be certain that these weapons will never be used? Well, of course not. We must bear this in mind and avoid such an outcome," he added.
Putin, who said he was ready for a trilateral meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping and U.S. President Donald Trump if a proper agenda was worked out first, ruled out the idea of stopping Russian strikes on Ukrainian targets in the Black Sea area, while conceding that Ukrainian strikes on oil refineries across Russia had cost Russia 1% of its gross domestic product (GDP).
He said Russia was now responding to Ukraine in kind.
But while he cast Western help to Kyiv when it came to launching deep strikes inside Russia as a future threat, he said Moscow was not planning to attack arms factories in Europe which supplied Ukraine "tomorrow."
