articles.title: MFA condemns Russian attacks on Ukraine's nuclear, scientific facilities, urges IAEA to respond firmly to escalation – statement
articles.body:
The Ukrainian Ministry of Foreign Affairs condemned yet another act of Russian nuclear terrorism after a Russian attack drone crashed on September 30 on the grounds of the Institute for Nuclear Research of the National Academy of Sciences of Ukraine in Kyiv, 100 meters from a research nuclear reactor. The ministry emphasized that this strike is a continuation of the Russian Federation's systematic attacks on facilities in Ukraine's nuclear sector.
A statement published on the Ministry of Foreign Affairs' website notes that in recent days, Russian attacks have targeted several key institutions of Ukraine's nuclear industry and scientific community. Buildings used by JSC national nuclear energy generating company "Energoatom" were hit. On September 28, a Russian drone struck the building of the Presidium of the National Academy of Sciences of Ukraine, causing significant damage and killing two people. Now, the Institute for Nuclear Research of the National Academy of Sciences of Ukraine, which houses a research nuclear reactor, has become a target.
"Ukraine views these actions as a continuation of targeted terror against Ukrainian nuclear science," the statement reads.
The Ministry of Foreign Affairs said as far back as 2022, Russian troops repeatedly shelled the National Scientific Center "Kharkiv Institute of Physics and Technology" and damaged the infrastructure of the Neutron Source nuclear facility.
"Russia is systematically destroying the conditions necessary for scientists to work. It is jeopardizing the safety of nuclear facilities, for which Ukrainian specialists are responsible on a daily basis. This escalation requires a clear response from the IAEA. It must be backed by concrete decisions from states and the international scientific community. We call on the IAEA Director General to unequivocally condemn this new Russian attack and demand that Russia immediately cease such strikes," the MFA said.
The ministry said Russia cannot destroy Ukrainian nuclear and scientific institutions while at the same time freely reaping the benefits of international cooperation in this field.
"We call on our partners to strengthen sanctions against the Russian nuclear sector, in particular against Rosatom. Partners should also restrict institutional cooperation with Russian scientific organizations, including their participation in international research programs and access to funding. Countries that maintain nuclear and scientific cooperation with Russia should use these ties to put pressure on Moscow," the statement reads.
At the same time, according to the statement Ukraine needs additional capabilities to protect facilities that remain under threat from Russian strikes.
"We call on our partners to expedite the delivery to Ukraine of air defense systems, missiles for those systems, and means to intercept attack drones. Defensive measures and sanctions must deprive Russia of the ability to continue its nuclear terror and force it to account for these attacks," the Foreign Ministry said.
As previously reported, on September 30, Russia launched a drone strike on the premises of the Institute of Nuclear Research of the National Academy of Sciences of Ukraine in Kyiv, where Kyiv research reactor is located. The State Nuclear Regulatory Inspectorate of Ukraine called this yet another war crime.
The State Nuclear Regulatory Inspectorate said the reactor itself and safety-critical systems were not damaged, and no changes in the radiation background were recorded-its readings remain within the natural background range (0.16-0.20 μSv/h) and have not changed.
The agency explained that, to minimize radiation risks, the reactor has been shut down since February 2022 with the core fully unloaded, and its operation is limited to routine maintenance of safety-critical systems.

The United States is sending the aircraft carrier USS Theodore Roosevelt and an additional Marine unit to the region. The decision comes amid threats by U.S. President Donald Trump that, after the midterm elections in early November, the United States will resume strikes on Iran.
The Hill reported that the Theodore Roosevelt departed San Diego on the Pacific coast on Sunday and is making its way to the Middle East to replace another aircraft carrier already operating in the region. According to the report, it will replace the USS George Washington, which is based in Japan and was sent last month to the U.S. Central Command, or CENTCOM, area of responsibility to replace the USS Abraham Lincoln, amid reports of a serious deterioration in the mental health of members of its crew.
The deployment comes amid the crisis in the Strait of Hormuz and escalating tensions between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis in Yemen. The United States is working to increase the flow of oil in the region, while U.S. vessels continue to impose a naval blockade off Iran’s coast.
Against this backdrop, Qatar is pressing for a breakthrough in negotiations between the United States and Iran aimed at ending the war between them, which began about seven months ago. However, according to various reports, those efforts have failed to produce significant progress.
Axios reported that U.S. officials believe the deadlock is reinforcing an assessment on both sides that the likelihood of renewed military confrontation is growing, amid an exchange of threats earlier this week.
The officials believe Trump could order a return to large-scale military operations after the midterm elections. Trump on Wednesday night reiterated his position that Iran must not be allowed to obtain nuclear weapons and said the war would end soon.
“I don’t know if they’re going to give up right now, but they will give up,” Trump told reporters. “They’re in very bad shape.”
By contrast, Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, attacked the U.S. administration Tuesday, saying: “The president of the United States is trapped. He cannot negotiate and he cannot go to war. Lacking the ability to act effectively, the U.S. administration has chosen to impose an aerial blockade on Iran. Many foreigners have come and gone throughout history, but Iran and the countries of the region have remained.”
For now, Qatar has not given up on the diplomatic track, and officials in Washington said Doha would continue its efforts despite frustration on all sides.
Doha has returned to its role as mediator after previously helping formulate a memorandum of understanding in June that led to a ceasefire, though the truce collapsed shortly afterward.

articles.title: Poland Simplifies Shoot-Down Rules as Russian Drones Threaten Its Airspace

Poland Simplifies Shoot-Down Rules as Russian Drones Threaten Its Airspace
Poland has introduced simplified rules allowing its military to identify and shoot down foreign objects in its airspace without visual confirmation, Gazeta Prawna reported on September 30.
The new procedures took effect on October 1 as Poland adapts its air defense rules to repeated risks from Russian drone and missile attacks on neighboring Ukraine. Defense Minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz confirmed that the military had completed preparations for the change.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
UNITED24 Media recently documented a sharp rise in Russian drone and missile incursions near NATO’s eastern flank, with 2026 recording almost as many confirmed and likely Russian-origin incidents as 2024 and 2025 combined. Poland has responded by strengthening air defenses and revising procedures for dealing with unidentified aerial threats.
Under the previous peacetime rules, Polish fighter pilots generally had to approach an unidentified object closely enough to identify it visually before engaging it. Gazeta Prawna noted that the requirement is being replaced by so-called positive identification.
Pilots or commanders will now be able to authorize an interception using information from radars and other surveillance systems, as well as data provided by Ukraine during Russian aerial attacks.
Kosiniak-Kamysz stated that Operational Commander General Ireneusz Nowak had reported that the new procedures were fully prepared and being implemented.
“October 1 is always a good moment not only to begin the academic year, but also to introduce new procedures,” Kosiniak-Kamysz stated.
The changes do not require amendments to Polish law and are being implemented at the military level, Gazeta Prawna wrote. The defense minister described the new rules as clear procedures that pilots and other personnel involved in air defense would be expected to follow.
Under existing Polish law, the Operational Commander of the Armed Forces remains responsible for protecting national airspace through the Air Operations Center. The commander can order an intruding object to be shot down or delegate that authority to fighter pilots.
Deputy Defense Minister Cezary Tomczyk earlier explained that the previous visual-identification requirement was designed to reduce the risk of mistakenly shooting down civilian aircraft during peacetime. Poland’s current security environment, however, required different procedures.
“Until now, we did not use this type of capability because it is usually reserved for a state of war or martial law,” Tomczyk stated.
“Poland today faces the possibility of drones entering our territory every day, so we have to introduce these changes for both our pilots and the security of the state,” he continued.
Poland has repeatedly scrambled aircraft and activated air defenses during large Russian attacks on Ukraine, particularly when drones and missiles approach its eastern border. The revised rules are intended to give Polish forces more time to respond when unidentified aerial objects enter national airspace.
Days earlier, a Russian jet-powered drone crashed near the Yahodyn crossing on Ukraine’s border with Poland, with the blast wave damaging the checkpoint area. Poland scrambled fighter jets and placed air defense and radar units on heightened readiness as the drone approached the border.

"We have never shied away from talks, and we never will, although the United States has targeted our country three times despite having signed an agreement," the semi-official Tasnim news agency quoted him as saying.
Tehran international flights drop 42 percent after US ban
Flights to and from Tehran's main international airport have fallen by nearly half, 42 percent, since a US ban on Iranian airlines, but some popular routes remain, tracking data up to Wednesday shows.
On average 53 daily international flights have operated to and from Tehran's Imam Khomeini International Airport since September 23, when the US ban took effect, compared to a daily average of 91 flights before the ban, according to data from tracking platform FlightRadar24.
Traffic had already fallen after Israeli-American strikes on Iran at the end of February led to the complete closure of its airspace.
Since flights resumed, only Iranian carriers operated services out of Iran.
Pre-ban September data shows that a typical week included services to 18 countries.
Since the ban, flights have completely stopped to Georgia, Oman and Azerbaijan, which normally have regular service to Tehran.
Iran is preparing a broader and more forceful response if the United States resumes large-scale military attacks, sources said, while continuing a diplomatic push that Iranian officials privately see as unlikely to succeed.
The planning reflects a conviction within Iran's leadership that any renewed US campaign must be met with a stronger response than before, even as Tehran seeks to avert escalation through talks.
Senior commanders are reviewing plans to expand potential targets beyond US-linked assets to countries that support US military operations and possibly to locations outside the Middle East, according to three senior Iranian officials and an insider familiar with the discussions.
Since President Masoud Pezeshkian returned from New York last week, commanders and senior officials have focused on the scope and timing of any response if Washington strikes again.
No final decision has been made, but planning has intensified as neither side shows signs of willingness to compromise.
Emirates suspends flydubai codeshare flights to Tel Aviv
Emirates airline announced that it is suspending all codeshare flights with flydubai to and from Tel Aviv’s airport until further notice.
“Passengers whose final destination is Tel Aviv will not be accepted for travel at the point of origin,” the UAE carrier says. “Customers already en route to Tel Aviv will be accommodated and provided with all possible support to complete their journeys.”
In practice, this means anyone who booked a flight to Israel through Emirates, which always requires a stopover in Dubai and a transfer to a flydubai jet, will now also be unable to board the Emirates plane for the first leg of their journey to Dubai.
'Taiz Axis': Violent battles in Bani Bakari and Himyar
In a statement carried by Anadolu, the Yemeni government forces said they "are engaged in violent battles in the Bani Bakari area in the Jabal Habashi District, and on the Himyar front in the Maqbanah District in the western countryside of Taiz, and in the Al-Aqroud front southeast of the governorate."
The statement added that the army forces "inflicted losses on the Houthi militia in lives and equipment," without details.
There was no comment from the Houthi as of yet.
EU diesel hits record 2.24 euros a litre as Iran war hits
The average price of diesel at the pump across the EU has hit a record of 2.24 euros per litre -- equivalent to $9.60 per US gallon -- compared with 1.59 euros before war erupted in the Middle East, according to EU Commission data published Thursday.
Twelve EU member states recorded fresh all-time highs, including Belgium, Italy, Romania and Poland, according to an AFP analysis of data submitted weekly to Brussels by national authorities since 2005.
The data reflect prices at filling stations, either at the start of the week or at the end of the previous week, depending on the country.
The price of diesel, the main fuel used by road freight transport and farming machinery, exceeded 2.50 euros per litre in Denmark, the Netherlands and Finland, and reached 2.44 euros in Germany.
In Belgium, where prices hit a record, diesel averaged 2.43 euros per litre on Monday, compared with 2.39 euros the previous week.
In Italy, it rose by seven cents to 2.35 euros. French filling stations, excluding overseas territories and Corsica, were charging an average of 2.37 euros per litre, a very slight decline.
Across the whole of the European Union, there was an average rise of one cent per litre over the last week.
Syrian officials and Hezbollah held secret talks in Turkey
Representatives of the Syrian government and Lebanese Hezbollah have held face-to-face talks in Turkey to try to calm tensions between them, according to six sources briefed on the first known meeting between the longtime foes.
The Syrian officials and the Iran-aligned group met secretly at least once last month, the sources—who include two Syrian officials, a US official and a senior Lebanese security source close to Hezbollah—told Reuters.
The internationally-recognised Yemeni government's stated that they "thwarted a massive Houthi attack on all fronts of the Tur al-Baha axis and eliminated all of its attacking groups," without mentioning additional details.
In another brief statement, the army said, "The armed forces' warplanes launched 6 raids on the positions and vehicles of the Houthi militia," noting that the raids targeted sites "in the Al-Akbush, Al-Ahkoum, and Haifan fronts, south of Taiz Governorate," without details.
UAE says investigation launched into flydubai incident
The United Arab Emirates' chief prosecutor on Thursday said an investigation had been launched into the incident on board a flydubai flight to Israel.
The state news agency WAM said the attorney general had ordered the probe, adding that "the investigation team has launched its work into the incident" that forced the plane to land in Saudi Arabia on Wednesday.
It also said the investigation would determine "the degree to which (the incident) was linked to any terrorist activity or intent".
Israel claimed on Wednesday that the co-pilot of the flight had tried to crash the aircraft but that the pilot and passengers intervened and averted the crash.
Passengers described rushing the cockpit after the plane suddenly plummeted, losing around 17,000 feet of altitude in the span of a minute, according to the Flightradar24 website.
Airline flydubai said all of the passengers—of whom 166 out of 174 were Israeli, according to media reports—were safe.
Israeli officials called the incident "an attempted terrorist attack" while Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu told US broadcaster Fox News it was "too early" to say who was behind the altercation and lauded those who prevented a crash.
"During the flight, as they approached the country, one of the pilots stabbed the other pilot, and apparently tried to crash the plane with everyone on board," Netanyahu said in a video message.
Hegseth says US cut number of generals, admirals by 20%
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth announced Wednesday that the United States has slashed the number of its generals and admirals by 20 percent, in a move he said is aimed at "accountability."
Hegseth suggested the cuts targeted officers who failed to get on board with his efforts to ensure the military is focused on war-fighting rather than the "woke" policies of previous administrations, describing the reductions as an "accomplishment."
"The number-crunchers say we fired 10 percent of the generals and admirals across the force," Hegseth told troops at the Quantico military base, saying: "We've also reduced the overall number of general officer slots by an additional 10 percent."
"So yes, 20 percent reduction across the board," he said. "The media calls that a purge. I call it accountability, and long overdue."
Since returning to office early last year, Trump has purged of top military staff. [Getty]
Saudi Arabia turned down Israeli requests to send planes
Saudi Arabia turned down multiple requests by Israel to send its own planes to retrieve passengers from a diverted flydubai flight, a Saudi source with knowledge of the matter told AFP Thursday.
"They asked to send military warplanes. Two or three direct to Tabuk airport," the source told AFP. "Turned down. Then asked to send [El Al] commercial one. Turned down as well."
The source also told AFP the message was communicated through the UAE and not directly with the Israelis.
The comments come a day after a plane heading to Tel Aviv from Dubai was forced to make an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia, after one of the pilots allegedly tried to crash the plane and kill everyone onboard.
The Saudi source said the kingdom fulfilled its "international obligation" and assisted the passengers of the flight after they made the emergency landing, emphasising that nationality of the travellers had no impact on their decision.
"We were to act the same way, regardless of the nationalities of flydubai passengers," the source added.
IRGC hail US withdrawal from Iraq as 'historic victory'
Iran's Revolutionary Guards on Thursday welcomed the withdrawal of US forces from Iraq as a "historic victory" and called for American troops to leave the Middle East.
The Revolutionary Guards "congratulate the proud nation of Iraq, the united front of the Islamic Resistance, and the revolutionary fighters of the Islamic world on this historic victory," the IRGC said in a statement carried by their official media.
The Israeli settler movement preparing to return to Gaza
Two decades after Israel evacuated its settlements from Gaza, a hardline settler movement is mobilising to return—and waiting for a green light, writes Fin de Pencier.
Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi on Thursday announced June 30 as a new deadline for armed factions to turn over their weapons to the state, following the end of the US-led coalition's mission in the country.
"October 1 is considered a serious beginning to address the issue of weapons outside state control... according to a clear roadmap and agreed timelines extending no later than June 30, 2027," Zaidi said in a statement, after having backed away from an initial September 30 deadline.
Rubio orders visiting Iranian UN delegation to leave NYC
Secretary of State Marco Rubio ordered Iran’s foreign minister and his delegation to the UN General Assembly to leave New York earlier than they had planned, two US officials said Wednesday.
The Trump administration had granted visas, albeit with severe restrictions, to Iran’s president and foreign minister and their delegations to attend the annual meeting of world leaders despite the hostilities between the two countries.
While President Masoud Pezeshkian left New York a day after speaking at the United Nations last week, Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi had remained behind ostensibly to participate in indirect talks with the US on opening the Strait of Hormuz, ending the conflict and resuming negotiations over Iran’s nuclear program.
According to some accounts, Araghchi had planned to stay in New York until Wednesday.
Iran-backed Iraq factions say 'not bound by any timeline'
Iraqi armed factions backed by Tehran said Wednesday that they were "not bound by any timeline or agreement" to surrender their weapons to the state, as the government seeks to disarm them under mounting US pressure.
A military spokesman for Kataeb Hezbollah, Jaafar al-Husseini, said at an event to celebrate the withdrawal of US-led coalition forces that the factions had been in talks on "regulating" their weapons but "have not yet received a response from the Iraqi government".
"Based on this, the Islamic Resistance declares that it is not bound by any timetable or agreement that any governmental or political party has spoken of or may speak of."
UK PM: 'strong indications' Iran involved in airbase
British Prime Minister Andy Burnham on Wednesday said there were "strong indications" Iran was involved in suspicious activity at a UK airbase that triggered a major security incident this weekend.
"There are strong indications that Iran played a part in what happened over the weekend at RAF Fairford," Burnham told the BBC, referring to Sunday's bomb scare near the airbase in southwest England, which is used by the US military in its war against Iran.
"Of course it remains an ongoing, complex, and serious police investigation," said Burnham.
Iran's embassy in London earlier said it "categorically rejects and strongly condemns" speculation it was involved in the incident, while Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi posted on X that Burnham was "barking up the wrong tree".
Police said on Tuesday that no explosives were found at the scene. The nature of the threat has not been explained by officials.
Burnham's comments are the first official confirmation from UK authorities that Iran may have had a hand in the incident, which saw three white vans appearing to head towards RAF Fairford in the early hours of Sunday.
A local resident who rang the police said she saw a group of masked men near the vans, which were blocking a road in a village next to the military base.

articles.title: Washington’s Iraq project ends where it began: in failure
articles.body:
Washington’s Iraq project ends where it began: in failure
American forces are completing their withdrawal from Iraq, yet the country that Washington once promised to turn into a model of democratic transformation in the Middle East is still facing questions that years of military presence never managed to answer.
For Iraq, this is a long-awaited political milestone, but the end of a foreign military mission does not magically fix the fragmentation of power it created. The consequences of the intervention, sectarian distrust, and competition among armed centers of influence are likely to remain part of Iraq’s political landscape for years to come.
How a military victory turned into a political dead end
Although the US had already fought Iraq in 1991, it was the invasion of March 2003 that marked the beginning of the occupation and the radical restructuring of the Iraqi state. The administration of George W. Bush justified the war primarily by pointing to the alleged threat posed by Iraqi weapons of mass destruction, yet the supposed stockpiles were never found. Saddam Hussein’s regime was overthrown with remarkable speed, but building a stable state proved to be a challenge that American military superiority alone could not solve.
The dissolution of the Iraqi army and the sweeping process of purging the influence of Hussein’s Ba’ath party deprived the emerging political system of a substantial number of people who had previously kept the state apparatus functioning. As tens of thousands of professionals, civil servants, and military personnel found themselves excluded from the new order, social resentment merged with armed resistance, while the struggle for power became increasingly sectarian. Hussein’s dictatorship had undoubtedly left behind a deeply troubled legacy, but decisions made under the occupation catalyzed violence as a means of reclaiming lost influence.
At the same time, it would be an oversimplification to attribute all the disasters that followed solely to Washington. Iraqi political leaders who institutionalized the distribution of offices and resources along party and communal lines also contributed to the alienation of significant sections of society, while neighboring states used Baghdad’s weakness to advance their own interests. Yet it was the intervention that dismantled the previous order before institutions capable of preventing the country from fragmenting into competing political and armed networks had taken shape.
The first withdrawal of American forces was completed in 2011, but by 2014 the US had returned at the invitation of the Iraqi government after ISIS seized Mosul and large areas of Iraqi territory. At that stage, American air power, intelligence capabilities and the training of local forces genuinely contributed to turning the course of the war. Denying that contribution would diminish both the role of the international coalition and the importance of the support it provided to Iraq. Even so, the principal burden of the fighting on the ground was carried by Iraqi forces, including the army, counterterrorism units, the Peshmerga and the Popular Mobilization Forces.
The destruction of Islamic State’s territorial rule in Iraq in 2017 was a genuine military achievement, but it did not eliminate the conditions that had previously allowed jihadist forces to establish themselves in the country. If American policy is judged against its promise of creating a stable and secure Iraq, the outcome appears considerably less impressive than one would think from all the declarations of military victory. All Washington did was help suppress a threat its own intervention had helped create.
The regional consequences were equally contradictory, since the removal of one of Tehran’s principal adversaries created new opportunities for Iran to expand its influence inside Iraq. The US invested enormous resources in building a new political order in which the position of its main regional rival ultimately became considerably stronger. This does not mean that Baghdad lost its own political agency, but it demonstrates just how far the actual consequences of the war diverged from the expectations with which Washington had entered it.
Sovereignty begins with bringing armed power under state control
The American withdrawal will inevitably be regarded by part of Iraqi society as the end of a long era of occupation, even though the military presence established after 2014 rested on a different legal and political basis and took place at Baghdad’s invitation. This distinction allows the Iraqi authorities to emphasise their sovereignty without denying that foreign assistance had been necessary at a particular stage.
The far more difficult challenge will be ensuring that decisions of war and peace are genuinely made by the state. The Popular Mobilization Forces, an Iranian-backed paramilitary group, emerged as a broad mobilization structure during the Islamic State offensive in 2014, although some of the organizations that became part of it had existed long before then. The organization was later incorporated into the state system, yet it retained considerable internal diversity, which is why treating the entire Popular Mobilization Forces as a single Iranian-controlled army would be misleading.
This is one of the most difficult contradictions of post-war Iraq. Groups that helped save the state from jihadist forces acquired their own sources of political and economic influence, while some commanders developed an interest in preserving a system under which the state finances armed formations without exercising complete control over their decisions. Disarmament in these conditions affects the position of political parties, access to state revenues and the personal security of individuals who have become accustomed to relying on their own armed networks.
The government of Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi is seeking to bring weapons under state control, while Iran-linked armed groups like Kataib Hezbollah are resisting these demands. The deadline imposed by the authorities has met direct opposition from several formations, while arrests of individual militia members have already prompted threats of retaliation.
Against the backdrop of the war between the US, Israel, and Iran, there is ever less space for compromise, since some armed groups view their weapons both as a means of supporting Tehran and as protection against American pressure. Baghdad, meanwhile, risks finding itself caught between Washington’s demands and the expectations of neighboring Iran, a country whose relationship with Iraq cannot be reduced simply to its ties with armed groups.
An attempt to disarm all formations simultaneously could unite against the government commanders whose interests had previously diverged, while endless concessions would merely institutionalize the autonomy of competing armed centers. A gradual process of bringing these forces under a unified chain of command, combined with tighter control over financing and credible guarantees for ordinary fighters, appears more sustainable. Otherwise, organizational rebranding may leave old networks of loyalty intact, while sovereignty remains little more than a political slogan.
New power vacuum
The Iraqi army today possesses experience that it catastrophically lacked in 2014, which is why it would be misleading to assume that the fall of Mosul could simply repeat itself. The number of Islamic State attacks in Iraq fell to a historic low in 2025 as a result of sustained pressure from Iraqi security forces. At the same time, the organization has not disappeared and continues to exploit instability in neighboring Syria.
The low intensity of attacks does not mean the underground networks are gone. The remaining cells of Islamic State, which itself grew out of the Iraqi branch of al-Qaeda, continue to pose a real security threat, whereas portraying the two organizations as separate and equally powerful underground movements in contemporary Iraq would distort the actual situation.
The most dangerous scenario would play out if confrontation between the government and armed groups began consuming the resources required for everyday security. If army units were redeployed towards the capital, intelligence services became increasingly focused on internal political opponents and local commanders stopped exchanging information, jihadist networks would gain opportunities to rebuild their supply routes and recruitment mechanisms. They would not need to seize major cities immediately. A sustained series of attacks on roads and in rural areas could already be enough to undermine public confidence in the authorities.
Such a vacuum could emerge in areas where several security structures are formally present but none assumes full responsibility for maintaining order. Territories where political rivalry obstructs cooperation between Baghdad, the Kurdish authorities and local security forces would be particularly vulnerable. If arbitrary measures and collective accusations against local communities were added to this environment, underground groups could once again attempt to present themselves as defenders of those who feel excluded or mistreated.
The central question, therefore, is whether the Iraqi leadership can preserve unity of command, public confidence and effective intelligence work while simultaneously reforming the country’s armed formations. Continued external technical assistance and intelligence sharing could make this task easier, but foreign advisers cannot substitute for a domestic political settlement. The withdrawal creates a genuine danger when it coincides with the collapse of such a settlement, although the departure of foreign troops does not in itself make another war inevitable.
At the same time, the army’s ability to conduct raids against underground cells should not automatically be equated with its ability to confront large armed formations that enjoy political protection. In the latter case, an order to use force could divide the governing coalition, while commanders would inevitably have to take into account loyalties and connections within their own political camp. It is precisely this dependence of military decisions on elite rivalry that makes the possibility of internal confrontation particularly dangerous.
Why Washington is reducing its presence
Explaining the American decision solely through the current conflict with Iran would be historically inaccurate, since the timetable for transforming the coalition mission was agreed as early as September 2024. The decision reflected the decline in the terrorist threat compared with the period when Islamic State controlled substantial territory, pressure from the Iraqi authorities and a broader intention to move towards bilateral cooperation. Washington was able to reduce its direct military involvement while maintaining its relationship with Baghdad through training programs, arms cooperation, and diplomatic instruments.
Nevertheless, the conflict with Iran has clearly shown the costs of maintaining a permanent military presence. In early March 2026, Iranian drones struck Erbil airport, where an American base was located, and a coalition facility housing Italian personnel was later attacked as well. These incidents go to show that overseas military bases, while designed to project power, can simultaneously become accessible targets for retaliation.
When an expensive military facility can be repeatedly targeted with comparatively inexpensive drones, protecting that facility requires a constant expenditure of resources, and every military casualty creates political pressure for another round of escalation. Under these circumstances, reducing the number of vulnerable American garrisons can be a rational choice for Washington even though the overall military capabilities of the US remain incomparably greater than those of its opponents. This, however, explains the incentives behind current American policy rather than proving that Iranian attacks were the original cause of the withdrawal.
Even after the last military unit departs, political responsibility for the consequences of the intervention will remain. The US is leaving at a moment when the Iraqi state has still not secured a complete monopoly over the use of force and when the foundations of lasting political reconciliation are still shaky. The issue is not whether American troops should remain indefinitely against the wishes of the host country, but rather that the political project proclaimed at the beginning of the intervention was never fully completed.
The Iraqi withdrawal also raises the question as to whether it is part of a wider change in the American role in the Middle East, as Washington concentrates more resources within a strategic security belt extending from Latin America to the North Atlantic and Greenland.
There are grounds for such an interpretation, since the US has increasingly emphasized the Western Hemisphere while reconsidering the geographic distribution of its military presence. The expansion of American military opportunities in Greenland is also consistent with a growing emphasis on the security of the American continent and the North Atlantic.
Yet these decisions do not mean that the US is abandoning the Middle East altogether or that it no longer has the capacity to maintain bases there. The continuing confrontation with Iran demonstrates the persistence of powerful strategic commitments, while the reduction of one military contingent can be accompanied by a stronger naval or air presence elsewhere. Rather, Washington is adopting a more selective approach, seeking to reduce the costs of prolonged deployments where military presence has failed to produce a proportionate political return.
For Iraq, the consequences of that shift will ultimately depend less on the number of American soldiers who remain than on whether Iraqi leaders can create a functioning and accountable state authority before competing armed actors begin struggling to fill the vacuum once again.

articles.title: Why the US Air Force Needs to Invest in Electronic Warfare
articles.body:
United States air forces are engaged in combat operations today, and not all the aircraft are modern stealthy platforms like the B-2, F-22, or F-35. The venerable Lockheed Martin F-16 Fighting Falcon remains the backbone of the U.S. Air Force fighter fleet and will be in service for two more decades, yet combat operations in Operation Urgent Fury prove it needs electromagnetic warfare (EW) upgrades to survive in modern threat environments.
Our knowledge of the frequencies and waveform characteristics across the Electromagnetic Spectrum (EMS) and our ability to manipulate them with hardware and software have grown tremendously. We harness our knowledge and capabilities continuously for tracking, intelligence, communication, jamming, radar, and many other applications. Unfortunately, so do our adversaries.
To survive and accomplish combat missions, F-16 pilots need to first detect enemy threat systems, like surface-to-air missiles or air-to-air radars, via a Radar Warning Receiver (RWR) and then counter the threat with Electronic Countermeasures (ECM) that manipulate radio signals to jam guidance systems outright or deceive them in such a way that makes them ineffective. If it were only that easy.
In 2023, Commander-in-Chief of the Ukraine Armed Forces, General Valerii Zaluzhnyi, wrote a paper listing five reasons why the war with Russia had ground into static trench warfare. He cited the critical importance and rapid adaptation of electromagnetic warfare along with air superiority, counter artillery battery fires, minefield clearing, and reserve forces.
The electromagnetic spectrum is the tissue that continuously connects all our systems together and allows us to coordinate our actions, detect adversaries, deceive threats, survive, and win. Acknowledging the EMS’s asymmetric impact, both Russia and China created separate branches of service and senior commands specifically focused on electromagnetic warfare.
While superiority in the EMS is critical across all warfighting domains: land, sea, space, and cyber, it is particularly important in air operations.
While the U.S. Air Force has re-prioritized EMS for a portion of the F-16 fleet, approximately 50% of the remaining F-16 aircraft fleet across the active duty, Air National Guard, and Reserves will not have EW protection with no clear plan going forward.
International partners have invested over $1B in procuring Viper Shield systems for their F-16s over the past seven years. The Air Force could add EW pods and leverage foreign investment to save taxpayer money. This foreign investment is funding development, lab testing, flight testing, and current production of operational Viper Shield systems, which presents the U.S. Air Force with a massive savings opportunity to avoid those upfront costs.
As the Air Force considers options to resolve the F-16 EW capability gap, a modest number of advanced EW pods would be a reasonable expense for near-term capability to mitigate against potential program delays, maximize flexibility across the F-16 fleet, and reduce invasive internal modifications.
Furthermore, the pod version of Viper Shield offers maximum flexibility to rotate systems across deploying squadrons, share them among operational units during training periods, and maintain them without taking an aircraft off the flying schedule.
F-16 pilots today – and for the next 20+ years – deserve the capability an EW pod like Viper Shield brings to the fight.
Lt. Gen. Lance Landrum, USAF (Ret.), served over 30 years as an F-16 Weapons Instructor and operational fighter pilot in several deployed locations developing firsthand combat experience on the importance of Electromagnetic Warfare. During his role as the Joint Staff J8 Deputy Director for Requirements and Capability Development, he stood up and led the interagency Electromagnetic Spectrum Operations Cross Functional Team that developed the current U.S. EMS Superiority Strategy and subsequent implementation plan. His insights are based on that experience and from his efforts to champion EMS capabilities as the U.S. European Command J3 and Deputy Chair of the NATO Military Committee.

articles.title: Forterra reveals lessons from 1,400 Lancer missions in Ukraine
articles.body:
- Forterra says combat use of its Lancer autonomous ground vehicles in Ukraine led to Starlink integration and remote AutoDrive updates for terrain and traction.
- The company confirmed some Lancers were lost to Russian drones and said Ukrainian troops teleoperate the vehicles when reacting to immediate threats.
Forterra says well over a thousand missions in Ukraine have shaped how it builds autonomous ground vehicles, from coping with jamming and mud to keeping them running under constant threat from Russian drones.
The company develops autonomy systems for military vehicles. Its Lancer is a Polaris Ranger 1500 utility vehicle fitted with Forterra’s AutoDrive self-driving software and Vektor communications system. Forterra delivered more than a hundred Lancers to Ukrainian forces under a U.S. government program, a deployment it first disclosed in July. Ukrainian troops use them for supply runs, casualty evacuation and other frontline tasks.
In written answers to questions from The Defence Blog, Forterra said running more than 100 vehicles in combat has taught it more about durability, supply chains and field maintenance than any test range could.
The company’s full answers appear below, unedited.
Q: Forterra has now accumulated experience from more than 1,400 Lancer missions in Ukraine. Looking beyond the mission count itself, what have been the most important lessons from operating autonomous ground vehicles in an active, contested battlefield?
A: A few things stand out for us at Forterra. Electronic warfare changes constantly. A solution that works one month may not work the next, so the system has to be updated quickly. That requires trust and good operational communication with the unit executing missions. We’ve built our comms and autonomy stack in a way that can be updated and adapted remotely, and often in near real time. So being able to iterate rapidly from a remote location is just as important as the hardware itself.
Terrain has been another major lesson. It is difficult to reproduce the combination of mud, poor traction, improvised routes, and recovery challenges in testing. In Ukraine, the best results have come from combining autonomy with human judgment. That experience is shaping how we design the next generation.
We’ve also learned that just because a vehicle can operate fully autonomously, there are times soldiers want to be in control. The troops in Ukraine choose to teleoperate the Lancers when reacting to an immediate threat. Our Lancers were designed to assist and support the troops in the best way they see fit, and when it comes to contested environments such as the ones they’re facing in Ukraine, autonomy combined with human judgment will like result in the greatest success, and it’s shaping how we design the next generation of the system.
And ultimately, reliability at scale matters more than any single capability. Keeping over a hundred vehicles running, maintained, and mission-ready for as long as we have, under combat conditions, has taught us more about durability, supply chains, and field maintenance than any test range ever could.
Q: What did Ukrainian operators teach Forterra about the system that the company could not have learned through testing in the United States? Were there assumptions made during development that had to be reconsidered once Lancer entered combat operations?
A: Testing can reproduce rough terrain, jamming, or a mechanical failure. It cannot fully reproduce the urgency, pressure, and improvisation involved in making those decisions under fire.
Operators constantly find practical fixes in the field. Operators would add armor plating or reflective tape with whatever they had on hand, faster than we could respond to one of their requests, and we’ve had to build our process to absorb that kind of frontline fix. This is something the US misses in each of its programmatic efforts. It underutilizes operational assessments where this ingenuity emerges and presses the government and industry teams forward with new solutions.
Trust in autonomy is earned incrementally. Soldiers wanted to retain control in certain situations and that has reshaped how we think about the balance between autonomous and remotely piloted modes. Ukraine’s electronic warfare environment also pushed us to accelerate work on resilient communications and made clear that maintainability has to be a core design requirement.
Q: Ukraine presents an unusually difficult environment for autonomous systems, with electronic warfare, disrupted communications, GNSS interference, drones, mines and rapidly changing front lines. Which of these challenges has been the hardest for Lancer and its autonomy stack to deal with?
A: The pervasive drone threat has been a challenge. There is a lot of surveillance and the coordination of these vehicles under near persistent observation means human judgment for when to move and when to pause is critical.
So, on a go forward basis looking at how this context of the battlefield, in a comms restricted environment, gets to operators and assets is critical. The information exists, the automated behaviors are in work.
Q: Forterra has acknowledged that some Lancer vehicles have been lost to Russian drones. What have those losses taught you about survivability, signature management, redundancy and the way unmanned ground vehicles should be designed for a battlefield saturated with UAVs?
A: We have lost Lancers. They demonstrate the value of using unmanned systems for missions that would otherwise resulted in a loss of life. Some of these assets have been resurrected and repaired. The thoughts around sustainment and reconstitution on the edge are important.
I think there is room for automated defensive measures which have proved to be effective. This seems like a natural next step.
Q: Has combat experience in Ukraine already resulted in hardware or software changes to Lancer, AutoDrive or Vektor? Can you give examples of improvements that originated directly from feedback from Ukrainian units?
A: Yes. This program has been able to move fast because we’ve treated frontline feedback as a direct input to engineering. Integrating Starlink into our comms architecture was a direct response to the environment. It gave operators another way to maintain connectivity to assets executing missions.
Another example is with our mobility capability AutoDrive. We’ve been able to push updates to AutoDrive around terrain handling, traction, and recovery behavior based directly on where and how vehicles were getting stuck in the field.
More broadly, the feedback we get and our ability to push these updates remotely in response has been one of the biggest benefits of this deployment.
Q: How quickly does that feedback loop work in practice? When Ukrainian operators identify a problem or new requirement, how does that information move from the battlefield back to Forterra and eventually into a software update, design modification or production change?
A: We have deliberately kept the feedback loop short. We treat the front line as a live input to engineering, not a lagging indicator. Operators flag an issue directly through the units and program touchpoints we have in place, and it gets to our engineering team almost immediately. For software, that often means a fix or update pushed remotely within days. For hardware or production changes, it is much faster than typical defense programs.
Q: Ukraine has become an operational environment for unmanned technologies on a scale and with a technological intensity that is difficult to reproduce elsewhere. From an engineering perspective, how has exposure to this environment changed Forterra’s understanding of what future ground autonomy needs to look like?
The biggest shift has been recognizing that autonomy is not a standalone capability. A vehicle can be great at driving itself and still fail the mission if it can’t handle jamming, can’t be fixed in the field, or can’t be updated fast enough to keep pace with new threats.
We believe that “good autonomy” is less about maximizing autonomous capability for its own sake, and more about knowing where autonomy helps and where human control still matters. Ukraine has made that split much clearer than any test range could.
It’s also changed our sense of pace. Traditional defense development cycles measure in years but this engagement demands fixes in days. Any future ground autonomy platform has to be built for that kind of iteration from day one. Future systems need to be designed as complete operational systems – from autonomy and communications to logistics, maintenance, human controls, and rapid updates.
Q: If Forterra were starting the Lancer program again today with everything the company has learned from Ukraine, what would you design differently from the beginning?
A: The core architecture has held up: a proven commercial platform with modular autonomy and communications. If we were starting again, I’d prioritize field maintenance and local supply chains, recovery, communications resilience, and operator control even earlier in the design process.

German authorities have warned repeatedly that Russia is conducting a hybrid campaign of drone and cyber attacks, accusing Moscow of being behind an attempted drone attack at Leipzig airport in August.
“We are preparing for further hybrid attacks, including serious ones,” Merz said, in a speech marking the award of the 2026 Westphalian Peace Prize to the NATO alliance.
Moscow has rejected the accusations from Western governments and intelligence services.

articles.title: Space Force Sunsets 1970s-Era Missile Warning Satellite Constellation
articles.body:
More than 50 years after the U.S. military launched its first Defense Support Program satellite, the Space Force has officially decommissioned the missile warning constellation as it prepares to start fielding its next-generation architecture.
In a swan song of sorts, the last two remaining DSP spacecraft participated in a U.S. Space Command exercise in early September, helping the command demonstrate dynamic maneuvers across multiple orbits. Following the demonstration, the satellites were decommissioned into a supersynchronous—or graveyard—orbit, the Space Force’s Combat Forces Command said Oct. 1.
“These last two satellites were the culminating end to over a half-century of space-based early warning,” Mission Delta 4 Commander Col. Brandon Davenport said in a statement. “The DSP constellation ensured deterrence during the Cold War and protected our deployed warfighters from the Gulf War until their retirement last month.”
The first DSP satellite was launched in 1970 to geosynchronous orbit, providing key ballistic missile warning capabilities amid Cold War tensions between the U.S. and the Soviet Union. The goal was to discourage a first strike from the Soviets and help stabilize the relationship between the two nuclear-armed states. As the U.S. built out the constellation, it was used to detect theater missile launches in Iraq during the Operation Desert Storm in 1991. Its infrared sensors have also been used to detect natural disasters like forest fires and volcanic eruptions.
The constellation eventually grew to 23 satellites, the last of which launched in 2007. However, the service life of that final spacecraft was cut short in 2008 when a component failure caused it to drift to an unintended orbit. The Defense Department had originally set out to launch a 24th satellite, but ultimately canceled that plan. A full-sized DSP test article is on display at the National Museum of the United States Air Force in Dayton, Ohio.
DSP’s immediate successor, the Space-Based Infrared System, is on orbit today and consists of six satellites in GEO as well as four in a highly elliptical orbit. The Space Force is on the verge of launching the first of two Next-Generation Overhead Persistent Infrared satellites in the coming months. The spacecraft will augment the SBIRS constellation with improved, more sensitive sensors to detect dimmer threats.
Those two Next-Gen OPIR satellites, going to geosynchronous orbit, are part of the Space Force’s plan for a multiorbit missile warning architecture, which will include proliferated constellations in medium-Earth orbit and low-Earth orbit developed by Space Systems Command and the Space Development Agency, respectively. The service also had plans to fly two Next-Gen OPIR Polar satellites, but proposed canceling the program in its fiscal 2027 budget request. House and Senate lawmakers have supported maintaining the effort in drafts of defense spending and policy legislation, but its future will remain undecided until a final appropriations bill passes both chambers.
In its press release, Combat Forces Command noted that sunsetting the last two DSP satellites will allow operators in the 2nd Space Warning Squadron to shift their focus toward preparing for launch and initial testing of the first Next-Gen OPIR satellites.
“Retiring our legacy DSP system allows us to best posture for the future,” said Lt. Col. Ann Hughes, the squadron commander. “Our crews are always ready on each and every system they operate to ensure seamless [missile warning and tracking]. Onboarding future systems requires training for every scenario from unforeseen software issues to countering adversary aggression on orbit. We’re focused on providing a reliable, consistent, and seamless picture of missile threats regardless of the operational environment.”

articles.title: Chinese invasion of Taiwan likely pushed past 2027 amid military purges, say US officials
articles.body:
US officials believe a Chinese invasion of Taiwan before 2028 is increasingly unlikely despite Chinese President Xi Jinping's instructions for his military to be ready by 2027 to take the democratically governed island by force, if needed, people familiar with US thinking said.
The main reasons include delays in military readiness amid the Chinese Communist Party's anti-corruption campaign as well as Beijing's eagerness to see the results of Taiwan's 2028 election, which some Chinese officials hope could usher in a government more amenable to bringing the island under Chinese control, according to two current US officials, one former US official and a person familiar with the matter.
Beijing may increasingly look to use force in 2028 and beyond if Taiwan's election sees the Democratic Progressive Party win a fourth consecutive term, and in particular if current President Lai Ching-te wins reelection, the people added.
"If that happens, I think 2028 becomes pretty sporty," said one of the US officials, who, like the other sources, spoke on condition of anonymity.
Lai, who took office two years ago, and his ruling DPP champion Taiwan's separate identity from China, a position that frequently angers Beijing, which views the island as an inviolable part of Chinese territory. Taiwan strongly objects to China's claims and says only its people can decide their future.
Taiwan 2027 invasion chosen to match centenary of PLA
The assessment, which has not previously been reported, is a significant update to the years-long understanding among US officials that Xi wanted his military ready to potentially take Taiwan by force in 2027, the centenary of the founding of its People's Liberation Army. China has never ruled out using force to bring Taiwan under its control but has never publicly confirmed a 2027 readiness order.
The Pentagon declined to comment.
China's US embassy and Taiwan's representative office in Washington did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
In a speech this week, Xi referred to Taiwan and talked about promoting the peaceful development of cross-strait relations to achieve "reunification."
The 2027 benchmark, which analysts say is about Chinese military preparedness rather than a timeline for invasion, has for years created a sense of urgency across multiple US administrations in countering China in the Asia-Pacific region.
The US intelligence community has hinted at Chinese wariness before. It said in its annual threat assessment in March that China did not, at least at that point, have a plan to invade Taiwan next year and still preferred to wrest control of the island without the use of force, if possible.
US elections may be a factor
The US is Taiwan's most important international backer and weapons supplier despite a lack of formal diplomatic ties, and US officials offered mixed assessments of the degree to which China might view the 2028 US presidential election as an important indicator for military action.
While three of the people familiar with the matter said Beijing may also want to evaluate the outcome of the US election, particularly given rising American voter antipathy toward US military action abroad, the first US official said Beijing viewed both Democrats and Republicans as largely aligned on Taiwan.
While China might have a preference in the 2028 US election, "it doesn't become as decisive a factor in my opinion, as it might have been 15 years ago," the official said.
US President Donald Trump has downplayed the likelihood of a Chinese invasion of Taiwan during his presidency, going so far as to say last year that Xi told him China would not invade while he was in office.
Trump made limited comments on Taiwan after hosting Xi in Washington last week, saying only that the issue of Taiwan came up when the two spoke and that Xi understood his position.
China calls Taiwan its single most important issue and a matter of Chinese sovereignty and territorial integrity.
It has called for an end to US arms sales to Taiwan. Since his May trip to Beijing, Trump has held off on approving a new arms package worth some $14 billion, describing it as a "negotiating chip."
For years, the US strategy has focused on arming Taiwan so that it can hold off Chinese forces long enough for the United States and others to come to its aid.
Goal remains to take Taiwan by next year, purge may push that back
China's Xi has not rescinded his goal for the People's Liberation Army to have the capabilities available to take Taiwan by force by next year, officials say.
But the military didn't accomplish as much last year militarily as it probably had intended because of the impact of China's anti-corruption campaign, the people said.
Since coming to power in 2012, Xi has unleashed a sweeping corruption and discipline crackdown. Millions within China's vast bureaucracy have been investigated, with scores of senior party, government and military officials ensnared and purged.
In recent years, the People's Liberation Army has been a target of the campaign. A string of investigations and expulsions has left just two active officials on the formerly seven-member Central Military Commission, including Xi himself, who serves as chair.
China draws lessons from Iran, Ukraine
China's military exercises last year were smaller and less threatening compared to the past several years, according to the US official. While they bounced back a bit this year, the official suggested Chinese military officials were dissatisfied with their readiness.
The official said China was believed to have drawn a lesson from the wars in Iran and Ukraine, which is the need to move quickly once any invasion begins and avoid getting bogged down in a sustained conflict.
More work remained for China.
"There are way too many pieces that aren't quite in place yet for what would be the most difficult military operation any military has attempted probably since the Allied invasion of Normandy," the official said.

Russian dictator Vladimir Putin made a number of statements concerning international politics and the war in Ukraine during the plenary session of the Valdai Discussion Club on October 1. He tried to absolve his country of responsibility for the peace talks that had reached an impasse and added: "the Russian Federation believes it will liberate the entire territory of the 'Donetsk People's Republic' much earlier than Ukraine and Europe expect," UNN reports.
In addition, Putin tried to convince his compatriots and the international community of the significant successes of the Russian Armed Forces on the battlefield.
What Putin said during the discussion club meeting
Putin tried to convince people that Russia allegedly sought to end the war against Ukraine as soon as possible through negotiations. At the same time, however, he confirmed that Moscow was not abandoning its key demands, including Ukraine's neutral status.
"We would like to end this (the war — ed.) as soon as possible, preferably through negotiations," he said.
At the same time, both Putin himself and his entourage repeatedly put forward demands on the Ukrainian side as part of the talks that are technically impossible to fulfill. For example, the Russian side has consistently and stubbornly demanded that Ukrainian leader Volodymyr Zelenskyy come specifically to Moscow. This is despite the fact that, among others, countries in the East and Turkey have repeatedly expressed their readiness to serve as a venue for peace talks.
The Russian dictator also stated that Ukraine's neutral status remains among Moscow's goals. According to his version, Russia had previously viewed Ukraine as a neutral state, but the situation changed after Ukraine's Constitution enshrined a course toward NATO membership. In practice, Putin once again confirmed that he wants to deprive Ukraine of independence on the international stage and prevent it, as a sovereign state, from making decisions about its own future.
Putin also outlined Moscow's position on the American proposals concerning the end of the war. According to him, they include decisions that are difficult for the Russian side and require compromises. Overall, however, the Kremlin views them as movement toward a possible settlement. However, the Russian leader did not specify exactly which decisions he was referring to. It is entirely possible that he meant potential compromises regarding the end of the war, which he discussed during his meeting with U.S. President Donald Trump in Anchorage. At the time, Moscow officially claimed that it had agreed with a number of approaches proposed by the American side, although no public comprehensive agreement was announced following the talks.
The Russian dictator separately accused Ukraine of being unwilling to suspend hostilities. He stated that he had allegedly been ready to resume the negotiating process immediately after Russia's parliamentary elections in September, but linked the absence of such dialogue to Ukrainian strikes on the territory of the Russian Federation and on regions of Ukraine occupied by Russia. Putin claimed that Ukrainian servicemen had allegedly deliberately targeted members of electoral commissions, resulting in the deaths of six people. It should be emphasized that Russia's authorities' claim that the strikes specifically targeted members of electoral commissions has not received independent confirmation.
At the same time, Putin spoke about the voting for the State Duma held in the temporarily occupied territories of Ukraine. The United Nations emphasized that such electoral processes in occupied Ukrainian territory have no legal basis and do not alter its internationally recognized status.
Putin also stated that, in Moscow's view, a possible peace settlement should address the Russian language and the activities of the church in Ukraine. Russia had previously repeatedly included linguistic, religious, and political issues in its list of demands toward Kyiv.
Putin announced an acceleration of the Russian forces' offensive
During his speech, Vladimir Putin also stated that the pace of the Russian army's advance was allegedly increasing. According to his claim, during September alone, Russian troops established control over 1,301 square kilometers of territory, which he described as approximately 2.5 times greater than the figure for the previous months.
In addition, the Russian leader emphasized that, allegedly, approximately 11% of the territory of Donetsk region, which Moscow illegally incorporated into the Russian Federation, remains under Ukraine’s control. According to him, the Russian leadership believes that the Russian armed forces will be able to seize this territory sooner than Ukraine and European countries expect. However, such statements contradict the actual course of events. In particular, Ukrainian troops are currently successfully conducting Operation "Vivaldi" and liberating occupied territories. The Russians themselves, according to assessments by a number of analysts, have "become bogged down" in Donetsk region and have no progress to boast about.
In his monologue, Vladimir Putin also referred to allegedly existing assessments in Ukraine and Europe according to which Ukrainian forces could hold these territories for another one and a half to two years. However, he did not name the sources of these assessments.

articles.title: Russian drones strike Kyiv’s Southern Bridge in first attack on the city’s bridges since the full-scale invasion. A subway train was crossing it at the time.

Russian drones strike Kyiv’s Southern Bridge in first attack on the city’s bridges since the full-scale invasion. A subway train was crossing it at the time.
Russian forces are keeping up their drone attacks on Kyiv. On the morning of October 1, a drone struck a school building in the Solomianskyi district. The students were in a shelter at the time and were unharmed. Later that day, Russian forces attacked bridges in Kyiv with drones for the first time since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine began. Two drones struck the Southern Bridge, which carries both road traffic and subway trains.
The blast wave sent dust from the ventilation system into the cars of a subway train crossing the bridge. No passengers were hurt. The train was also undamaged, according to preliminary reports, but was sent to a depot for further inspection.
Subway and bus service across the bridge has been suspended. Subway trains are running only on underground stretches: between the Syrets and Vydubychi stations and between Osokorky and Chervonyi Khutir, the Kyiv City Military Administration said. Buses have been temporarily rerouted. Experts are inspecting the bridge to assess damage from the strikes. The administration said preliminary findings showed no critical damage.
UNIAN noted that subway service across the Southern Bridge used to be suspended during air raid alerts. Since September 9, however, trains have been allowed to cross the bridge during “yellow” alerts, with service suspended only during “red” alerts.
It also emerged on October 1 that a Russian drone had attacked the Institute for Nuclear Research of Ukraine’s National Academy of Sciences in Kyiv the previous day. Ukraine’s nuclear regulator, the State Nuclear Regulatory Inspectorate, said the strike hit the grounds where a research reactor is located. A fire broke out but was quickly extinguished. No one was hurt, the reactor was undamaged, and radiation levels are normal.
On September 28, a Russian drone struck the building housing the academy’s governing body in central Kyiv. Two people were killed and several were injured. Among the injured, according to the BBC Russian Service, was former National Security and Defense Council Secretary Volodymyr Horbulin.

articles.title: US Congress ought to fix the flawed Saudi nuclear deal
articles.body:
The confusion surrounding a proposed civil nuclear deal with Saudi Arabia has not exactly disappeared: The White House is still claiming it depends on the country normalizing relations with Israel, even if that is not part of the written agreement. At least the US Congress now has the text for review. Having seen its flaws, legislators should demand changes.
The 30-year nuclear cooperation pact would allow US companies not only to build new reactors in the kingdom, but possibly also a uranium enrichment facility — needed to produce the fissile material for a bomb. The two governments would have up to two years to decide whether an indigenous enrichment program makes sense, both commercially and in terms of US national interests. If so, the US would introduce, but restrict the sensitive technology, keeping it in a metaphorical “black box” to prevent transfer to the Saudis. Congress has 90 days in session to decide whether to oppose the deal; otherwise, it will go into effect automatically.
Proceeding on such terms would be risky. For decades, the US and other nuclear suppliers have refused to provide customers with the technology to enrich uranium or reprocess spent fuel, precisely so they could not assemble the working materials for a bomb. Saudi Crown Prince Mohammad bin Salman has already said his nation would “have to” match Iran if it develops a nuclear weapon; the mere possibility that the Saudis might do so would encourage other countries in the region to pursue one as well. Any restricted facilities would be vulnerable to leakage, if not outright seizure.
It is unclear why the US even needs to offer such a concession. Other suppliers are not threatening to provide the same access to enrichment technology; Russia and China compete mainly on cost. Besides, the Saudis have been pursuing access to US nuclear technology for nearly two decades. They have had plenty of time to seek alternatives if they wished. Breaking with precedent, on the other hand, could liberate US rivals to do the same. (Russia is already leading major reactor projects in Egypt and Turkey.) It would also dramatically weaken the US case against allowing Iran a domestic enrichment program.
While a joint resolution opposing the agreement seems unlikely to muster a veto-proof majority, Congress should still use this chance to press for greater clarity and stronger safeguards against proliferation.
At minimum, lawmakers should thoroughly scrutinize the classified documents linked to the deal, including two secret side letters, and insist on answers to unresolved questions such as whether the Saudis would be allowed to pursue an independent enrichment program if the joint study decides against one. Congress should insist on input into that study, to ensure the arguments against allowing nuclear fuel-making are fully absorbed.
Legislators should continue to push for the Saudis to sign an Additional Protocol with the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA), allowing for expanded international inspections. Failing that, they should press the administration to work with the IAEA on expedited procedures to investigate any suspicions that the Saudis might be pursuing a hidden enrichment or weapons program. Perhaps most important, Congress should lay out severe consequences for such cheating — including asset freezes and cutting off access to other US technology.
The administration should be commended for looking for ways to boost US nuclear exports, but that goal should not be pursued at any cost — and Congress should say so clearly.

A Russian drone struck Kyiv’s Southern (Pivdennyi) Bridge the second time on Thursday, damaging a bridge support and forcing authorities to halt metro and surface transport across it.
Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko first reported the strike at 9:50 p.m. local Kyiv time, saying the drone had hit the bridge’s roadway and that emergency services were heading to the scene.

articles.title: Ukraine carries out first logistics mission using an amphibious UGV
articles.body:
Ukrainian service members have completed the country’s first logistics mission using an amphibious unmanned ground vehicle (UGV), according to an announcement from Ukraine's Defense Ministry.
Such platforms are designed to maintain mobility in areas where conventional unmanned ground vehicles cannot operate due to flooding, deep channels, or unstable ground.
According to the ministry, the system traveled more than 40 km. while carrying ammunition and food supplies to frontline positions, moving across terrain that included rivers, canals, and marshland.
The vehicle operated as a wheeled platform on land and switched to swimming mode when encountering water obstacles. The cargo remained onboard throughout the transition, allowing the route to be completed without relying on bridges.
Ukraine’s Brave1 defense innovation cluster said in a statement that operators of the "Alter Ego" unit of the 93rd Mechanized Brigade deployed the robotic system.
While the ministry did not identify the vehicle’s developer, it said that the platform had been developed and refined over several months in cooperation with the military and took into account “real-world missions, operational experience, and the specific characteristics of front-line terrain.”
The Brave1 defense innovation cluster, which recently introduced a dedicated funding track for amphibious unmanned systems, supported the development of the platform through grant funding.
Although the ministry did not specify the model used, there is a growing number of domestically manufactured amphibious UGVs, including platforms such as the UNEX, Triton, Rage Robot, Dodger multi-purpose UGVs.
The UNEX system, which became operational last year, is built on a specialized chassis and can cross water, floodplains, swamps, sand, ice, and other difficult terrain. The ministry claims that the weight distribution across its axles and its wide tires “generates less surface pressure than an infantry soldier’s foot, preventing the activation of mines designed to target automotive equipment and armored vehicles.”
The platform is fully electric, has an autonomous operating time of up to six hours and a payload capacity of up to 1,700 kg. It can be placed in various configurations, tailored for logistics, evacuation, and demining, and can be equipped with a weapons station or electronic warfare system.
Ukrainian forces have expanded their use of unmanned ground vehicles for logistics and evacuation missions over the past year. Ukrainian media have reported that the number of frontline units using UGVs has increased from 67 in late 2025 to 167 by the spring of 2026.
On its website, Brave1 says that UGVs are already carrying out over 7,000 combat missions per month. In April, the country’s former Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov said that it aims to have UGVs carry out all front-line logistics operations.
UGVs have become one of the most consequential technologies in modern warfare. Once limited to bomb disposal and remote reconnaissance, UGVs now support frontline combat, logistics, electronic warfare, and casualty evacuation across multiple conflict zones. Their rapid evolution is transforming how militaries fight, supply, and survive on increasingly lethal and electronically contested battlefields.
According to Brave1, troops from the Alter Ego UGV battalion of the 93rd Mechanized Brigade engineered a variation of the Desantnyk UGV along with a precision drop mechanism for heavy drone bombers. The entire process, from initial concept to combat application, took 10 days.
Earlier this month, troops used heavy bomber drones to air-drop those UGVs several miles behind Russian positions in a surprise assault called Operation Vivaldi.
The use of the UGVs, which acted as suicide ground robotic systems, helped Ukraine take back 125 sq.km. from Russian control. Business Insider reported that UGVs completed over 15,700 different missions, delivering around 3,300 tons of cargo during the offensive.

articles.title: Ukraine Strikes Russian Forces With FP-7 Ballistic Missile for the First Time
articles.body:
Ukraine has used its own FP-7 tactical ballistic missile, manufactured by Fire Point, in combat for the first time.
This was announced by Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, who also released a video of the missile launch.
“Ukrainian tactical ballistic missile. FP-7. First combat use. Thank you for the result,” Zelensky said.
The president stated that following its successful combat use, the missile is set to enter production.
The missile is designed for the rapid engagement of targets at medium ranges.
Fire Point first announced the development of its own FP-7 and FP-9 ballistic missiles at a press conference during the MSPO international exhibition in September 2025 in Poland.
The FP-7 ballistic missile has a range of up to 200 km, a maximum speed of 1,500 m/s, and a circular error probability of 14 meters.
Its payload will be 150 kg, and its maximum flight duration will be 250 seconds.
In Februaryi 2026, Fire Point conducted flight tests of the new FP-7 tactical ballistic missile.
To launch the missiles, the company does not use a specialized launcher based on a multi-axle truck chassis which is standard for such systems, but, similar to the FP-5 cruise missiles, a conventional rail guide mounted on a trailer.
As part of the Freyja project, an interceptor designed to shoot down ballistic missiles is also being developed based on this missile.
The missile’s relatively low cost is expected to be one of the advantages of Freyja compared to the use of expensive American interceptor missiles.
