On September 30, a Russian attack drone struck the territory of the Institute for Nuclear Research of the National Academy of Sciences of Ukraine in Kyiv. The site of the strike is located approximately 100 meters from a research nuclear reactor. The Foreign Ministry noted that in recent days, Russian attacks had hit several important facilities of Ukraine’s nuclear industry and scientific sector at once. In particular, buildings used by the National Nuclear Energy Generating Company "Energoatom" came under attack.
Also, on September 28, a Russian drone struck the building of the Presidium of the National Academy of Sciences of Ukraine. According to the Foreign Ministry, it sustained significant damage, and two people were killed.
The ministry believes these attacks are a continuation of Russia’s targeted strikes against Ukrainian nuclear science.
The Foreign Ministry also recalled that back in 2022, Russian forces repeatedly shelled the National Science Center "Kharkiv Institute of Physics and Technology." At that time, the infrastructure of the "Neutron Source" nuclear installation was damaged. The ministry called on the IAEA Director General to clearly condemn the new attack and demand that Russia stop striking Ukrainian nuclear and scientific facilities.
In addition, the ministry called on partners to strengthen sanctions against Russia’s nuclear sector, particularly against "Rosatom," and to limit cooperation with Russian scientific institutions. This includes, in particular, their participation in international research programs and access to funding.
Separately, ministry representatives emphasized that Ukraine needs additional means to protect facilities that remain under threat of Russian attacks. Partners were urged to speed up the delivery of air defense systems, missiles for them, and means of intercepting attack drones.
"Defense measures and sanctions decisions must deprive Russia of the ability to continue its nuclear terror and force it to answer for these attacks," the Foreign Ministry emphasized.

articles.title: China’s Military Open New Logistics and Training Facility in Laos
articles.body:
This week, the Chinese military opened a new logistics and training facility at an airport in Laos, further expanding its regional security presence and establishing the first overseas presence of the Chinese air force.
In a statement, China’s Ministry of Defense said that the China-Laos Military Joint Support and Training Center was inaugurated on Tuesday, in a ceremony that was attended by Lao Defense Minister Khamlieng Outhakaysone and a delegation from the Chinese People’s Liberation Army (PLA).
The facility, which is based at Ban Keun Airport, which sits close to the Nam Ngum River around 50 kilometers north of the capital Vientiane, also includes a China-Laos Friendship Aviation Academy.
“The center, jointly maintained and operated by both sides, is aimed at helping Laos strengthen the training of its air force pilots,” the Ministry said, but offered no details about what personnel or equipment would be based at the airport.
“The construction and use of the center reflect mutual respect and equal consultation between China and Laos, comply with both countries’ domestic laws, relevant international law and common practice,” it said. “It is not directed against any third party and contributes to enhancing practical military cooperation as well as promoting regional peace and stability.”
Satellite imagery of the Ban Keun facility shows it also includes the construction of an extensive airfield. According to Reuters, work began on the new airfield in late 2025 and work was ongoing as of early September. “In place of green fields,” it reported, “a large paved runway and a parallel taxiway and apron were visible, along with a number of new buildings.”
The airport was built on the site of an airfield known as Lima Site 44, one of a network of airstrips that were used by the U.S. military and Central Intelligence Agency during the Vietnam War, when the U.S. secretly supported an insurgency by anti-communist Hmong rebels. However, satellite images show that the new airfield expands far beyond the narrow, red-earthed strip established during the Vietnam War.
The new center adds to the handful of overseas facilities now operated by the PLA, since the opening of its first official overseas military base in Djibouti in 2017. It also complements a similar training and logistics facility that has been established at Cambodia’s Ream Naval Base on the Gulf of Thailand. The Cambodian facility was officially inaugurated by Prime Minister Hun Manet in April 2025, after three years of Chinese-funded refurbishments that include a 300-meter-long deep-water pier, a 5,000-ton dry dock, and a 1,000-ton slipway.
China’s involvement at Ream has attracted the suspicion of Western, and particularly American, security officials, who fear that the base may evolve into a full-blown Chinese base. Cambodia has sought to allay these fears by inviting foreign navies, including those of Japan, Vietnam, and the U.S., to visit the base.
Collin Koh, a scholar at the S. Rajaratnam School of International Studies in Singapore, said in a post on X that unlike Ream, the base in Laos is “more ostensibly similar to the one in Djibouti.” He added, “It may not be wrong to conclude this is the first full-fledged PLA overseas base in Southeast Asia.”
The development at Ban Keun is perhaps unsurprising given the rapid expansion of China’s influence in Laos over the past 15 years. During that time, the north of the country has become economically fused to southern China, as new highways and an impressive China-built railway have improved overland connections. The Chinese investment presence is clearly visible in most parts of the country, and there is a large Chinese expatriate community in Vientiane and the provincial towns of northern Laos.
Defense relations have proceeded more slowly, perhaps due to the sensitivities of Vietnam, Laos’ traditional defense patron, which has had close ties with Laos dating back to the communist struggle of the 1960s and 1970s. In June, however, Lao President Thongloun Sisoulith visited Beijing for meetings with Chinese President Xi Jinping, during which the two leaders agreed to enhance defense cooperation.
Xi also suggested that China and Laos should establish a “3+3” strategic dialogue mechanism involving their foreign, defense, and public security ministers, “as an opportunity to strengthen law enforcement and security cooperation and crack down on cross-border crimes.” (A similar mechanism was established with Cambodia earlier this year.) Last month, Beijing and Vientiane also concluded “Peace Train 2026,” a 16-day joint military exercise aimed at “humanitarian assistance and military medical services.”
One Chinese security analyst told the state-run Global Times that the base at Ban Keun was a means of providing the Lao People’s Liberation Army Air Force, which operates a small and obsolescent fleet of Chinese and Russian craft, with a “systematic training system for pilots, maintenance crew and flight personnel” that will reduce its reliance on overseas training. More broadly, the analyst said, the facility will deepen “practical exchanges” between the two militaries, “upgrading from simple equipment assistance to long-term integrated cooperation in talent training, joint exercises and equipment support.”
Perhaps most tellingly, the analyst drew an explicit parallel between Ban Keun and the facility at Ream Naval Base, noting that together they “cover inland airspace in the Indochina Peninsula and the maritime direction in the Gulf of Thailand.”
In both cases, the Chinese military has emphasized that the facilities have been established on the basis of “mutual respect” and are not directed at any
Nonetheless, the Ban Keun facility has the potential to alter the strategic map of mainland Southeast Asia, pulling Laos and Cambodia further out of the Vietnamese sphere of influence.
Nguyen Khac Giang, a visiting fellow at the ISEAS-Yusof Ishak Institute in Singapore, told Bloomberg that in light of the recent expansion of China’s military presence in Cambodia and the South China Sea, Vietnam in particular could have “serious grounds for concern” if the Ban Keun facility becomes a foothold for a more permanent PLA presence in Laos.
“These developments could give Beijing greater leverage over strategic access routes around Vietnam, raising concerns about its ability to monitor, and potentially constrain, Vietnam’s room for maneuver in time of crisis,” Giang told the newspaper. “Much depends on how the facility is used.”
Vietnam has not yet officially commented on the opening of the new facilities in Laos.

articles.title: Amnesty Report Documents Morocco's Sustained Spyware Campaign Against Civil Society
articles.body:
Amnesty International has released a new report showing how, despite official denials, Moroccan authorities used surveillance spyware against civil society between 2017 and 2021, and possibly continued to use it later.
The rights watchdog’s report, titled “We start with the verdict”: Inside Morocco’s surveillance machine, details how the government deployed Israeli firm NSO Group’s Pegasus spyware to target civil society figures both domestically and abroad in what Amnesty described as “unlawful surveillance attacks.”
“The report presents extensive technical and forensic evidence confirming the DGST acquisition of Pegasus, confirms that civil society members were the primary target of Morocco from the very beginning of their Pegasus use in 2017,” Donncha Ó Cearbhaill, leader of the Security Lab told OCCRP.
According to the findings, the government's deployment of Pegasus evolved in tandem with the technological development in the spyware. Amnesty documented the use of sophisticated attack vectors, ranging from “one-click” phishing links requiring user interaction to advanced “zero-click” exploits capable of compromising devices without any action from the target.
While Pegasus represents the most technically advanced system documented in the report, Amnesty emphasized that it is merely one of the “digital tool[s] among many in Morocco’s repressive surveillance ecosystem.”
The report traces the government's use of digital espionage tools over two decades, citing the mass surveillance system Eagle, acquired in the early 2010s from French firm Amesys; the Remote Control System (RCS) spyware from Italian vendor Hacking Team, used in 2012 against journalists with the citizen media group Mamfakinch; and FinSpy software developed by the Anglo-German company Gamma Group and FinFisher.
As early as 2012, “Morocco was among the first countries where activists and journalists were found to be targeted with advanced spyware tools,” Amnesty said.
The Moroccan government has not responded to OCCRP’s request for comment.
Evidence suggests that national security agencies purchased these spyware systems even earlier. In 2015, emails included in a major leak from Hacking Team revealed that two Moroccan
security agencies, the internal intelligence service, the Direction Générale de la Surveillance du Territoire (DGST) and the National Defence Secrets Committee (CSDN) had contracted with Hacking Team since at least 2009. The records also show that the DGST was licensed to infect up to 2,000 devices, with support for Windows, Mac and mobile devices.
An OCCRP investigation published in July in collaboration with the Paris-based nonprofit Forbidden Stories revealed new evidence of Morocco’s secret service’s use of surveillance technology, particularly how the internal intelligence service DGST were using Pegasus and other surveillance tools to spy on activists.
A whistleblower who worked inside Morocco’s secret services added new evidence to the allegation that the government was behind the spying on a journalist, shedding light on the inner workings of state-backed surveillance operations and how the tool was used. His account was corroborated by other sources with knowledge of Moroccan intelligence operations, and documents.
According to the whistleblower, Moroccan intelligence agents utilized a private intermediary firm to contract with NSO Group, the Israeli cyber-intelligence company that created Pegasus. This arrangement was designed to shield the state from leaving a paper trail directly linking it to NSO Group or the spyware.
The latest evidence stems from a multi-year investigation led by Moroccan journalist Hicham Mansouri, whose own device was infected with Pegasus. Mansouri partnered with Forbidden Stories, the newsroom dedicated to continuing the work of threatened, silenced, or imprisoned journalists. Forbidden Stories organized a media collaboration titled "Pegasus Project: Inside the Moroccan Spying Machine," bringing together 39 journalists across 14 media outlets.
Amnesty’s report builds on this and the 2021 Pegasus Project, a global investigation involving 17 media organizations and coordinated by Forbidden Stories. The landmark reporting revealed that the spyware had been systematically deployed worldwide against journalists, human rights activists, and politicians.
Despite the increasing evidence presented in these publications, the Moroccan government responded to the July reporting with a familiar pattern of denials. Pro-government Moroccan media outlets launched a campaign of disinformation, dismissing the reports as based on “an unverifiable anonymous source, flimsy documentary evidence, and a persistent confusion between technical detection and state attribution.”
The pro-government website Al Barlamane similarly dismissed the investigation as incitement seeking to undermine relations between Morocco and France, stating that the report was published at a time when relations between Rabat and Paris were “undergoing a period of restructuring following successive signs of rapprochement.”
A third website, Le 360, again labelled the evidence as “very fragile,” claiming that the provided evidence was “aggregated under the same biased and politically assumed narrative.”
Corroborating data published in the July investigation, Amnesty’s latest report presents technical evidence that an NSO Group VPN server was deployed within Morocco’s DGST IP range in September 2017. This timeline aligns with earlier testimony and technical leaks from the Pegasus Project that showed DGST officers testing the system on their own phone numbers that same month.
Furthermore, the report says that the Apple iCloud accounts used to target Spanish ministers were the same as those used to target journalist Hicham Mansouri and Claude Mangin, the partner of Naama Asfari, a Sahraoui activist who is imprisoned in Morocco. Since NSO assigns accounts exclusively to single customers, Morocco is the only plausible operator, said Amnesty.
“The forensic evidence and analysis [presented in the report] allows for the high-confidence attribution of Pegasus attacks against Hicham Mansouri and other French-based civil society, the targeting of French and Spanish politicians, and Western Sahara activists as all have been carried out by Morocco's Pegasus system,” said Amnesty's Ó Cearbhaill.

articles.title: Satellite imagery reveals suspected hideout for ultra-secret Losharik submersible at Russian deep-sea research base
articles.body:
A researcher at the Foreign Policy Research Institute analyzed satellite and declassified intelligence imagery of a base on the Kola Peninsula belonging to the Russian Defense Ministry’s Main Directorate for Deep Sea Research (GUGI). He identified a deep-sea vehicle that appeared to be a Losharik submersible vehicle being towed toward specialized covered docks. According to the researcher, the structures are used to shield secret Russian submarines from satellite surveillance.
A Planet Labs image taken last year shows two tugboats moving an underwater vehicle roughly 70 meters long — about the same length as the AS-31 Losharik nuclear-powered deep-sea station. The researcher notes that the vehicle rarely appears in satellite imagery from the Olenya Guba area, where the base is located, suggesting it typically stays under the docks’ canopies.
GUGI and Losharik
GUGI handles deep-sea operations that include seabed mapping, underwater rescue work, and activities related to underwater infrastructure. It has deep-sea vehicles at its disposal, as well as larger carrier submarines to deliver them to operation sites. The reconnaissance ship Yantar also makes regular visits to Olenya Guba.
Losharik is one of Russia’s most secretive nuclear-powered deep-sea vessels and one of GUGI’s key vehicles for seabed operations. Available estimates suggest it can operate at depths of over 1,000 meters, allowing it to be used for exploring and potentially tampering with underwater infrastructure, including communication cables. To reach an operation area, Losharik can employ specialized carrier submarines, including the Podmoskovye. The study’s authors call it Russia’s most advanced vehicle for seabed operations and believe that in the event of a conflict between Russia and NATO, the Losharik could play an important role in actions against critical underwater infrastructure.
What the images show
Having examined Cold War-era American intelligence imagery, images from the French SPOT satellite system, and recent commercial satellite imagery, the study’s author concluded that specialized shelters for deep-sea vehicles appeared in Olenya Guba as early as September 1991. A ground-level photograph near one of these floating docks also shows a Project 1910 Kashalot deep-sea submarine belonging to GUGI. The researcher calls the appearance of these structures the earliest reliable visual evidence of GUGI’s presence at this base.
Since then, the base’s infrastructure has not expanded significantly, though the capabilities of the forces stationed there have grown. Besides the Yantar, GUGI carrier submarines can be seen at Olenya Guba, including the Podmoskovye, designed to transport deep-sea vehicles.
The study comes amid reports of GUGI activity near critical underwater infrastructure belonging to NATO countries. In April, UK Defence Secretary John Healey stated that British forces, together with Norway and other allies, tracked a Russian attack submarine, two special-purpose submarines, and the Yantar near undersea cables and pipelines.
Reuters later reported that the U.S. helped drive off Russian special-purpose submarines that were allegedly conducting a covert operation using technology designed to disable undersea cables. No visible signs of tampering were found after the incident.

articles.title: UN Member States weigh latest Security Council veto, this time on Iran
articles.body:
UN Member States weigh latest Security Council veto, this time on Iran
The General Assembly met on Thursday to examine the Security Council’s latest veto, cast by China and Russia over a United States-backed sanctions panel of experts on Iran nuclear facilities.
What you need to know
- The right to use a veto is held by permanent Security Council members – China, France, Russia, United Kingdom and United States – whereby if any votes against a resolution or decision, it automatically fails
- Council vetoes wielded over the past few years have included multiple resolutions for a ceasefire in Gaza and to end the war triggered by US and Israeli strikes on Iran in February
- The veto initiative – established in 2022 – requires the General Assembly to meet within 10 working days of any veto in the Security Council
‘Poster child’ for global gridlock
Many nations have called for removing or limiting veto power in the Council, but reform of the 15-member organ remains a work in progress.
At last year’s annual veto debate, then-General Assembly president Annalena Baerbock called repeated veto use a “poster child” for global gridlock.
Thursday’s debate was triggered by the assembly’s landmark veto initiative, established in 2022.
No substitute for action
Khalilur Rahman, president of the assembly’s 81st session, said the veto initiative “cannot substitute for effective Security Council action”.
Each invocation of the initiative “highlights both the value of this mechanism and the circumstances that make it necessary” and affirms the assembly’s complementary role, ensuring that veto use is accompanied by transparency, explanation and consideration by the wider membership.
While the initiative does not override the veto, it guarantees a public and accountable debate on each use and its implications in the General Assembly, where there is no veto power.
Watch the meeting on UN Web TV:
Divergent views
During the debate, Deputy Permanent Representative Sun Lei of China said that his delegation voted against the draft resolution to “uphold a correct sense of right and wrong”.
The current impasse on the sanctions panel arises from the United States’ unilateral withdrawal from the Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action on Iran’s nuclear facilities – the Iran nuclear deal of 2015 – its campaign of “maximum pressure” and its “two rounds of strikes against Iran in the midst of negotiations”.
Meanwhile, other delegates argued for extending the panel’s mandate.
“No UN Member State should prevent the UN Security Council from functioning properly and being fully operational,” said Hedda Samson, Deputy Head of the European Union delegation, noting that the need for a panel of experts is “even great today”.
Next step? Delivering
Following Thursday’s debate, the assembly president will send a summary of discussions back to the Security Council.
At the outset of the meeting, Mr. Rahman said the assembly and the council “serve humanity best when they operate in balance”, each fulfilling its distinct but complementary responsibilities under the UN Charter.
“Let us, therefore, use this debate not to exacerbate tensions or assign blame, but to clarify positions, identify common ground for constructive solutions and chart a credible path forward to support dialogue and diplomacy and ultimately restore trust in the organization and its ability to deliver,” he said.

articles.title: Gaza documentary NAZA tops Italian box office, beats Avengers
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Gaza documentary NAZA tops Italian box office ahead of 'Avengers Endgame: Encore'
Award-winning Gaza documentary NAZA, directed by Israeli filmmakers Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, has beaten Avengers Endgame: Encore to top the Italian box office at number one.
The documentary, which examines the mass killing of Palestinian civilians in Gaza through testimonies from Israeli military and intelligence personnel, topped the Italian box office during its first two days in cinemas.
Its debut marked its first theatrical release following its premiere at the Venice Film Festival, with ticket sales reaching nearly €1.1 million ($1.24 million) by Tuesday, according to Italian box office tracker Cinetel.
Meanwhile, Avengers Endgame: Encore, an extended re-release of the 2019 Marvel film, grossed €356,000 ($404,000) over the same period in Italy.
NAZA was initially released as a three-day cinema event across 515 cinemas in Italy, with many screenings selling out.
However, strong demand has led to screenings continuing beyond the initial run.
More than 150 cinemas have extended the film’s programming, according to The Guardian, which produced the documentary, with further extensions expected.
Interest in Italy was already high ahead of the film’s release after it won the Special Jury Prize at the Venice Film Festival earlier this month, with a premiere that was followed by a 25-minute standing ovation, a festival record.
NAZA features testimony from 24 Israeli military and intelligence personnel whose identities, voices and appearances were digitally altered for allegedly for their protection.
The interviews were conducted over three years and focus on the use of AI-powered surveillance and targeting systems in Gaza, including how targets were identified and struck despite expected civilian casualties.
According to reports about the documentary, some of those interviewed describe witnessing Palestinian civilians being killed and residential areas used as shelters being set ablaze.
The film’s title is derived from an acronym used by Israel’s intelligence service to indicate the number of civilians expected to die in an airstrike, according to The Guardian.
The documentary has faced significant backlash from senior Israeli officials since its Venice win.
Israeli Culture Minister Miki Zohar called for Abraham and Szor to have their citizenship revoked, accusing them of “treason against the state”.
“I will act immediately to revoke the Israeli citizenship of these despicable creators for treason against the state,” Zohar posted on X.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu subsequently said he would pursue legislation allowing citizenship to be revoked in cases involving people who "defame" Israeli soldiers abroad.
Netanyahu also proposed a second bill that would increase damages in defamation cases involving the Israeli military or state.
Simiarly, Israeli military chief Eyal Zamir said the military was examining possible legal measures over the film.
Israeli media subsequently reported that the military was considering a leak investigation and seeking assistance from the Shin Bet.
Abraham and Szor were among the co-directors of the 2025 Oscar-winning documentary No Other Land, which focused on Israeli settler violence and the destruction of Palestinian villages in the occupied West Bank.

articles.title: Russian Drone Attacks Kyiv Institute for Nuclear Research
articles.body:
A Russian drone struck the grounds of Kyiv Institute for Nuclear Research of the National Academy of Sciences of Ukraine.
The State Nuclear Regulatory Inspectorate of Ukraine reported that the attack occurred on September 30.
The attack caused a fire, which has been extinguished. There were no casualties. An investigation and assessment of the damage are underway. The VVR-M research nuclear reactor is located on the institute’s grounds.
“The reactor itself and the safety-critical systems were not damaged. No changes in the radiation background have been recorded; its levels remain within the natural background range (0.16–0.20 μSv/h) and have not changed,” the statement reads.
The State Nuclear Regulatory Inspectorate of Ukraine noted that to reduce radiation risks, the reactor has been shut down since February 2022, with the core fully unloaded.
Its operation is limited to routine maintenance of safety-critical systems.
Kyiv Institute for Nuclear Research of the National Academy of Sciences of Ukraine is a leading research institution in the fields of nuclear physics, nuclear energy, and radioecology. The VVR-M nuclear reactor is used as a neutron source for fundamental and applied research in nuclear physics.
The State Nuclear Regulatory Inspectorate of Ukraine described the UAV strike on the territory of Kyiv Institute for Nuclear Research as “an attack on a peaceful nuclear facility that serves exclusively scientific and research purposes, and represents yet another cynical disregard by Russia for internationally recognized principles and standards of nuclear and radiation safety, as well as a war crime.”
This is not the first Russian attack on critical facilities. Last year, a Russian strike drone carrying a high-explosive warhead struck the shelter of the number 4 reactor unit at the Chernobyl Nuclear Power Plant.

articles.title: Hegseth military cuts fuel fears of Trump loyalty purge
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Hegseth military cuts fuel fears of Trump loyalty purge
US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has announced a 20 percent cut to the number of generals and admirals in the US military, intensifying concerns that the Trump administration is reshaping the armed forces around its political and ideological agenda.
Hegseth portrayed the cuts as an exercise in "accountability", suggesting that officers who failed to embrace his drive to purge what he calls "woke" policies from the military had been removed.
"The number-crunchers say we fired 10 percent of the generals and admirals across the force," Hegseth told troops at the Quantico military base on Wednesday.
"We've also reduced the overall number of general officer slots by an additional 10 percent."
"So yes, 20 percent reduction across the board," he added. "The media calls that a purge. I call it accountability, and long overdue."
The announcement comes amid mounting concerns among Democratic lawmakers and some current and former military officials that the Trump administration is eroding the traditionally non-partisan character of the US armed forces and making adherence to its political agenda increasingly important for senior officers.
Since returning to office last year, President Donald Trump and Hegseth have removed a succession of senior military leaders, often without publicly explaining the reasons for their dismissal.
They include former chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff General Charles "CQ" Brown, who Trump fired without explanation in February 2025, as well as the heads of the US Army, Navy and Coast Guard, the general who headed the National Security Agency, the vice chief of staff of the US Air Force, a Navy admiral assigned to NATO and three senior military lawyers.
Hegseth has also fired or blocked the promotions of scores of generals and admirals during his tenure, according to US media reports.
The upheaval has prompted warnings from some former senior officers about the potential creation of a loyalty culture within the military.
H.R. McMaster, a retired Army general who served as Trump's national security adviser during his first term, recently warned against creating "a climate in which everything's a loyalty test".
Hegseth rejects accusations that the changes amount to a political purge, insisting that Trump is entitled to select the military leadership he wants and that his reforms are intended to restore an apolitical force focused on combat effectiveness.
In Wednesday's address, however, he explicitly linked the fate of senior officers to their response to his previous efforts to reshape military culture.
Hegseth said officers who "responded positively" to a speech he delivered to senior commanders last year were now "leading newly focused and newly empowered and disciplined formations", while those who did not "no longer work here".
"We are no longer the woke department, or the weak department," Hegseth said.
"Simple translation of that: no fatties, no trannies, no beardos, no weirdos, no wimps, no radicals. Just warriors -- just tough, ready, committed troops."
Hegseth ordered major cuts to the military leadership in May 2025, including a 10-percent reduction in the overall number of generals and admirals and a 20-percent cut to the highest four-star ranks.
During his confirmation hearing in January 2025, Hegseth argued that the Pentagon bureaucracy was top-heavy and that resources should instead be directed towards combat capabilities.
"It's going to be my job, working with those that we hire and those inside the administration, to identify those places where fat can be cut, so it can go toward lethality," he told lawmakers.
His campaign has extended beyond the military's senior ranks. The Pentagon has dismantled diversity programmes and Hegseth this week moved to end tenure for future civilian faculty at US military academies, saying the institutions should refocus on their "warfighting" mission.
Critics argue that the combination of ideological changes and unexplained dismissals risks encouraging officers to tailor their conduct to the political preferences of the administration.
Hegseth, meanwhile, has cast the changes as necessary to reverse what he regards as years of misplaced priorities at the Pentagon.
"The media calls that a purge," he said on Wednesday. "I call it accountability."

articles.title: Syria denies holding secret talks with Hezbollah in Turkey
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Turkey and Syria deny report of secret talks with Hezbollah
Turkey and Syria have denied a Reuters report that Syrian government officials and representatives of the Hezbollah militant group held secret talks in Turkey to try to ease tensions between them.
The Turkish presidency on Thursday rejected the report as baseless, while Syria also denied that such a meeting took place. The Reuters report, citing six sources briefed on what it described as the first known meeting between the longtime foes, said the Syrian officials and Hezbollah representatives had met secretly at least once last month.
"The claims circulating in some international media outlets and social media platforms to the effect that "Syrian government officials and Hezbollah executives met in Turkey under the auspices of the MİT" are entirely baseless," Turkey’s Presidential Communications Directorate’s Center for Combating Disinformation said in a post on X.
It added that "the allegations regarding the date, location, content, and topics of discussion featured in these posts do not reflect any reality whatsoever and are completely fictional and speculative in nature".
In a post on its official English-language account for its Foreign Media Department on X, Syria Response, the Syrian Information Ministry also wrote: "These claims are false. No such meeting took place".
Hezbollah for years dispatched fighters to Syria to support former dictator Bashar al-Assad’s regime during the country’s civil war.
After Assad was ousted in late 2024 in a lightning rebel offensive, tensions rose between Syria’s new government and Hezbollah, with Damascus accusing the group of transferring arms through Syria, and the United States encouraging Syria’s military to send forces into Lebanon to fight Hezbollah.
According to the Reuters report, last month’s meeting involved Hezbollah representatives and Syrian intelligence and foreign ministry officials and took place at the invitation of Turkish security and intelligence agencies in an effort to de-escalate, the six sources said.
All the sources spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss the sensitive meeting, which has not been previously reported.
Syria’s Foreign Ministry, Turkey’s foreign and defence ministries and the US State Department did not immediately respond to Reuters' questions about the meeting. Hezbollah’s media office declined to comment.
Mutual security concerns
The meeting focused on resolving points of tension between the two parties and went well, according to the US official, the Syrian officials and the Lebanese source.
One of the Syrian officials said both sides agreed they held no hostility towards one another, and that Syria assured Hezbollah that it would not intervene militarily in Lebanon to disarm the group.
In turn, Syrian officials asked Hezbollah to help stop cross-border smuggling attempts and dismantle its remaining sleeper cells, particularly in southern Syria, the official said.
Syria said on Tuesday it had captured a Hezbollah cell preparing to launch rockets in southern Syria. Hezbollah denied on Wednesday that it was involved and said it "has no presence whatsoever on Syrian territory and has no involvement in any security or military activity there".
The Syrian official said Hezbollah’s representatives had not given a direct answer on the request to halt arms smuggling and dismantle its Syria-based cells, but did pledge not to interfere in Syria’s affairs.
The Lebanese source, who has direct knowledge of the reported meeting and its outcomes, said the two sides "made a lot of progress on security issues".
"Hezbollah wants to protect its flank," the source said, referring to concerns about a Syrian attack on the group within Lebanon.
Both the Syrian official and the Lebanese source said no final agreement had been reached and that no announcement had been planned.
The Lebanese source told Reuters that contact between the two parties via Turkey had begun about two months ago. Reuters could not confirm where in Turkey the September meeting was held, how long it lasted or whether other meetings had been held before or since.
Turkey pushed for meeting, Iran absent
Both Hezbollah and Syria’s government had previously signalled they would be open to speaking to one another.
In July, Syrian Foreign Minister Asaad al-Shaibani said Damascus was open to meeting the group. A month later, Hezbollah chief Naim Qassem said in a televised address that the group had no objection to meeting Syria’s leadership.
Both Lebanon and Syria have territories occupied by Israel, and face near-daily strikes by the Israeli army.
Ankara portrays itself as a key regional stakeholder in rebuilding and stabilising Syria. Under President Tayyip Erdogan, it has also sought to position itself as a facilitator of regional dialogue and is keen to boost stability in the region.
Three of the sources said it was Turkey, a key ally of Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa, that pushed for the meeting as it was keen to be directly involved in those efforts.
Absent from the reported meeting, however, was Hezbollah’s main sponsor, Iran.
The Lebanese security source claimed that Hezbollah attended the meeting with Iran’s knowledge, but said Tehran was disappointed that it was not a direct participant and that Sharaa had rebuffed any notion of direct ties to Iran for now.
That disappointment was the main reason that no final agreement was reached and no announcement about the reported meeting was made, the source said.
(Reuters, The New Arab)

articles.title: By Putin’s own estimate, Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries have cost Russia 1% of GDP. But he says stopping them isn’t worth halting attacks on Ukrainian vessels.
articles.body:
By Putin’s own estimate, Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries have cost Russia 1% of GDP. But he says stopping them isn’t worth halting attacks on Ukrainian vessels.
Russian President Vladimir Putin rejected the idea of halting attacks on Ukrainian ships in exchange for Ukraine ending its strikes on Russian oil refineries. He made the remarks at the Valdai Forum.
Putin estimated Russia’s losses from the refinery strikes at 1% of GDP. He said Russia has enough diesel to meet its own needs, but sanctions would keep any surplus off the global market — even if Ukraine stopped the strikes.
“How is our diesel supposed to reach the global market with sanctions still in place? It can’t. And in return for that, we would have to stop striking targets important to their economy. You have to admit, that just looks absurd,” Putin said.
Putin also said Russia had begun striking targets important to Ukraine’s economy in response to the refinery attacks. He said the strikes had inflicted significant damage on Ukraine. In particular, he said, the country now has “virtually no metals industry.”
In recent weeks, U.S. President Donald Trump has repeatedly urged Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky to stop striking Russian oil refineries. Trump has linked rising diesel prices to the war between Russia and Ukraine. He said Zelensky responded to his most recent request by saying, “Maybe we’ll do that.”
In mid-September, Trump said Russia and Ukraine had agreed to halt strikes on energy facilities. That claim was not confirmed. Russian presidential spokesman Dmitry Peskov, however, called the idea “good.”

articles.title: Lithuania Ready to Pay for Permanent U.S. Troop Presence in Country
articles.body:
Lithuania is ready to pay for the permanent deployment of U.S. troops on its territory.
Lithuanian Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevičius said this in an interview with Bloomberg.
The country is ready to build the necessary infrastructure and provide U.S. troops with suitable conditions.
The United States currently deploys troops to Lithuania on a rotational basis. U.S. units regularly arrive in the country, and their presence has been continuous since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
About 1,000 U.S. servicemen are expected to arrive in Lithuania at the end of October. They will remain in the country for nine months.
At the same time, the future of the U.S. military presence in Europe remains uncertain.
The Pentagon is conducting a six-month review of the deployment of U.S. troops in Europe and considering various options for their future deployment.
Allies are concerned about a possible reduction in the U.S. troop presence.
NATO Supreme Allied Commander Europe Alexus Grynkewich said that the United States would continue to support the Alliance but could provide ‘critical but more limited capabilities’ going forward.
Lithuania previously said it was ready to host up to 1,500 U.S. troops. Overall, Lithuania and Poland are interested in maintaining and strengthening a permanent U.S. military presence in Eastern Europe.
Against this backdrop, a new rotation of U.S. troops is heading to Lithuania, while Poland is ready to pay for the deployment of U.S. troops on its territory. The United States has been deploying battalion units in Lithuania since 2019.
At the same time, Poland also wants to establish a permanent U.S. military base on its territory. Polish Deputy Minister of National Defence Paweł Zalewski said Warsaw is ready to pay $15,000 per year for each U.S. service member and cover the costs of the necessary infrastructure.

articles.title: Syrian officials and Hezbollah held secret talks in Turkey
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Syrian government officials and Hezbollah held secret talks in Turkey
Representatives of the Syrian government and Lebanese Hezbollah have held face-to-face talks in Turkey to try to calm tensions between them, according to six sources briefed on the first known meeting between the longtime foes.
The Syrian officials and the Iran-aligned group met secretly at least once last month, the sources—who include two Syrian officials, a US official and a senior Lebanese security source close to Hezbollah—told Reuters.
Hezbollah for years dispatched fighters to Syria to support former dictator Bashar al-Assad's regime during the country's civil war.
After Assad was ousted in late 2024 in a lightning rebel offensive, tensions rose between Syria's new government and Hezbollah—with Damascus accusing the group of transferring arms through Syria, and the United States encouraging Syria's military to send forces into Lebanon to fight Hezbollah.
Last month's meeting involved Hezbollah representatives and Syrian intelligence and foreign ministry officials, and took place at the invitation of Turkish security and intelligence agencies in an effort to de-escalate, the six sources said.
All the sources spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss the sensitive meeting, which has not been previously reported.
Syria's foreign ministry, Turkey's foreign and defense ministries and the US State Department did not immediately respond to Reuters' questions about the meeting. Hezbollah's media office declined to comment.
Mutual security concerns
The meeting focused on resolving points of tension between the two parties and went well, according to the US official, the Syrian officials and the Lebanese source.
One of the Syrian officials said both sides agreed they held no hostility towards one another, and that Syria assured Hezbollah that it would not intervene militarily in Lebanon to disarm the group.
In turn, Syrian officials asked Hezbollah to help stop cross-border smuggling attempts and dismantle its remaining sleeper cells, particularly in southern Syria, the official said.
Syria said on Tuesday it had captured a Hezbollah cell preparing to launch rockets in southern Syria. Hezbollah denied on Wednesday that it was involved and said it "has no presence whatsoever on Syrian territory and has no involvement in any security or military activity there."
The Syrian official said Hezbollah's representatives had not given a direct answer on the request to halt arms smuggling and dismantle its Syria-based cells, but did pledge not to interfere in Syria's affairs.
The Lebanese source, who has direct knowledge of the meeting and its outcomes, said the two sides "made a lot of progress on security issues."
"Hezbollah wants to protect its flank," the source said, referring to concerns about a Syrian attack on the group within Lebanon.
Both the Syrian official and the Lebanese source said no final agreement had been reached and that no announcement had been planned.
The Lebanese source told Reuters that contact between the two parties via Turkey had begun about two months ago.
Reuters could not confirm where in Turkey the September meeting was held, how long it lasted and whether other meetings had been held before or since.
Turkey pushed for meeting, Iran absent
Both Hezbollah and Syria's government had signalled they would be open to speaking to one another.
In July, Syrian Foreign Minister Asaad al-Shaibani said Damascus was open to meeting the group. A month later, Hezbollah chief Naim Qassem said in a televised address that the group had no objection to meeting Syria's leadership.
Both Lebanon and Syria have territories occupied by Israel, and face near daily strikes by the Israeli army.
Ankara portrays itself as a key regional stakeholder in rebuilding and stabilising Syria. Under President Tayyip Erdogan, it has also sought to position itself as a facilitator of regional dialogue and is keen to boost stability in the region.
Three of the sources said it was Turkey, a key ally of Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa, that pushed for the meeting as it was keen to be directly involved in those efforts.
Absent from the meetings, however, was Hezbollah's main sponsor, Iran.
The Lebanese security source said Hezbollah attended the meeting with Iran's knowledge, but that Tehran was disappointed that it was not a direct participant and that Sharaa had rebuffed any notion of direct ties to Iran for now.
That disappointment was the main reason that no final agreement was reached and no announcement about the meeting was made, the source said.

articles.title: Beyond the Bunker: Lessons from Survivalist Architecture on Resilience
articles.body:
"Let us take a hard look at the facts." With this direct and hardly reassuring sentence, the director of the Office of Civil and Defense Mobilization opened The Family Fallout Shelter, a 32-page manual published by the U.S. government in 1959 amid Cold War tensions. The document taught families how to build shelters capable of protecting them from radioactive fallout after a possible nuclear attack and, through technical drawings and sketches, outlined solutions using concrete blocks, walls filled with earth or sand, underground structures, and ventilation systems. It was a survival manual that, in many ways, also functioned as a construction manual.
The logic of preparedness did not disappear with the end of the Cold War. Instead, it began responding to threats that were more diffuse and often more familiar: economic and energy crises, natural disasters, pandemics, prolonged disruptions to supply networks and infrastructure, and even speculative fears surrounding artificial intelligence, including scenarios in which autonomous systems could escape human control or even turn against humanity. Contemporary survivalism emerged in response to this wider range of risks, encompassing practices that range from keeping several days' worth of supplies on hand to seeking remote properties, adapting homes for greater autonomy, or, at the more extreme end, building bunkers and other fortified shelters.
This differs from the off-grid architecture we have previously explored, where water collection, energy generation, and sewage treatment must be resolved by the building itself. While off-grid architecture assumes a reduced or permanent dependence on certain networks, survivalism introduces another possibility: that networks normally taken for granted may stop functioning altogether.
Related Article
A Guide to Off-Grid Architectures
For Raphael Cozzi, founder of the Preppers Brasil community, preparedness does not necessarily begin with the expectation of an apocalyptic scenario, but with a simple question: "How long could I keep my family functioning normally if what is outside stopped working?" This can include prolonged power outages, flooding, or interruptions to the water supply, alongside economic crises, difficulties accessing food, and family emergencies. The goal, he explains, is to anticipate consequences rather than predict exactly what the next disaster will be.
Preppers, however, are far from a homogeneous group. Geographer Kezia Barker notes that the figure of the prepper is often ridiculed by the media and framed in pathologizing or dismissive ways. Her research places prepping within vulnerabilities that are already familiar, especially our dependence on infrastructure networks and the inequalities that shape who can or cannot rely on protection during a crisis. Supplies, tools, skills, and equipment can therefore form a kind of "parallel infrastructure," capable of taking over certain functions when conventional systems stop responding.
Once this parallel infrastructure outgrows a backpack or closet and begins to require dedicated space, technical systems, and construction solutions, survivalism becomes an architectural question. Unlike an off-grid house, designed to operate continuously with less dependence on conventional networks, survivalist architecture generally considers two possible states: everyday operation and the eventual interruption of those networks. For Cozzi, this possibility could be anticipated from the design stage, including "the possibility of the residence operating partially without the electrical grid."
When the House Becomes Infrastructure
These priorities begin to reshape the house itself. Cozzi places water at the top of the hierarchy: "We can go some time without electricity or with limited food, but water is an immediate necessity." Energy comes next, not necessarily to keep the entire house operating as if nothing had happened, but to "ensure essential functions: lighting, communication, charging equipment, preserving certain foods, and operating important devices."
Preparedness often starts small. Many people begin by storing water, food, medication, flashlights, and batteries. Then other questions emerge: where to store these resources, how to filter water, how to cook without electricity or gas, how to maintain communication, and which functions should have alternatives in case one system fails.
Cozzi summarizes much of this logic in one word: "redundancy." As he explains, "if I have only one way of obtaining water, I have a single point of failure." The same logic applies to energy, communication, and other essential functions.
"The organization of the house itself changes," he observes. "You begin to see the residence not simply as a property, but as an infrastructure that needs to continue providing certain basic functions even when some external services temporarily cease to exist."
Even so, the bunker occupies a much larger place in the popular imagination than it does in everyday preparedness. "It represents a very small portion of the prepper universe," Cozzi says. For him, a resilient home is a more useful reference than an underground fortress: an apparently conventional house can incorporate water reserves, alternative energy, storage, communication, and emergency equipment. Preparedness can also involve mobility, since remaining in the building will not always be the appropriate response. "Preparedness does not necessarily mean building a fortress. It means creating options."
Survivalism also has an escapist dimension. If many speculative architectures of the 20th century imagined other worlds in which it might be possible to live, certain forms of preparedness make an almost inverse move: they attempt to create a relatively autonomous world within the one that already exists. In this case, the alternative world is not on Mars, at the bottom of the ocean, or in virtual reality. It may instead be underground, in the countryside, or behind the walls of an apparently ordinary house. A remote property, a residence capable of operating for long periods without conventional networks, or, at the extreme, a bunker can reduce exposure to external instability. The goal is not always to abandon society. Still, there is a clear tension between autonomy and isolation: to what extent does becoming less dependent on collective systems also mean withdrawing from them?
Many of the qualities associated with preparedness-oriented architecture are already familiar to the discipline: durability, thermal insulation, weather tightness, resource efficiency, energy independence, repairability, and redundancy. Under extreme conditions, these characteristics are pushed to their limits, but many are also becoming relevant in the face of more severe climate events, power outages, or buildings located in remote areas.
Repairability matters too. Cozzi points to our growing dependence on complex systems that users can rarely repair themselves. In his view, more resilient architecture should consider solutions that can remain operational, even at reduced capacity, during an emergency, while also providing alternatives for certain critical functions from the design stage onward.
The same questions apply well beyond bunkers. As materials and technologies expand what a building can produce, store, filter, and control on its own, autonomy and resilience are taking on a larger role in architectural design. Survivalism pushes this logic to an extreme, exposing dependencies that usually remain out of sight.
Cozzi reduces this principle to an almost banal question: "What if this stops working?" What if the power goes out? The water? Communications? What if the street becomes inaccessible? Asked during design, these are no longer exclusively prepper questions. They are also questions about whether a building can continue providing basic conditions when the systems around it fail.
If, in 1959, The Family Fallout Shelter asked readers to "take a hard look at the facts," it was responding to a threat that was easier to identify and name. Today, risk is more diffuse, shaped by forecasts, misinformation, alarmism, and competing interpretations of what may happen next. For architecture, predicting the next disruption may matter less than understanding how dependent buildings already are on systems beyond their walls. Water tanks, batteries, filters, stored supplies, backup systems, and other forms of redundancy make those dependencies visible. That may be the most useful architectural lesson of prepper culture.
This article is part of the ArchDaily Topic: The Lure of Escapism in Architecture and Alternative Worlds. Every month we explore a topic in-depth through articles, interviews, news, and architecture projects. We invite you to learn more about our ArchDaily Topics. And, as always, at ArchDaily we welcome the contributions of our readers; if you want to submit an article or project, contact us.

articles.title: Italian Army tests Ukrainian gun-armed robots in assault drill
articles.body:
- Ukrainian company DevDroid demonstrated its Droid TW 7.62 and Droid TW 12.7 combat ground robots during the Italian Army's AEGIS 26 exercise on Sept. 17.
- The robots worked alongside Italy's ULISSE UGV and were linked to a NATO situational awareness system, sharing positions and live video.
Ukrainian defense company DevDroid put two of its armed ground robots through their paces with the Italian Army during AEGIS 26, a major exercise watched by Italian President Sergio Mattarella, operating them alongside an Italian robot and infantry in a simulated assault and linking them to a NATO battlefield information system.
AEGIS 26 was held on Sept. 17 at the Monte Romano training area in Viterbo province, north of Rome. Mattarella attended with Defense Minister Guido Crosetto and Undersecretary of Defense Isabella Rauti, and was received by the Army’s chief of staff, Gen. Carmine Masiello.
About 850 soldiers took part, drawn from every unit of the Folgore Parachute Brigade along with the Acqui Division, special forces, army aviation, engineers, signals, air defense artillery and tactical intelligence units, with aircraft from the Italian Air Force. The Italian Army says the exercise tested its units’ ability to plan and run integrated tactical operations, including offensive maneuvers supported by remotely piloted systems, some of them built by soldiers themselves, for reconnaissance and attacks on defensive positions, along with artillery, anti-tank fire, cyber and electronic protection.
DevDroid brought its Droid TW 7.62 and Droid TW 12.7 unmanned ground vehicles, whose names refer to the caliber of the machine guns they carry. They operated alongside the ULISSE unmanned ground vehicle built by Italian company ABET HTS in a scenario that included artillery support, coordination between the robots and an infantry unit during an assault on enemy positions, evacuation of a casualty and a further advance.
The teams also connected the Ukrainian-made robots to a NATO situational awareness system, sending each vehicle’s position and live video into the network, and controlled them over a tactical military network. DevDroid says the robots worked with the Italian system and carried out joint tasks within a single scenario, and its specialists trained Italian soldiers on the controls and on how armed ground robots are used in combat.
The company said it shared lessons from the use of unmanned ground vehicles in Ukraine, where both sides now rely heavily on ground robots to carry supplies, evacuate wounded troops, lay mines and fire on enemy positions while keeping soldiers out of the line of fire.
“For us, it is important that Ukrainian robotic systems can operate alongside solutions developed by our European partners. Trials like these allow us to test platform interoperability in joint scenarios and move from technology demonstrations toward practical industrial cooperation. The next step is to deepen technological and manufacturing cooperation with our Italian partners,” DevDroid said in a statement.
The demonstration grew out of a partnership between DevDroid and ABET HTS. The two companies have signed a memorandum of cooperation and are preparing the documents for a joint venture, which they say would combine Ukraine’s battlefield experience with ground robots with the Italian company’s manufacturing and engineering capacity.

articles.title: Why the U.S. Must Simultaneously Compete—and Cooperate—With China on AI
articles.body:
Last week, President Donald Trump hosted Chinese President Xi Jinping at the White House. It's their second meeting this year, following the May summit in Beijing. This visit, the stakes were even higher.
We have learned about security incidents from nearly every major AI company, American and Chinese, built on both open and closed models. The leading AI labs are openly debating whether to pace their frontier model development, and the government is working out what role it plays in that decision.
I spent four years as Secretary of Commerce focused intently on America’s economic, technological, and security competition with China—instituting first-of-its-kind export controls on the sale of chips and chipmaking equipment to China to protect our national security, and leading implementation of the CHIPS Act to onshore chip manufacturing. I also created the AI Safety Institute so we could accelerate our AI development responsibly and safely. I have sat across the table from China, and I have an understanding of how they think about AI.
I believe AI companies are right to want to pace the frontier. But we need to stay ahead of China while we pace, because a world where China leads the global AI competition threatens America’s interests.
The challenge is this: We need to outcompete China on the technology itself, while also working with China on addressing the risks posed by AI. Competition and cooperation are often in tension, but the stakes are too high in this case to pick only one.
How we cooperate—while staying ahead
China has its own reasons to take AI safety seriously. The Chinese Minister of State Security recently said publicly that the greatest risk advanced AI poses to China is the risk it poses to the stability of the Chinese Communist Party (CCP). Beijing is no more interested in powerful AI systems wreaking socio-political havoc than Washington is; both countries have incentives to align on certain safety standards or even just a shared understanding of AI risks. It is in neither country’s interest for companies to lose control of their AI systems or for AI to be used to create bioweapons by rogue actors. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent’s announcement of a possible AI dialogue with Chinese counterparts after his meeting with Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng is a tangible sign that China sees at least some space for cooperation here.
I would argue that now is the moment to fully establish that dialogue and keep the momentum going. We should do this by convening experts from both countries. I’m well aware that we’d be foolish to trust People's Republic of China (PRC) leaders. But that doesn’t mean we shouldn’t try. It just means we need to develop verification mechanisms to ensure agreements work even in the absence of trust.
Even if we don’t reach agreement on a shared set of standards, starting a dialogue and opening those lines of communication are critical—just as we did in 2008 during the financial crisis, when it was in our mutual benefit to coordinate. And we spent decades during the Cold War in careful, ongoing dialogue with the Soviet Union about nuclear arms control because the risks to both countries were enormous. During that time we developed zero-trust methods to verify arms control agreements even while locked in an adversarial relationship.
None of that changes the need to vigilantly and continuously update our controls as technology changes so China can’t access our most sophisticated compute in ways that threaten our national security. That includes continuously updating our export controls on leading-edge chips, addressing the risks of China accessing controlled compute remotely in data centers around the world, and cracking down on diversion of technology that is controlled.
We also need to tighten remaining gaps in our semiconductor manufacturing equipment controls so China can less capably obtain tools to manufacture powerful chips at scale and service their pre-existing equipment. That work has to happen with our Dutch, Japanese, and German allies and partners who manufacture and service this chipmaking equipment.
American AI
Finally, the U.S. government should put a greater burden on the AI companies to take adversarial distillation much more seriously. Distillation—coordinated, industrial-scale efforts by AI labs to train their weaker models on the outputs of frontier models—has become a significant issue in the past year. Anthropic has attributed more than 16 million Claude exchanges to distillation campaigns, and has estimated that over 3 million of these distillation campaigns can be traced back to China’s Moonshot AI (the company behind China’s version of ChatGPT, Kimi) along with other Chinese AI labs like Alibaba and DeepSeek. Moonshot, for instance, was later caught forwarding user prompts to Claude to answer and feeding those answers back through Kimi.
China has certainly indigenized much of its AI stack, something Xi publicly made a priority in his Made in China 2025 plan, many years before the U.S. government was talking openly about chips or models. And China has made progress on this plan. But it is clear to many that China’s most competitive models, to some degree, are ripping off American ones. American AI labs should be allocating even greater amounts of their money and compute towards finding and exposing this kind of activity so that policymakers—and the public—can adapt accordingly.
The risks and benefits of AI are enormous, something more and more Americans have come to realize as AI advances more quickly than we previously thought possible. There is much to do on AI safety at home, to ensure our society and economy are resilient to the dramatic changes AI will bring. But I also know that safe deployment of AI is only possible if we successfully manage our relationship with China—both by maintaining our technological lead and working towards collaboration.

articles.title: Europe wants drones that actually work in war, so Ukrainian maker is moving in to build them in Belgium and Luxembourg
articles.body:
A Ukrainian drone maker is preparing to build unmanned systems in the heart of western Europe. TAF Industries and Luxembourg's LUXUAV have signed a memorandum to jointly develop, industrialize, and field weapons in Belgium and Luxembourg, under the Build with Ukraine initiative, TAF said.
The deal is part of Build with Ukraine, an initiative that enables Ukrainian arms manufacturers to take their operations to a new level by scaling up production beyond the country’s borders. This involves exporting Ukrainian military technologies to partner countries that support Ukraine financially and politically. In return, joint production lines will be established on their territory, according to Ukraine's Arms Council.
The deal targets the Benelux
The memorandum is a first step, TAF said, with joint work on autonomous systems in the two countries to follow. The aim is to move from signed intent to shared production lines and fielded drones.
TAF Industries, a Ukrainian unmanned-systems maker, and LUXUAV, a Luxembourg defense-tech firm, plan to develop, industrialize, and deploy drone solutions across Luxembourg and Belgium, pooling Ukraine's battlefield experience with European manufacturing muscle.
Build with Ukraine spreads west
TAF's chief executive, Volodymyr Zinovskyi, framed the memorandum as a way of "combining Ukrainian innovations, proven by war, with European industrial and technological capabilities," arguing that European security now depends on industry, states, and research working across borders.
Belgium has already contracted a Ukrainian producer to build drones and counter-drone systems on Belgian soil.
Europe wants the know-how
The timing fits Europe's new urgency. Russian drones have strayed into Polish, Romanian, and Moldovan skies in recent weeks, and member states scrambling to build defenses increasingly look to Ukraine, the one country fighting a mass drone war, for the technology and the lessons.
Earlier, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk warned of very difficult weeks and months ahead, “linked to Russia’s extremely aggressive stance toward Ukraine," according to TVP Info. As he emphasized, Polish security services were on heightened alert due to the situation along the country’s eastern border.

articles.title: Major General Nikitushkin, Responsible for Modernizing Tank Training Ranges, Arrested in Russia
articles.body:
In Russia, a military court remanded Major General Sergey Nikitushkin, head of the Training and Material Support Department of the Main Directorate for Combat Training of the Russian Armed Forces, into custody.
This was reported by the Russian newspapers Kommersant and The Moscow Times.
The high-ranking Russian military officer was arrested and sent to a pretrial detention center as part of a criminal case, the details of which have not yet been disclosed.
It is known that 51-year-old Nikitushkin was directly involved in the war against Ukraine.
The Russian officer was awarded the rank of major general by Vladimir Putin in December 2024.
According to the propaganda Telegram channel Mash, the Major General was responsible within the agency for the modernization of tank training grounds on the territory of the Russian Federation.
The Main Directorate for Combat Training of the Russian Armed Forces is responsible for training military personnel and coordinating the activities of military command structures.
This agency also oversees the development of training facilities and equipment and provides Russian troops with the necessary resources for training.
Previously, Nikitushkin complained about a lack of funding to purchase the training simulators for armored vehicle crews, communications specialists, UAV operators, and personnel using night-vision devices.
In addition, the Main Directorate for Combat Training oversees the “Patriot” fleet, where large-scale embezzlement had previously been uncovered.
In this case, former Deputy Minister of Defense, Army General Pavel Popov, and former Deputy Chief of the Main Directorate for Innovative Development of the Russian Ministry of Defense, Major General Vladimir Shesterov, have already been sentenced to prison terms.
In August, Yevgeny Grigoryev, the CEO of the TulaDrone Scientific and Production Center for Unmanned Aerial Systems, was detained in Russia.
