articles.title: Trump's Board of Peace: Can it deliver a future for Gaza?
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Trump's Board of Peace: Can it deliver a future for Gaza?
Khan Younis - Nearly a year after a ceasefire halted the heaviest fighting in Gaza, Palestinian analysts say the recovery plan unveiled last week by the US-led Board of Peace will not make any progress before Israelis vote on 27 October.
Its fate, they argue, will depend largely on the next Israeli government and the positions it takes on Gaza, and still faces a series of political and security obstacles before it can move from paper to the ground.
The Board presented the six-month, $2.45 billion program on 23 September on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York. It sets out 66 costed programs across six clusters: infrastructure, human development, economic acceleration, digital transformation, legal recovery, and peace and security.
Chaired by US President Donald Trump, the Board operates under a UN Security Council mandate adopted in November 2025. The program was drawn up under its supervision by the National Committee for the Administration of Gaza (NCAG), the Palestinian technocratic body meant to take over the Strip's daily affairs.
The plan hinges almost entirely on Hamas handing over its weapons and its control of Gaza to the new administration. Meanwhile, Israel's military still controls more than 60 percent of the territory.
Experts who spoke to The New Arab expect the plan to be amended and doubt it will be implemented in its current form or at the announced pace. Some believe its success depends on full Israeli approval.
Others describe it as a "major deception" intended to prolong Gaza's catastrophe and push its people to ask the world to let them emigrate.
Meanwhile, Nickolay Mladenov, the Board's high representative for Gaza, has described three possible paths for the Gaza Strip. The Palestinian territory could remain in its current state, Israel could expand its military operations and reoccupy it, or the parties could implement the Board's roadmap.
He warned that failure to move forward could make a two-state solution practically impossible.
Waiting for the Israeli elections
Israeli affairs expert Ismat Mansour argues that implementation of the plan is "definitively linked to the Israeli elections," saying Netanyahu is postponing major decisions until after the vote because he does not want to appear to have withdrawn from Gaza, eased pressure on Hamas, or ended the war without achieving what he can present as a victory before the election.
“Until then, Netanyahu will keep political options open,” he told The New Arab. “He is not allowing any concessions or even allowing the NCAG to intervene.”
Board officials describe a similar picture. Netanyahu largely cooperated with the Board for most of the past year, one Israeli official said, but stopped entirely about two months ago when the election campaign officially began.
Nickolay Mladenov, the Board's high representative for Gaza, acknowledged in New York that talks with Israel have been difficult during the campaign.
Abu Rahma agrees that the plan is heavily tied to the vote, because the current government treats Gaza as both a security file and a domestic political issue.
He warns, however, against assuming that a new government would transform the situation.
"It cannot be said that a change of government will automatically improve the situation in Gaza. A change could open a new political space, but it will not be sufficient on its own," he told The New Arab.
Much will depend on the composition of the next government and its positions on withdrawal, disarmament, Palestinian administration, an international presence, and reconstruction.
The opposition is led by former army chief Gadi Eisenkot, whose centrist Yashar party is running alongside the joint list of former prime ministers Naftali Bennett and Yair Lapid. A government led by Eisenkot or Bennett could open more room for the Board.
Such a government would be less dependent on settler and ultra-Orthodox partners. It would therefore likely find it easier to accept the full sequencing of the disarmament and reconstruction plan, including withdrawal to the original Yellow Line.
“The outcome of the election will determine the course ahead,” says Mansour. “Netanyahu is more hardline than Eisenkot, so what happens after the election will be crucial.”
A Jerusalem Post column argued that a new government would create an immediate opening for the Palestinian technocratic committee to take over civilian authority and for reconstruction to begin.
Mansour agrees with this position, seeing more room for change. A new Israeli government, he argues, could give the Palestinian Authority a broader role, explore ways to strengthen the Board if international forces cannot be secured, or draw on the Palestinian Authority's security capabilities in Gaza.
But so far, the outcome is far from certain. Israel faces a real possibility of a stalemate in the 27 October vote, which would complicate efforts to advance the recovery program even further.
The vote looks set to end in deadlock. Neither the bloc led by Netanyahu's Likud, which includes the far-right Religious Zionism and Otzma Yehudit (Jewish Power) parties and the ultra-Orthodox Shas and United Torah Judaism, nor the opposition, is close to the 61 seats needed to govern.
The Palestinian-majority parties could tip the balance, but a 23 September ban by Israel's Central Elections Committee, which voted to bar Ra'am and the Joint List from running, despite the attorney general's opposition to barring Ra'am. The Supreme Court, which has overturned similar bans before, must rule by 4 October.
Without their roughly 12 seats, the opposition's path to a majority narrows. Even with them, much of the Zionist opposition has ruled out governing with Palestinian parties, and Eisenkot has said Ra'am will not be part of his government.
For Netanyahu, the campaign leaves little room to show any flexibility on Gaza. His far-right partners have campaigned against any withdrawal from the Strip, any public sign he would reduce Israel's control there, or make concessions to Hamas, would likely cost him his voter base.
Hamas weapons or Israeli withdrawal first?
Hamas accepted the Board's disarmament plan on 30 July, but its implementation stalled after Israel rejected it. The plan linked disarmament to a phased Israeli withdrawal, while Netanyahu insists Hamas must give up its weapons before Israeli forces pull back.
In August, Netanyahu said Israeli forces would stay in their current positions until Hamas had fully disarmed. After meeting him, the Board hardened its position and tied any pullback beyond the Yellow Line to the complete decommissioning of light weapons, heavy weapons, and tunnels, dropping the phased approach it had presented days earlier.
Mansour says the election is the plan's main obstacle but not its only one. Other unresolved questions include how withdrawal and disarmament would be synchronised, how and when weapons would be collected, which areas Israel would leave, how Hamas would be removed from government, and when and where the Board would assume its responsibilities.
The Yellow Line itself has become part of the problem. It is the demarcation set by the October 2025 ceasefire as the position to which Israeli troops would initially withdraw. Israel's military has since confirmed that it controls 60 percent of Gaza, up from the 53 percent agreed in the ceasefire talks. In July, Israeli control had reached nearly 70 percent.
The International Crisis Group (ICG) said this month that Israeli forces are levelling neighbourhoods behind the line and enforcing it as a no-go zone as they push it toward the sea.
“I do not expect a complete or rapid Israeli withdrawal from the areas behind the Yellow Line without a binding US decision involving all parties and a clear political agreement on disarmament and security arrangements,” Abu Rahma says.
He also warns against a piecemeal approach, adding that continued reconstruction in some areas but not others would be a major problem, as it would create geographically fragmented reconstruction and make Gaza appear as if it consisted of multiple areas in terms of administration, security, and services.
"The most stable solution is for the Israeli withdrawal and reconstruction to take place as a synchronised and gradual process," he told The New Arab.
Board of Peace: A strategic deception
Academic and political analyst Talal Abu Rokba reads the plan very differently. He believes that "everything that is happening is an attempt to deceive the world into believing that solutions are coming for Gaza while Israel continues with its plans to displace its people".
The killing has indeed continued. Gaza's Health Ministry said on 26 September that 1,145 Palestinians had been killed since the ceasefire took effect, bringing the war's toll to around 74,000 killed and 175,000 wounded, although the unofficial death toll is thought to be much higher.
Speaking at the UN General Assembly on 24 September, Netanyahu rejected accusations that Israel had committed genocide in Gaza and ruled out Palestinian statehood under present conditions.
Mansour shares part of Abu Rokba's concern. He links the success of the recovery plan to Israel's intentions for Gaza's population, saying that "the displacement issue remains on the table and will remain so as long as the recovery phase does not genuinely begin".
Israel's defence minister has confirmed the government's intention to move large numbers of Palestinians out of Gaza "at the right time and in the right manner”.
“It’s like throwing dust in the eyes to cover up the ongoing genocide, a strategic deception carried out by the Board of Peace to sustain Israeli policy in Gaza,” says Abu Rukba.
He also argues that the Board was designed to meet Israel's core demand that Gaza should not come under any genuine Palestinian rule, with the Board and the technocratic committee serving as alternatives to the Palestinian statehood Netanyahu seeks to eliminate.
“Israel is not allowing the committee to operate. They meet with the Americans, Europeans and Arabs, issue statements, and are in contact with the UN and even officials in the Palestinian Authority, but they have no presence on the ground,” says Abu Rokba.
Mansour expects changes after the Israeli vote, and within the Palestinian Authority and its structures as well, including possible elections for the Palestinian Legislative Council.
Palestinian elections and any reconciliation within Fatah, he says, could change the course of Gaza as a whole, and could transform the recovery plan completely.
Mohamed Solaimane is a Gaza-based journalist with bylines in regional and international outlets, focusing on humanitarian and environmental issues
This piece is published in collaboration with Egab.
Edited by Charlie Hoyle

articles.title: Exclusive: Inside Lebanon's 200-page Israeli war crimes dossier
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Exclusive: Inside Lebanon's 200-page dossier on Israeli war crimes
A report obtained exclusively by The New Arab documents suspected Israeli war crimes and crimes against humanity during the latest war on Lebanon, detailing attacks on civilians, journalists, medical personnel and infrastructure, as well as widespread destruction and forced displacement.
The more than 200-page report, compiled by Lebanon's National Committee for International Humanitarian Law, was handed to Parliament Speaker Nabih Berri on Tuesday by Deputy Prime Minister Tarek Mitri, who heads the committee.
The findings come despite Lebanon agreeing to waive its right to pursue legal action against Israel over war crimes under a framework ceasefire agreement, with Article 13 of the agreement, signed in Washington on 26 June, requiring Lebanon to end "all hostile or harmful actions in international political or legal forums" against Israel.
According to information obtained exclusively by The New Arab, the report focuses on Israeli violations committed after 2 March 2026, placing them within the broader context of the conflict in Lebanon since 8 October 2023.
It examines numerous incidents classified by the committee as war crimes and crimes against humanity, supported by an independent evidence file containing screenshots, original links, statements from official bodies and human rights organisations, published photographs, maps, witness testimonies, press materials and other sources used to assess the incidents in accordance with international standards.
The report also outlines the methodology adopted by the National Committee for International Humanitarian Law to collect information and document and verify violations. It evaluates Israeli accounts of the incidents and provides legal assessments and analysis of the documented violations.
The violations examined include the destruction of infrastructure, bridges and crossings; attacks on cultural property, civilians, civil defence personnel, rescue teams, journalists and media workers; attacks on hospitals, health facilities and medical and humanitarian services; attacks on civilian property; and forced displacement.
The committee faced significant difficulties in compiling the report, particularly because the Lebanese authorities had not opened investigations into the crimes and therefore had no official investigative records. In many cases, the names of those killed were unavailable, with only casualty figures recorded.
The lack of cooperation from relevant ministries, which failed to provide the assistance required to complete the documentation, created further obstacles.
Despite these challenges, the committee intensified its efforts to document the violations and prepare a comprehensive report that could support future legal proceedings against Israel.
Killing of journalist Amal Khalil
Among the cases examined was Israel's killing of Lebanese journalist Amal Khalil during attacks on the southern town of Al-Tayri on 22 April 2026.
Journalist Zeinab Faraj, who was accompanying Khalil, was also wounded in the attack.
The report concluded that the incident constituted a blatant violation of international humanitarian law on several grounds, including the deliberate and direct targeting of Khalil, who was left surrounded at the site for several hours while emergency teams were prevented from reaching her, despite her still being alive.
Several organisations, including Human Rights Watch, described the 22 April attack as a deliberate targeting of civilians that would constitute a war crime.
They also highlighted the Israeli army's obstruction of rescue efforts, including the use of a stun grenade dropped from a drone, which forced Lebanese Red Cross personnel to withdraw temporarily without rescuing Khalil or providing potentially life-saving medical assistance.
Deadly Israeli attacks on 8 April
Another major case examined in the report was Israel's large-scale bombardment of Lebanon on 8 April 2026, which the committee found had involved attacks in the absence of military targets.
Israeli forces launched around 100 attacks within a short period, striking Beirut, its southern suburbs, Mount Lebanon, the Bekaa Valley and southern Lebanon.
The attacks killed more than 303 people and wounded over 1,200 others, including dozens of women and children.
Lebanon subsequently submitted an urgent complaint to the UN Security Council over the 8 April bombardment and Israeli attacks on medical and emergency facilities since 2 March 2026 as a blatant violation of the principles of international law.
UN experts, in a statement published by the UN Human Rights Council, also condemned Israel's bombardment of Lebanon on 8 April, saying it was unlawful aggression and a campaign of indiscriminate bombing.
Systematic destruction and forced displacement
The report also documents the systematic destruction of Lebanese cities and villages, including the destruction of cultural heritage, which it classifies as crimes against humanity and serious violations of international humanitarian law.
Among the examples cited is the extensive bulldozing and destruction of the southern city of Bint Jbeil. Satellite imagery, maps and field reports document the scale of the damage to the city's landmarks, infrastructure and residential areas.
The committee also found that Israel had violated fundamental principles of international humanitarian law through unlawful evacuation orders that triggered unprecedented waves of mass displacement, emptied entire villages of their residents and left them uninhabitable.
According to the report, the available evidence indicates that Israeli attacks were indiscriminate, particularly where their effects extended beyond the intended targets into wider civilian areas or where weapons with wide-ranging effects were deployed in environments in which their impact could not be contained.
The evidence also provides sufficient information for a preliminary assessment of the weapons used, with the documented damage consistent with the use of highly explosive munitions, most of them dropped from aircraft on civilian residential areas.
Geographical analysis identifies three main areas where evidence of the violations is concentrated.
The first is central Beirut, where footage of direct attacks, images recorded in their aftermath and victims' testimonies provide evidence of strikes in densely populated residential neighbourhoods.
The second is Beirut's southern suburbs, where repeated footage of attacks, widespread destruction and testimonies documenting continued bombardment and displacement indicate that civilian areas were subjected to sustained military pressure.
The third is southern Lebanon, where attacks on villages, damage to infrastructure and civilian testimonies reveal a similar pattern of harm inflicted on residents.
The committee concluded that these findings raise serious concerns about violations of the fundamental principles governing the conduct of hostilities, as established by the Geneva Conventions and international humanitarian law.
The report also examines a series of Israeli attacks on major bridges and crossings over the Litani River and its tributaries, as well as roads leading to them, during March and April 2026.
According to the committee, the evidence indicates that the destruction constituted unlawful attacks on protected civilian infrastructure and crossings vital to the civilian population, violating the principles of distinction, proportionality and precaution, as well as obligations concerning the facilitation of humanitarian relief.
Other incidents examined include attacks on medical services in the town of Mifdoun in the Nabatieh district, civil defence personnel in Majdal Zoun in the Tyre district and a residential apartment in the hills of Ain Saadeh on 5 April 2026.
Legal avenues for prosecuting Israel
Separately, the Arab Centre for Research and Policy Studies in Beirut, headed by former minister Nasser Yassin, has been documenting Israeli violations and assessing the cost of the war on Lebanon, particularly the direct and indirect damage inflicted on the country's vital sectors.
During a discussion hosted by the centre on 27 August under the title "Israeli violations of international humanitarian law", Mitri addressed the legal options available for pursuing accountability for Israeli crimes, including the possibility of bringing cases before the International Criminal Court (ICC).
"Lebanon is not a party to the Rome Statute, which established the International Criminal Court, preventing the Lebanese state from resorting to it to prosecute Israel under the current circumstances," he said.
Mitri nevertheless explained that the ICC could, under specific circumstances and through established legal mechanisms, exercise jurisdiction over crimes committed during a particular period, even if the state concerned had not fully joined the Rome Statute.
"The inability of the Lebanese state at present to turn to the International Criminal Court does not remove the right of Lebanese individuals to pursue Israel before several European courts, such as those in Spain, Belgium and France, where some European judicial systems allow, under specific conditions, the filing of cases related to international crimes or serious violations," he said.
He stressed that some individuals had already begun taking such steps.
Mitri also called on civil society associations, human rights organisations and other bodies that have documented Israeli violations to submit their research and reports to the government.
He said coordinating official and civil society efforts was essential to consolidating the evidence and preparing legal cases to pursue accountability for Israel's actions.

articles.title: How does the Kremlin want the loyalist media to report on Russia’s 2027 federal budget? Start with social benefits. Don’t mention that 44% goes to the military and security agencies.
articles.body:
How does the Kremlin want the loyalist media to report on Russia’s 2027 federal budget? Start with social benefits. Don’t mention that 44% goes to the military and security agencies.
Russian state-run and government-aligned online news outlets have received guidelines on how to cover Russia’s proposed 2027 budget. The government submitted it to the State Duma on September 30.
The guidelines, which Meduza has reviewed, recommend telling readers that the authorities continued to put “people” first when drafting the budget and that “the state will fulfill and expand all its social obligations” to them. The document says the budget proposal’s “main feature” is that those obligations will be met “without fail.”
The authors advise citing specific figures to support this claim. For example, they suggest telling readers that pensions will be adjusted for inflation twice next year: by 6.7% in February and another 3.3% in April.
Planned spending on new schools and kindergartens is also meant to show that the authorities care about their citizens. But the document cites plans for 2030 rather than targets for next year. Those plans call for another 150 schools and more than 100 kindergartens nationwide.
The guidelines recommend comparing the planned budget deficit of 2% of GDP with deficits in “Western countries”: 5.5% in France, 3.6% in the U.K., and more than 3% in Germany.
After distributing the guidelines, presidential administration staff also verbally warned employees of government-aligned outlets against “going off script” in their budget coverage. Their reporting and forecasts must be based on government press releases and announcements.
The journalists may seek comment on the approved budget proposal only from pro-government experts, who have themselves received instructions from the cabinet. These experts include staff at the Financial University under the Government of the Russian Federation, such as lead researcher Dmitry Morkovkin; the Russian Presidential Academy of National Economy and Public Administration, including senior researcher Vladimir Yeremkin; and the Higher School of Economics.
On the eve of the budget’s approval, the government-aligned outlet Vesti had already sought comment from Yeremkin. He gave the proposal a “generally positive” assessment and singled out the very points the guidelines emphasized:
In my view, all the budget items are very well balanced. One thing worth highlighting is the strong social support. The social spending provisions look quite good, and the budget provides for two pension increases next year, with pensions rising by 10% on average.
In reality, the proposal cuts social spending while increasing military spending yet again. The guidelines say nothing about this. Government-aligned journalists are forbidden to raise the subject.
The proposal calls for 17.1 trillion rubles in defense spending in 2027. That is more than a third of the country’s total spending and 27% more than last year’s budget plans allocated for 2027.
Defense and security together account for 44% of total spending in the approved proposal, according to senior fellow Alexandra Prokopenko of the Carnegie Russia Eurasia Center in Berlin. The total includes spending on other law enforcement and security agencies: the Interior Ministry, Russia’s National Guard, and the security and intelligence services.
The “social obligations” that the guidelines urge journalists to highlight account for 21%. Spending on them has been cut from the levels the government planned last year, even though propagandists have been instructed to tell readers it has increased.
Spending under “Social Policy,” which includes pensions, payments to combat veterans, and maternity benefits, will fall by 7%. Education spending will fall by 6%, and health care spending by 6.8%.
Spending under “National Economy” will also fall by 7.4%. This category includes road construction, infrastructure projects, and subsidies for agriculture and other industries.
At Meduza, we are committed to transparency about our use of artificial intelligence in the newsroom. The story you’re reading was written by one of our living, breathing journalists and translated from Russian using an AI model configured to follow our strict editorial standards. This translation process is the result of extensive testing and refinements to ensure our English-language coverage is timely and accurate. A Meduza editor reviews every draft before publication.
If you find any errors in this translation, please contact us at [email protected].

articles.title: Third Army Corps releases testimonies of Russians captured during operation Vivaldi
articles.body:
The Third Army Corps has released a video showing a mass surrender of Russian soldiers, in which the occupiers explain their decision to surrender by citing hunger, exhaustion, administrative chaos, and threats from their own commanders; it is also noted that it is increasingly not infantrymen but specialized personnel of the Russian Armed Forces who are being taken prisoner.
"The Third Army Corps has released a video showing the mass surrender of Russian soldiers and their interaction with Brigadier General Andriy Biletsky. During the three phases of Operation 'Vivaldi,' more than 250 enemy soldiers were captured alive, including dozens of officers. The occupiers attribute their decision to surrender to hunger, exhaustion, administrative chaos, and threats from their own commanders, who, under pressure from the Third Corps, are losing control of the situation," according to a statement from the corps' press service received by Interfax-Ukraine.
In a video released by the corps, the prisoners claim that due to a lack of provisions at their positions, they are forced to eat nettles and tree bark and hunt wild animals. To stave off dehydration, the Russians resort to rainwater and, at times, their own urine. The wounded are not being evacuated from their positions: their only chance of survival is to crawl to the evacuation point on their own. During a conversation with Biletsky, the commander of the Third Army Corps, one of the Russian officers confirmed that troops are dying en masse from exhaustion and starvation. Another reason for capture is the administrative chaos in Russian headquarters, which, under pressure from the Third Corps, have begun to lose control of the battlefield.
It is increasingly not infantrymen but specialized personnel who are being taken prisoner. "Several Russian regiments are now falling apart. That is precisely why it is not even infantrymen who are being taken prisoner, but UAV pilots, mortar gunners, and electronic warfare specialists. We encounter infantry in the trenches less often than specialists," Corps Commander Biletsky said.
Captured Russian officers report that eight months ago, the situation on the front changed dramatically – the advance halted, and it became impossible to carry out orders from the command. Addressing the Russians, Biletsky said: "Capture is the best thing that could have happened to you, because in the near future your troops will face an even worse hell."
As previously reported, over the course of three phases of operation "Vivaldi," the Third Army Corps liberated 176 square kilometers in Lyman sector, eliminated over 5,000 enemy troops, and captured 250 Russian servicemen.
As part of this operation, the Third Army Corps is facing off against the forces of three Russian armies: Russia's 20th Combined Arms Army, Russia's 25th Combined Arms Army, and Russia's first Guards Tank Army. As a result, the offensive by the West Troop Group – formed from troops of the Moscow Military District – was halted, and the enemy was exhausted, defeated, and pushed back.
The 20th Combined Arms Army of Russia has been the main adversary of the third Assault Corps ever since a unit of the third Assault Brigade shifted its operations from Avdiivka to Borivka sector.
"Throughout its participation in the full-scale invasion, the 20th Army under Yurchenko's command has been responsible for numerous crimes against the Ukrainian people. In Ukrainian human rights databases and projects documenting war crimes, Yurchenko has been included in the relevant registries. Among other things, there is a documented case in which Ukrainian prisoners of war were executed using shovels. The execution was captured on thermal imaging. "The army commander at the time reported this incident to higher command, and those who carried out the execution were awarded (by the previous army commander, Alek Mityaev)," according to the reference section of the third Army Corps' statement.
It is noted that personnel of Russia's 25th Combined Arms Army were involved in mass war crimes on the territory of Ukraine, including the torture of civilians, the execution of prisoners of war, and the terrorization of the civilian population in Kharkiv region in 2022, while occupiers from Russia's first Guards Tank Army have committed numerous war crimes against the civilian population and infrastructure in Kyiv, Sumy, and Kharkiv regions.

articles.title: Pentagon orders 14,000 attack drones from Neros
articles.body:
- Neros said the U.S. Department of War ordered 14,000 drones and explosive payloads, valued above $100 million, after Drone Dominance Gauntlet II.
- The company also received a bonus order for 800 Gauntlet I drones reallocated from competitors that missed production deadlines.
The U.S. Department of War has ordered 14,000 attack drones and explosive payloads from California drone maker Neros after the company finished near the top of both events in the Pentagon’s latest Drone Dominance competition, a deal Neros values at more than $100 million.
Neros announced the order on Sept. 30 and said it had also received a second bonus order for 800 more drones from the program’s first round, reassigned from competitors that could not meet their production deadlines. The Pentagon has not published the value of either order.
The Gauntlet II order is split between two versions of the company’s Archer drone. Archer AI is a 10-inch first-person-view attack drone, a size class named for its propellers, with terminal guidance that lets it fly itself to a target the operator has picked, which helps when jamming cuts the link to the pilot, while Archer 5 is a smaller variant built for close-quarters fighting in towns and inside buildings.
“We’re proud to be the only manufacturer to have placed top three in both Gauntlet II mission sets, and are already fulfilling this next tranche of orders,” Neros said in a post on X.
Gauntlet II, held in August at Fort Carson, Colorado, tested 23 drone designs from 19 companies across 1,858 sorties flown by military operators, and the program’s leaderboard now shows 60,000 drones ordered, split evenly between its two events. In deep strike, Perennial Autonomy, the drone company backed by former Google CEO Eric Schmidt, won with 80.1 points and an 8,000-drone order, followed by Hyperscale with 7,000, Neros with 6,000, Skycutter with 5,000 and Swarm Defense Technologies with 4,000. In close-quarters battle, Neros won with 88.1 points and 8,000 drones, ahead of ORQA US with 7,000, XTEND Reality with 6,000, Vector with 5,000 and ModalAI with 4,000.
Neros’s combined 14,000 drones account for nearly a quarter of the 60,000 total, well ahead of the 8,000 ordered from Perennial Autonomy, the next-largest single order.
Neros’s figure of more than $100 million is higher than the program’s own prices suggest. At the Gauntlet II unit prices of $3,500 and $4,500, 14,000 drones would cost between $49 million and $63 million, DroneXL calculated, and Neros has not explained the difference, though its order also covers explosive payloads.
The 800-drone bonus comes from a problem that has dogged the program’s first round. Gauntlet I, held at Fort Benning, Georgia, earlier this year, produced orders for about 30,000 drones from 11 companies, which had to deliver half within two and a half months and the rest within four and a half. By August, only three of the 11 had finished, as most struggled to find motors, sensors, batteries and chips that meet U.S. rules barring certain foreign parts, Inside Unmanned Systems reported.
Neros was the first to finish, completing its 2,400-drone order in July and earning a 2,000-drone bonus, and the new 800-drone award brings its Gauntlet I total to 5,200 drones. The company was building about 1,200 Archers a week in August, the same month it raised $250 million at a $2.5 billion valuation.
Drone Dominance is a $1.1 billion, four-round Pentagon effort to buy cheap one-way attack drones in large numbers and push U.S. manufacturers to produce them at scale, with each round pairing field testing by troops with fixed-price orders and tight delivery deadlines.
The program opened its third round on Sept. 28 with $450 million for about 60,000 drones and an option for up to 40,000 more, and companies that want to compete must first deliver a 400-drone order within about two months.

articles.title: CX2 turns FPV drones into hunters of enemy drone pilots
articles.body:
- CX2 launched Vadris SDR, a software-defined version of its FPV-mounted RF direction-finding payload that adds TBS Crossfire and DJI OcuSync detection.
- The company says more than 450 Vadris systems have been fielded to the U.S. Department of War.
U.S.-based defense technology firm CX2 has released a new version of Vadris, a small radio sensor that rides on an FPV drone and steers it toward the source of an enemy drone’s control signal, now able to pick up several of the most common drone control systems instead of just one.
CX2 announced Vadris SDR on Oct. 1. The original Vadris was built to detect ExpressLRS, an open-source radio control link widely used on first-person-view drones by hobbyists, commercial users and militaries. The new software-defined radio version adds TBS Crossfire and DJI’s OcuSync, two other widely used control links, and CX2 says it can add more through software updates as new links appear, without fitting new hardware each time.
Vadris is mounted directly on an FPV drone. It detects radio activity, works out the direction it is coming from, and overlays directional cues on the operator’s video feed, letting the pilot fly toward the transmitter. CX2 describes the goal as “Hunt the Archer, Not the Arrow,” meaning the system goes after the ground station or pilot controlling an enemy drone, rather than chasing the drone itself.
“Drones speak different languages. If you want to hunt drones, you need sensors that can speak all of those languages. Vadris does that. Moving ahead, Vadris can speak any language for counter-UAS,” said Porter Smith, CEO of CX2.
The company says more than 450 Vadris systems have already been fielded to the U.S. Department of War. It did not say which units have them, how they have been used, or whether any customer has ordered the new SDR version. It also did not give prices, detection ranges or a delivery date.
The pitch rests on cost. Attaching a cheap sensor to an expendable FPV drone gives small units their own way to find and strike enemy drone teams, a task that otherwise requires larger, dedicated electronic warfare equipment. CX2 calls Vadris a low-cost, attritable payload, meaning the military can afford to lose it.
The update targets a problem seen on the battlefield in Ukraine, where both sides change drone radios, frequencies and control links quickly to stay ahead of jamming and detection. A sensor tuned to a single protocol can become far less useful once the other side switches. Radio-based hunting also has a clear limit: drones guided over fiber-optic cable, now common on the front in Ukraine, give off no control signal for a sensor like Vadris to follow.

articles.title: Oil Exports Find A Way Past Iranian Attacks, But Refinery Bottleneck Persists
articles.body:
Exports of crude oil from the Middle East hit their highest level in September since the war with Iran began, reinforcing a trend of increased supplies despite Iranian attacks on shipping in the Strait of Hormuz, according to analysis of shipping and commodity market data by industry observers.
But while crude levels have risen, the refinery bottleneck that has caused a global spike in diesel prices persists. European Union figures published on October 1 showed diesel pump prices at record levels. Prices have also surged in the United States despite the recovery in oil exports.
"More oil is coming out of the Middle East Gulf than many expected that would be possible even just a few months ago," Richard Meade, chief editor of Lloyds List, told an online briefing on October 1.
Roll Out The Barrel
Lloyds List data shows a steady upward curve of crude tanker transits through the Strait of Hormuz since mid-July, following a sharp fall that coincided with the collapse of the US-Iran memorandum of understanding aimed at ending the conflict, now in its eighth month.
Investment bank JP Morgan said Middle East crude exports in September were at 98 percent of pre-war levels, describing it as "a remarkable recovery for a region still at war."
Commodities analytics firm Kpler reported Saudi oil exports were at average levels for 2025, while maritime intelligence company Windward said Saudi terminals loaded four times more oil than in August -- a big increase but still nearly 40 percent lower than in January.
There appear to be a number of factors behind the revival, including the Saudi East-West oil pipeline, the use of oil shuttles and ship-to-ship oil transfers, and a willingness by some in the industry to accept higher risk.
The Saudi pipeline, which pumps its crude to the Yanbu port on the Red Sea to bypass the Strait of Hormuz, was damaged in an attack by Iran-aligned Houthi militants on September 10. An uptick in shipments from Yanbu later in the month, however, suggested the pipeline had regained at least some of its lost operational capacity.
The United Arab Emirates has found a similar solution, using its pipeline to the port of Fujairah on the Gulf of Oman. It has been targeted in Iranian attacks but is far less vulnerable than Hormuz.
Another route to market has been to use smaller shuttle vessels to transport crude through the Strait of Hormuz, using a route hugging the Omani coastline patrolled by the US Navy. These ships, often traveling in a convoy, pump their cargoes onto tankers in the safety of the Gulf of Oman.
Meanwhile, refineries in India have reportedly begun commissioning tankers to use the route directly.
Attacks Continue
The risks to shipping have not disappeared. In the latest incident, three Liberian-flagged tankers were struck by unknown projectiles when transiting the Strait of Hormuz on September 30. Industry analysts suggest the dangers have simply been priced in.
"Higher exports do not necessarily mean that the Strait of Hormuz has become safe. They simply show that the oil industry has become accustomed to working around that danger," Meade said.
Crude prices have retreated from recent highs, but refinery bottlenecks remain a global issue. According to the International Energy Agency (IEA), much of this is in the Persian Gulf.
Iranian attacks on refineries combined with Hormuz shipping disruption have led to a collapse in output, the IEA said.
"In 2025, Middle East producers exported 3.3 million barrels per day of refined oil products. But since the conflict began, as much as 3 million barrels per day of refining capacity has been unavailable," the IEA wrote in a note on September 21.
This global diesel shortage has been compounded by Ukrainian attacks on Russian oil refineries, leading the Kremlin to impose a diesel export ban.
"Refineries around the world are already stretched to capacity," the IEA said. "This leaves few available options to prevent a further tightening of supplies and higher prices in the coming months."

articles.title: Russian diesel exports via the Black Sea fall to zero for the first time on record
articles.body:
Russian exports of diesel fuel and gasoil through the Black Sea fell to zero in the week ending Sept. 24, the first such occurrence since records began, according to data from S&P Global Commodities at Sea that were reviewed by The Insider. A week earlier, 66,000 metric tons of fuel were shipped from the port of Novorossiysk, while in 2025 Black Sea ports exported an average of about 200,000 tons a week.
Russia’s total seaborne exports of diesel and gasoil nearly halved over the week, falling to 81,000 tons. All of those volumes were loaded at the Baltic port of Primorsk and were headed to Morocco and Venezuela. A week earlier, Russian diesel was being shipped to at least five countries, including Turkey, Morocco, and Singapore.
From Sept. 1 through Sept. 24, Russia exported 448,000 tons of diesel and gasoil by sea. By comparison, S&P put the figure at 535,000 tons in August and 713,000 tons in July. Russian ports also went a second consecutive week without shipping gasoline or jet fuel.
The Black Sea has become more expensive to insure
The drop in shipments coincided with a sharp increase in threats to shipping in the Black Sea. On Sept. 16, the Joint War Committee, which brings together representatives of the London insurance market, expanded its high-war-risk zone to cover nearly the entire Black Sea — Turkish, Romanian, Bulgarian, and Georgian territorial waters were excluded, but Russian and Ukrainian waters fell inside the risk zone.
According to calculations by maritime security company Ambrey, 45 commercial vessels were struck outside the previous risk zone in the 12 months from Sept. 21, 2025 to Sept. 21, 2026. There were no such incidents during the preceding 12-month period.
As a result, shipping insurance costs are rising, with the additional war-risk premium for loading oil at Black Sea ports reaching $2.90 a barrel by Sept. 21, up from 90 cents at the end of 2025, according to a Platts estimate. The rate has more than tripled over nine months.
In August, The Insider reported that following Ukrainian attacks, Russian oil shipments to India from Novorossiysk fell by a factor of 4.4, while freight costs rose by about 50%.
Exports restricted after Ukraine strikes Russian refineries
At the same time, Russia itself is restricting fuel exports. The government extended a ban on diesel exports by producers through the end of October, though shipments under intergovernmental agreements remain exempt. The Russian authorities say the measure is necessary in order to secure supplies for the domestic market amid high seasonal demand.
The Insider also reported in August that the restrictions had been tightened after a series of Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries. In July, Russia’s seaborne exports of petroleum products had already fallen by nearly 22%, reaching their lowest level since S&P began keeping the data in 2016. Exports of diesel and gasoil fell by about one-third.
At the same time, the drop in petroleum-product exports has been accompanied by an increase in crude oil shipments. In the four weeks through Sept. 27, Russia exported an average of 3.71 million barrels of crude a day by sea, while weekly revenue from those sales reached its highest level since the start of the full-scale invasion of Ukraine, as strikes on refineries reduce Russia’s domestic processing capacity, leaving more crude oil available for export.

articles.title: Xi’s rhetoric on Taiwan not new: official
articles.body:
Chinese President Xi Jinping’s (習近平) phrasing to “combat Taiwanese independence forces” is not new despite a perceived escalation in Beijing’s rhetoric, Mainland Affairs Council Deputy Chairman Liang Wen-chieh (梁文傑) yesterday said.
Xi yesterday reiterated his firm opposition to Taiwanese independence and external interference in a speech marking the 77th anniversary of the founding of the People’s Republic of China.
He called for efforts “to resolutely fight secessionist forces seeking ‘Taiwanese independence,’ oppose external interference and promote the peaceful development of cross-strait relations to advance national reunification,” the state-run Xinhua news agency reported.
Photo: Taipei Times
Xi called on China to “take solid steps to achieve the great national rejuvenation” in remarks made at a reception at the Great Hall of the People in Beijing, Xinhua reported.
Some observers have interpreted Xi’s remarks on Taiwan as an escalation in rhetoric, pointing to him replacing the term “oppose” Taiwanese independence, which had been commonly used in the past, with a pledge to “resolutely fight Taiwanese independence separatist forces.”

articles.title: U.S. Navy buys more 30mm guns to shoot down drones
articles.body:
- The U.S. Navy awarded MSI Defence Systems US a $197 million sole-source contract for MK88 MOD4 30 mm gun mounts and MK48 MOD2 sights.
- Most of the work will be done in Norfolk, England, with deliveries due by January 2031.
The U.S. Navy has awarded British-owned MSI Defence Systems a $197 million contract for 30mm deck gun mounts and the electro-optical sights that aim them, the weapons the service is fitting to its warships to shoot down small drones and fast attack boats.
The firm-fixed-price contract, issued by Naval Surface Warfare Center Indian Head Division in Maryland, covers MK88 MOD4 gun mounts, MK48 MOD2 electro-optical sights, related hardware and spares. The Department of War did not say how many systems it buys. Deliveries are due to finish by January 2031.
Together with an operator console, the gun mount and sight make up the MK 38 MOD 4 gun weapon system, which replaces the 25 mm MK 38 MOD 3 on U.S. Navy ships. The U.S. Navy has said the older system fell short of its requirements for countering drones, and the new version adds a larger 30 mm MK44 Bushmaster II cannon, with an optional coaxial .50-caliber machine gun. The mount holds 400 rounds in two separate ammunition bins, letting the crew switch between ammunition types.
Unlike earlier versions, the MOD 4 places its camera sight away from the gun rather than on the mount itself, so the system can track a target independently and pass aiming data to the gun. The design is based on MSI’s Seahawk DS30M A2 mount, a family of guns already used by the Royal Navy and other fleets.
The destroyer USS Mustin (DDG 89) became the first U.S. Navy warship to receive the system, with two mounts installed during a maintenance period in San Diego, Naval News reported in April 2024. The U.S. Navy plans to replace the 25 mm guns on its Arleigh Burke-class destroyers with the new system, and the U.S. Coast Guard also uses it.
The new contract is far larger than earlier orders. MSI received about $23.5 million in September 2023 for 15 gun mounts in low-rate production and about $34.5 million in late 2025 for 18 more, along with separate deals for the sight system. The company first delivered eight prototype systems for testing.
The U.S. Navy awarded the contract without competition under a legal exception for production that follows prototypes successfully completed under an other transaction agreement, a faster contracting route used for experimental work.
Most of the work, 73%, will take place at MSI’s facilities in Norfolk, England, with 19% at its U.S. subsidiary in Rock Hill, South Carolina, and the rest in Bozeman, Montana, and Eagleville, Pennsylvania. MSI Defence Systems is part of British company MS International.
The U.S. Navy obligated about $61.3 million at the time of award, drawing on weapons procurement and shipbuilding funds from fiscal 2023 through 2026, including money from accounts used to build new ships.

Trump deploys third US aircraft carrier to Middle East

articles.title: Hong Kong invests billions to accelerate innovation of impactful solutions as an AI-powered future comes into focus
articles.body:
Hong Kong invests billions to accelerate innovation of impactful solutions as an AI-powered future comes into focus
•    The HK$3 billion Artificial Intelligence Subsidy Scheme aims to accelerate the transformation of AI R&D projects into impactful practical solutions.
•    Over 30 projects have been approved, backed by a total of HK$1.7 billion.
[The content of this article has been produced by our advertising partner.]
Artificial intelligence has rapidly evolved from an emerging technology into a cornerstone of Hong Kong's economic transformation strategy. Under the Government's AI+ initiative, further reinforced by the First Five-Year Plan for Economic and Social Development of the HKSAR (2026-2030), the city is stepping up efforts to integrate AI across industries, public services, scientific research, healthcare, finance and smart-city development, with the ambition of becoming a leading innovation hub in the Greater Bay Area and beyond.
At the heart of this strategy is the HK$3 billion Artificial Intelligence Subsidy Scheme (AISS), a three-year programme that supports universities, research institutions, enterprises and government departments in harnessing the immense computing power of Cyberport's Artificial Intelligence Supercomputing Centre, the city's largest AI computing facility and a key piece of digital infrastructure. Hong Kong's total computing capacity has now surpassed 5,000 petaFLOPS.
The scheme marks a strategic shift from supporting AI research alone to accelerating real-world applications capable of generating tangible economic and social benefits. .
Against this backdrop, a new generation of researchers, scientists and innovators is translating cutting-edge breakthroughs into practical solutions.
Since the launch of AISS in 2024, more than 50 applications have been received and over 30 projects approved, spanning local universities, R&D centres, government departments, technology companies and start-ups. Total subsidies granted have exceeded HK$1.7 billion.
Speaking at a sharing session featuring approved AISS projects, Daniel Cheung, Acting Commissioner for Digital Policy, highlighted the scheme's role in supporting Hong Kong's broader development goals. "The AISS closely aligns with the National 15th Five-Year Plan by advancing ‘industries for AI’ and ‘AI for industries,’ promoting the transformation and upgrading of traditional sectors such as finance and healthcare. Since its launch, the AISS has received enthusiastic responses, with subsidised projects demonstrating immense potential in technological innovation and industrial application," he said.
 
Echoing this view, Hendrick Sin, Chairperson of the Committee of AISS, said: "The approved projects not only showcase scientific breakthroughs but are steadily being transformed into practical applications that benefit society and industry, enhancing citizens' quality of life and exemplifying the power of collaborative innovation among government, industry, academia and research."
One of the highlights of the sharing session was a multimodal large language model for medical diagnosis and surgery developed by the Centre for Artificial Intelligence and Robotics (CAIR) under the Hong Kong Institute of Science & Innovation of the Chinese Academy of Sciences.
Focused on advancing innovation at the intersection of AI and life and health sciences, CAIR has built a comprehensive medical AI ecosystem centred on CARES 3.0, a multimodal medical model equipped with continual learning and trustworthy decision-making capabilities. The platform pioneers a new "copilot" approach to intelligent healthcare.
Among its innovations is EchoCare, an ultrasound foundation model trained on four million ultrasound datasets. Adaptable across a wide range of clinical applications, the model can accurately identify lesions in more than 50 organs. CAIR's technological advances have helped overcome critical technical bottlenecks.
Financial innovation
AI is also reshaping Hong Kong's financial sector. The Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) and Cyberport launched the first and second cohorts of the GenA.I. Sandbox in 2024 and 2025 respectively, focusing on use cases in anti-fraud operations, risk management and customer experience enhancement.
Trial results demonstrated significant operational gains across the banking sector. Participating institutions recorded a 30 to 80 percent reduction in preparation time for suspicious transaction reports, while document processing times were cut from one day to approximately five minutes. The technology also reduced risk assessment report production time by 60 percent, enabled more comprehensive risk analysis workflows, and resulted in more than 70 percent of GenAI-generated credit assessments being regarded as useful references by adopting institutions.
Building on this momentum, the HKMA joined forces with Cyberport, the Securities and Futures Commission, the Insurance Authority and the Mandatory Provident Fund Schemes Authority to launch GenA.I. Sandbox++ in March 2026, with a strong emphasis on exploring Agentic AI applications.
Moving beyond content generation, selected use cases under Sandbox++ are examining how AI systems can responsibly take on greater autonomy across end-to-end processes, including customer onboarding, payments, insurance claims and customer interactions.
Collaborative Generative AI Platform
Another project demonstrating the breadth of Hong Kong's AI ambitions comes from InfiX.ai, which has independently developed the Collaborative Generative AI (Co-GenAI) Platform. It enables enterprises, research institutions and industry partners to train domain-specific AI models using their own datasets at significantly lower computing costs. By avoiding the centralisation of proprietary data while safeguarding privacy and intellectual property, Co-GenAI allows specialised intelligence distributed across organisations and devices to be connected and integrated into a continuously evolving collaborative intelligence network.
This approach enables AI technologies to be co-created, co-developed and shared among participating organisations. Supported by high-efficiency computing resources, model engineering, knowledge bases and application workflows, the platform offers capabilities ranging from local deployment and model fine-tuning to evaluation, inference services and multi-model collaboration.
Designed as a scalable, secure and controllable AI infrastructure, the platform has applications across sectors including manufacturing, public administration, finance, healthcare and education, helping drive digital transformation and strengthen the broader AI ecosystem.
These three projects illustrate how government support, world-class computing infrastructure and research excellence are converging to address pressing challenges, unlock new opportunities and demonstrate the transformative potential of artificial intelligence for Hong Kong's future.
The city's ambitions are set to grow further with the planned commissioning of the Sandy Ridge Data Facility Cluster in the Northern Metropolis by 2032. Once fully operational, the facility is expected to propel Hong Kong into the ranks of the world's leading centres for computing capacity, strengthening its position as a regional and global AI powerhouse.

articles.title: Drowning in Data: New Report Says Space Force Needs Lasers Comms to Beat the Bottleneck
articles.body:
The Space Force is preparing to launch hundreds of satellites with countless sensors into orbit over the next few years—sensors that will give commanders vast troves of data.
But the long-standing method for communicating data down from space via radio frequencies has the potential to create deadly data bottlenecks that could slow and stymie future operations, according to a new report.
The report, to be rolled out Oct. 1 by AFA’s Mitchell Institute for Aerospace Studies, makes the case for combining RF with optical communications technology, or laser comms, for a “hybrid” system.
Retired Air Force Col. Jennifer Reeves, now Mitchell’s senior resident fellow for space studies, authored the 37-page analysis and recommends that USSF get moving soon.
Her findings show that the military’s space-based sensors and communications systems are generating as much as 200 times more data than the force consumed two decades ago.
The ability to collect data, however, has not been matched yet by the ability to deliver it quickly to users, Reeves said.
The Space Force has made some moves to field laser comms, which advocates say is harder to disrupt and capable of transmitting more data faster. The Space Development Agency plans to field hundreds of data transport satellites with optical communications terminals in low-Earth orbit for its Proliferated Warfighter Space Architecture.
In a Sept. 29 media briefing, Reeves called that effort “an important step towards … building a proliferated network designed to move data across space and ultimately to the warfighter. But that’s one piece of a much larger communications architecture.”
The first batch of operational data transport satellites is in orbit, and scores more are already under contract and being prepped for launch. The problem is that all of that data is being pushed through a legacy network never designed for that volume, according to Reeves’ report.
“I think the space layer is getting out ahead of us, and we’re going to have too much information to be able to manage effectively,” Reeves said. “We really need to earnestly move forward.”
Yet even as Reeves and others argue for the Space Force to develop laser comms even more, there has been pushback. In 2025, Air & Space Forces Magazine reported on a Government Accountability Office report that dinged the service for spending too much on the not-yet-ready-for-prime-time tech.
“Without demonstrating key laser communications technology capabilities, or [minimum viable products], SDA is risking not being able to leverage past experiences into the investments either under contract or planned for in the future,” GAO wrote. “These investments are substantial—nearly $35 billion.”
RF and Lasers
Radio frequency methods work by broadcasting RF down from space, which makes signals easy to detect, intercept, and jam with the right equipment and skills.
“The [laser] link is so much safer just because of that beam spread, that’s so tiny compared to what you’re getting with RF,” Reeves said in a Sept. 28 media briefing. “Whereas anything inside the footprint of RF, all you have to do to overcome is use power, and you are turning that off.”
As an example, she showed RF communications from space blanketing much of the United States East Coast, while a laser comms shot covered the equivalent to the size of Ellis Island, home of the Statue of Liberty.
“A much smaller footprint reduces spillover and the opportunity for detection, interception, or interference,” she said.
Laser comms can transport data 10 to 40 times faster using a beam nearly 1,000 times narrower. But that precision comes with reliability tradeoffs.
Satellites in low-Earth orbit travel at about 17,000 miles per hour. At that speed, the time window to find another satellite and blast a laser beam to it while keeping the link steady is small. Any physical movement, even small vibrations, can disrupt the signal.
Reeves doesn’t want to ditch RF. The report highlights the technology’s capabilities and its widespread use and applications. But it can’t be the only method, she said.
Moving Data Smarter
Additionally, the report identifies a need for on-platform edge processing to use AI tools and data filtering in space.
“Edge processing and artificial intelligence can help identify and prioritize what’s operationally relevant,” Reeves said.
That will avoid raw data eating up tons of bandwidth on the front end, she said.
The edge processing challenge is that most space assets currently still rely on ground station downlinks for complex command-and-control decisions and target processing, among other tasks. That’s largely due to thermal, power, and radiation thresholds on much space hardware.
In the near-term, USSF’s work building the Space Data Network aims to standardize optical intersatellite links and edge routing.
By using onboard sensor triage methods, USSF hopes that equipment can better process high-resolution imagery and other data on the space asset.
While the paper notes tech fixes such as laser comms and edge processing to move data around space and down to and back up from Earth, Reeves also advocates for reducing data flows and building self-healing, smart networks that reroute information to the best possible pathway to deliver relevant information to operational commanders in minutes, not hours.
“The goal isn’t simply to move every bit faster. It’s to move the right information towards the right user for the most effective available pathway,” Reeves said in the media briefing.
Time Sensitive
Building out a hybrid RF/laser space communications network isn’t an overnight affair. But Reeves argues an initial operational capability could be running within the next five years if Congress and DAF prioritize funding to mature the technology.
That, she said, is critical because the Chinese military isn’t ignoring this capability.
The Chinese government and People’s Liberation Army have two major satellite projects, both utilizing laser communications— the Guowang Constellation (National Network), and the Qianfan Constellation (Thousand Sails).
Guowang began launches in 2024 and currently has as many as 204 active satellites, with plans to deploy nearly 13,000. It uses standard broadband RF, high-resolution radar, and high-capacity laser cross links. The Chinese government views this network as an unjammable military communications backbone for the PLA.
Qianfan has 248 active satellites, Reeves said. It aims to contain 15,000 satellites by 2030. This network is the Chinese government’s testbed for optical terminals with high-speed laser nodes and has secondary military communication lines and maritime tracking assets.
For the U.S., optical communications are already in use among industry and some NASA satellites.
The agency has used the technology on its Orion spacecraft during the Artemis II mission, testing high-bandwidth video transmission from the distance of the Moon, or nearly 240,000 miles away.
The NASA Psyche spacecraft has conducted experiments with laser communications on deep-space laser links. And in 2021, the agency launched the Laser Communications Relay Demonstration and has conducted more than 2,600 experiments with its two ground stations.
The Space Force is also working on its Enterprise Space Terminal program, a $100 million prototyping initiative to build smaller, lighter laser comms terminals that use a standardized waveform.
Mitchell Report Recommendations
- Accelerate and Sustain Communications Modernization Through Stable Resourcing and Adaptive Acquisition.
- Operationalize Hybrid RF-Optical Architectures Across the Force
- Lead Interoperability and Standards Development for the Future Communications Ecosystem

articles.title: Turkey detains suspect in 2013 attack by Syria border
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Turkey detains suspect in 2013 attack by Syria border: state media
Turkey's intelligence agency has captured a key suspect from a deadly 2013 attack near the Syrian border while he was attempting to flee to Europe, state media said Thursday, citing a security source.
The twin bombing in the southern Reyhanli district, which killed 53 people, was the deadliest attack in Turkey linked to fallout from Syria's civil war, which began two years earlier.
Omar al-Khatib, a Syrian who was the subject of an Interpol red notice, is believed to have coordinated between the attackers and intelligence officials loyal to Syria's then president Bashar al-Assad, Anadolu news agency reported.
Turkey's National Intelligence Organisation (MIT) detained al-Khatib as he prepared to leave for Europe by sea, Anadolu said, without saying exactly where or when he was caught.
Ankara blamed Turkish extremist groups allegedly backed by the Syrian government for the Reyhanli attack, accusations Damascus denied.
Before the attack, he crossed into Turkey to scout potential locations where it could be carried out, Turkish media reports said.
He also allegedly supplied the device used in the attack to the perpetrators. The participants were reportedly paid by the Syrian regime at the time, the reports said.
Turkey was a strong supporter of Syrian rebels seeking to overthrow Assad and has hosted millions of Syrians who fled the conflict.
Since Assad's ouster nearly two years ago, Ankara has built close ties with Syria's new leadership under President Ahmed al-Sharaa.

Putin reportedly asked Russian business leaders to help fund the war. Moscow expects 471 billion rubles in ‘voluntary’ contributions from companies this year.
Russian authorities expect to receive 471.4 billion rubles in voluntary contributions from businesses to the national budget in 2026, according to an explanatory note accompanying the draft 2027–2029 budget reviewed by The Bell.
The budget forecasts much smaller voluntary contributions in 2027–2029: 1.9 billion rubles each year.
In March, The Bell reported, citing sources, that Vladimir Putin had met with businesspeople behind closed doors and proposed that they voluntarily finance the war. The Kremlin called the report “untrue” but said Putin had welcomed the idea of voluntary contributions to the budget.
By mid-August, authorities had already collected 384 billion rubles from businesses. The bulk of the money began coming in after March, Vedomosti reported.
Business contributions totaling nearly half a trillion rubles will set a record, The Bell reported. In 2025, authorities collected 251.3 billion rubles from companies.
“Nonrepayable receipts” from private companies fall into two categories: mandatory payments businesses make when selling assets in Russia and voluntary contributions to the budget.

articles.title: Sen. Hawley: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman declined to testify at rogue AI hearing
articles.body:
OpenAI CEO Sam Altman declined an invitation to appear at a Senate subcommittee hearing on Wednesday on the risks of rogue artificial intelligence, according to Sen. Josh Hawley, R-Mo.
Hawley, who chairs the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs subpanel that held the hearing, sent a letter to Altman on Sept. 25 requesting his presence to "help shed light on 
the Subcommittee's ongoing investigation into recent rogue AI incidents involving OpenAI models." NBC News first reported that Altman did not accept the invitation to testify.
"He turned us down," Hawley said of Altman at the hearing. "I think that's unfortunate because I think the American people deserve to know exactly what's going on at all of these companies. And to give us the sort of transparency that I think is needed for not just comfort, but to have an understanding of what these companies — that are the most powerful companies in the world — are doing right now with the most powerful technology ever known to man."
A spokesperson for OpenAI noted that Altman received the invitation to testify on Friday, just five days ahead of the hearing. Altman on Tuesday appeared at the company's annual DevDay developer conference in San Francisco as other AI officials — including OpenAI President Greg Brockman — were in Washington meeting with President Donald Trump.
"OpenAI is deeply engaged with Congress on federal policies to advance AI safety, including through dozens of meetings in recent weeks with members of both parties in both chambers," the spokesperson said. "We look forward to continuing to work constructively and proactively with Senator Hawley and members of Congress on federal AI safety legislation that materially raises the safety bar."
Hawley's overture to Altman comes weeks after he opened an investigation into OpenAI earlier this month. Hawley sought information on a cyberattack involving hundreds of OpenAI agents that broke out of their testing sandbox and hacked into the systems of another AI company called Hugging Face.
The cyber attack was one in a series of recent hacks involving frontier AI models that have raised alarms and prompted calls for Congress to act to rein in the rapidly evolving technology.
Hawley requested information from Altman on the cyber attack and on the existential risks of the technology and set an Oct. 1 deadline. A spokesperson for Hawley said OpenAI is expected to provide additional documents by the end of the week.
"The American people deserve to know the details of what went on in the Hugging Face incident and other incidents of AI models going rogue. This investigation will seek those answers," Hawley said in the Sept. 10 letter.

SpaceX launches 13th long-duration astronaut crew to International Space Station

- The Falcon 9 rocket successfully delivered the Crew Dragon capsule into orbit, with a reusable booster returning safely to Earth after launch from Cape Canaveral.
