CAPE CANAVERAL, Florida - A SpaceX rocket lifted off from Florida on Oct 1 with a crew of two US astronauts, a Canadian astronaut and a Russian cosmonaut headed to the International Space Station (ISS) for a science mission devoted to human health and performance in orbit.
The two-stage Falcon 9 rocket, topped with an autonomously operated Crew Dragon capsule carrying the four-member crew, was launched from the Cape Canaveral Space Force Station, along Florida’s Atlantic Coast.
A live webcast showed the 25-storey-tall rocket thundering off the launch pad as its nine Merlin engines roared to life in billowing, incandescent plumes of vapour.
Falcon 9’s reusable lower-stage booster separated from the rest of the vehicle within three minutes of launch and flew itself back to Earth for a return landing.
The rocket’s upper stage climbed higher and released into orbit the Crew Dragon carrying NASA astronauts Jessica Watkins and Luke Delaney, Canadian astronaut Joshua Kutryk and Russian cosmonaut Sergey Teteryatnikov.
“Dragon separation confirmed. Jessica, Luke, Josh, Sergey, welcome to orbit,” SpaceX mission control in Hawthorne, California, told the crew.
The capsule is thrusting itself along an eight-hour orbital voyage to the space station and is set to dock with the orbiting laboratory platform some 400km above Earth around 7pm EDT (7am on Oct 2 in Singapore).
The mission marks the 13th long-duration space station team that NASA has flown aboard a SpaceX launch vehicle since the rocket venture founded in 2002 by Elon Musk began sending US astronauts to orbit in May 2020. The company went public in a record-breaking IPO in July.
The launch also comes days after SpaceX launched its next-generation Starship spacecraft on its first trip to orbit and first commercial satellite deployment, marking the vehicle’s 14th uncrewed test flight since 2023.
Crew 13 is led by geologist-turned-astronaut Watkins, 38, making her second voyage to space and becoming the first NASA astronaut to fly twice aboard a Crew Dragon.
Seated beside her in the pilot’s chair is Delaney, 47, a former test pilot and fighter pilot making his debut in space.
Rounding out Crew 13 are two other spaceflight rookies ranked as mission specialists - Kutryk, 44, a former test and fighter pilot, and Teteryatnikov, 37, an engineer who specialised in the operation of submarines.
The four crewmates are to be welcomed aboard the space station by seven current occupants of the orbital outpost, including the four members of Crew 12 who are due to fly back to Earth as soon as their seven-month-plus mission comes to an end.
The latest arrivals are expected to focus their attention on a series of biomedical and human performance studies, including research on how microgravity affects blood circulation and clotting, and gathering health data to inform future space missions.
The ISS, which spans the length of a football field and ranks as the largest human-made object in space, has been continuously operated by a US-Russian-led consortium that includes Canada, Japan and 11 European countries.
The first hardware for the outpost was launched more than a quarter-century ago. NASA has said it is committed to keeping the space station operating through 2030. REUTERS

articles.title: System sprang into action within seconds: Behind the scenes of the Flydubai terror drama
articles.body:
A single distress signal sent from the cockpit of a Flydubai plane carrying 174 passengers was enough to send Israel’s security establishment into one of its most tense and complex operations in recent memory.
The activation of various security bodies follows an orderly, almost automatic mechanism linking events aboard the aircraft directly and immediately to IDF command centers, putting the system on maximum alert within seconds.
At first, there was genuine concern that an aircraft bound for Israel had been hijacked. Even before the full picture became clear, the first contingency plan was activated — the protocol for a suspected hijacking. The plan’s code name is barred from publication.
Two Israeli Air Force fighter jets were scrambled to intercept the aircraft, escort it and isolate the surrounding airspace. At the same time, Home Front Command units were placed on alert and General Staff negotiation teams were put on full readiness in case the plane landed in Israel.
Within minutes, however, the situation changed dramatically.
The “hijacked” plane made a sharp U-turn and moved away from Israel’s borders, heading back toward Saudi Arabia. Initial reports sent to the operations command center indicated that a violent confrontation had erupted inside the cockpit between the captain and the co-pilot — a fierce struggle during which passengers and crew members managed, with considerable resourcefulness, to overpower the attacker.
As the aircraft headed for an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia, Israel’s course of action shifted completely.
At that stage, a second contingency plan was activated — a readiness order for a complex hostage-rescue operation in a foreign country. The code name of that plan is also barred from publication.
Once the alert was received that the aircraft was expected to land in Saudi Arabia, Israel’s security forces raised their readiness further. Air Force transport aircraft, including three Hercules planes, were prepared for immediate takeoff, and additional steps were taken as part of hostage-rescue procedures.
Shortly afterward, the IDF Operations Directorate and the broader security establishment concluded that the aircraft was landing in Saudi Arabia without having been hijacked and that its passengers were not being held hostage.
A senior military official said the options were examined with great caution, and three main alternatives were prepared for bringing the Israeli citizens home.
The first was a direct military evacuation using three Air Force Hercules aircraft that were standing by as part of the hostage-rescue order. The second was dispatching a designated civilian aircraft carrying military rescue teams. The third was relying on a civilian Flydubai flight.
In the end, after detailed assessments and complex coordination behind the scenes, officials decided to use what they considered the fastest and safest option for the passengers: evacuation aboard a civilian flight.
Security officials said the main consideration for decision-makers was to avoid unnecessary diplomatic friction on Saudi soil.
At the same time, security officials stressed that all physical and operational systems were fully prepared to carry out any of the other options, including a direct military landing, if difficulties or security risks had emerged.
Senior Israeli security officials said the Saudi government’s conduct during the tense hours was very positive.
“Behind the scenes, there was a great deal of willingness on the Saudi side,” senior Israeli officials said, “and in the end, they took very significant action from our perspective.”
Although military officials have avoided describing the incident as a diplomatic breakthrough and have left such interpretation to the political leadership, the ongoing and positive coordination in such a sensitive setting demonstrated the ability of the two sides to work together in real time.
The IDF said afterward that the operational orders and automatic mechanisms designed to protect Israeli airspace functioned adequately. The General Staff is expected to carry out a routine lessons-learned process in the coming days to further improve the system, with an emphasis on responding appropriately to rapidly developing and changing events.
Still, much remains unclear about the investigation, and difficult questions remain for Israeli security mechanisms that work with international airlines.
Officials will have to determine how an Omani pilot came to be flying Israeli passengers and entering Israeli airspace, and how the relevant security authorities were unaware of his recruitment by an airline that operates extensively in Israel, particularly in recent years.
Another question is whether he was part of a terrorist infrastructure or cell capable of deploying attackers in similar scenarios against Israelis abroad.
The investigation into the apparent security gap comes against the backdrop of the Shin Bet having barred Israeli airlines for months from landing in Dubai because of security concerns. However, the scenarios officials had considered were not similar to what ultimately unfolded aboard the Flydubai flight.
The expectation is that, following the unusual incident, changes will be made primarily behind the scenes in the relationship between the airline, similar carriers and Israeli security bodies.
The screening, questioning and vetting mechanisms relating to pilots carrying Israelis to Israel and other destinations are expected to undergo significant review and overhaul.

articles.title: U.K. Sanctions Four Georgians Over Occupied Ukraine Visit
articles.body:
The U.K. has sanctioned four Georgians—including the brother-in-law of Tbilisi’s mayor—for “legitimising Russia’s occupation of Ukrainian territory” after they met with the head of a Russian-backed separatist republic.
The designations are part of a broader British sanctions package announced in response to intensifying Russian drone strikes against Ukraine in September. According to a press release Thursday, the wider measures target Russia’s “shadow fleet,” Kremlin propagandists, and individuals allegedly involved in human rights abuses against Ukrainian civilians.
“The U.K. will not flinch in our support for Ukraine,” said Europe Minister Lord Wood of Anfield.
The U.K. sanctions notice states the four men “joined a delegation of Georgian politicians who met with the head of the so-called Donetsk People’s Republic, and subsequently publicised the visit.” All four now face U.K. asset freezes and travel bans.
The sanctioned delegates include political commentator Paata Abuladze, Mamuka Pipia, leader of the minor Solidarity for Peace party, party member Giorgi Iremadze, and Nikoloz Mzhavanadze, founder of a Georgian Russian-language TV channel.
Separatist leader Denis Pushilin praised the September 2025 meeting on Telegram, referring to the delegation as “likeminded people from Georgia.”
“It was pleasant to hear words of support for our region’s residents from the Georgian guests, who wished for the swift liberation of all the territory of the Donetsk People’s Republic,” he wrote.
According to a video of the meeting, Pipia told Pushilin: “We hope in the very near future the Donetsk People’s Republic will be free.”
Abuladze added: “You won't be able to show me a single country in the world that is such a small country, yet has endured and is doing whatever it takes to restore diplomatic relations.”
Three of the four delegates have so far responded to the U.K. measures, some using profanity and insults.
Mamuka Pipia told the Georgian TV channel Pirveli that he considered the sanctions a “reward” and that he was “very happy.” Mzhavanadze told his Facebook followers that the decision was “shameful,” and said the U.K. was “afraid that the positions expressed by a person will harm their politics.” Iremadze did not respond to Monitori’s request for comment.
Abuladze also took to Facebook following the news of his designation. “Britain sanctioned me… and congratulated me,” he told his followers, “I am grateful to the British for sanctioning me.”
Contacted by Monitori, he added: “So what? Like I won’t go to Donbas now?”
“I have never been to [Britain] in my life,” he said. “It’s just a formality.”
In his Telegram post, Pushilin referred to Abuladze as a “member” of the ruling Georgian Dream party. While Monitori was unable to verify his formal party membership and he holds no elected office, Abuladze has family ties to an influential Georgian Dream figure: he is the brother-in-law of Kakha Kaladze, the Mayor of Tbilisi.
Manana Toqmajishvili, the head of the Tbilisi City Hall Press Service, confirmed to Monitori that Abuladze is Kaladze’s “half-sister’s husband” but that he has “absolutely no connection to Tbilisi City Hall.” She did not comment further.

articles.title: Russian war spending keeps rising while some regions slash death benefits for soldiers’ families by up to 95%
articles.body:
Russian war spending keeps rising while some regions slash death benefits for soldiers’ families by up to 95%
In the fifth year of its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Russia is spending more on its military and looking for new ways to fund the war. In recent months, however, several Russian regions have sharply cut payments to the families of those killed in the war. Here are a few examples.
- In the Ulyanovsk region, payments to the families of service members killed in the war were cut from 1 million rubles to 500,000 in February 2026, then to 50,000 in April.
- In the Kemerovo region, the payment was cut to a third of its previous amount in February, from 3 million rubles to 1 million.
- In the Omsk region, the payment was cut from 1 million rubles to 500,000 in February.
- In Bashkortostan, the payment was cut to a fifth of its previous amount in May, from 500,000 rubles to 100,000.
- In the Saratov region, the payment was cut to a tenth of its previous amount in late September, from 1 million rubles to 100,000.

articles.title: Money transfers between Russia and Kazakhstan fall nearly 12-fold after EU sanctions on Zolotaya Korona payment service
articles.body:
Money transfers between Russia and Kazakhstan fall nearly 12-fold after EU sanctions on Zolotaya Korona payment service
Money transfers between Russia and at least two former Soviet republics — Kazakhstan and Georgia — fell sharply after the EU imposed sanctions on the operator of the Zolotaya Korona payment system in late July, according to data from regulators in both countries reviewed by RBC.
In August, the value of transfers by individuals from Russia to Kazakhstan fell nearly 12-fold to 239 million tenge (45.5 million rubles). Transfers from Kazakhstan to Russia fell more than 14-fold to 1.2 billion tenge (228.2 million rubles).
Transfers by individuals from Russia to Georgia fell to $5.1 million (about 426 million rubles) that month, their lowest level in more than 20 years. Transfers in the opposite direction fell to zero in August for the first time since records began.
Experts interviewed by RBC said sanctions had hurt Zolotaya Korona’s business.
Zolotaya Korona is an international payment system that has operated since 2003. It lets users send and receive money without opening an account, either online or in cash through its network of partners.
Before Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, one of Zolotaya Korona’s main lines of business was handling money transfers from foreign nationals in Russia to countries in the Commonwealth of Independent States. Following the start of the war, the imposition of sanctions and the departure of Visa, Mastercard, and Western Union — the oldest player in the international money transfer market — Zolotaya Korona became one of the main channels for Russians, including those who had left the country, to send money out of Russia.
Until recently, Zolotaya Korona remained one of the last major Russian payment systems to escape sanctions. The EU sanctioned its operator in July 2026. The service then stopped processing transfers to Azerbaijan, Belarus, Georgia, Kazakhstan, and other countries.
Georgia and Kazakhstan are popular destinations for Russians who left the country because of the war.

articles.title: Europe more aggressive towards Russia than US — Putin
articles.body:
MOSCOW, October 1. /TASS/. The top European nations are currently taking a much more aggressive stance towards Russia than the United States, President Vladimir Putin said during the plenary session of the Valdai Discussion Club.
"Now, of course, the main leading European countries are taking a much more aggressive stance towards Russia than the United States," the president said.
Putin added that if the United States "is striving to end the conflict, then, apparently, many European countries, as I have already said today, based on the unfavorable economic development in their countries, and consequently on the position of the ruling political class at this time, and based on the changes in public sentiment within their countries, are now perhaps the ones leading the aggressive behavior towards Russia and creating additional crises between Russia and Europe."
According to him, Europeans are doing this "precisely to justify the need to prepare for war and to mobilize as many supporters as possible around themselves to stay in power. The logic is very simple – I am sure that this is a significant part of the rationale behind the behavior of European countries towards the Russian Federation," the president explained.
Commenting on the possible influence of the EU on US policy, Putin expressed confidence that it is "excessive" to assume that "someone from the outside determines US policy in certain areas." As he noted, with regard to "the influence of European countries on US policy towards Russia," the EU countries remain NATO allies for Washington. "And they influence the US position in one way or another. But the US ruling class has its own understanding of how to shape [policy]. Yes, there is influence, and there always has been. But ultimately, the US will be guided by its own national interests, especially under President [Donald] Trump.
"This, by the way, also applies to the relations between the US and Europe. Look at the pragmatic decisions the US is making in the sphere of economic interaction with Europe, to put it mildly, so as not to offend anyone. You understand what I’m talking about. So yes, there is influence, but first and foremost, the US is guided by its own interests. Before that, under [US President Joe] Biden, I think it was the opposite – the US government had a greater influence on Europe’s position regarding Russia. Later, the dynamics of the events began to unfold according to their own laws."

articles.title: Israeli strikes kill eight Palestinians across Gaza
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Israeli strikes kill eight Palestinians across Gaza
Israeli strikes killed at least eight Palestinians and wounded more than 20 others across the Gaza Strip on Wednesday, including five people travelling in a civilian vehicle and a journalist who was reportedly working on a story about Quran education.
Five Palestinians were killed when an Israeli strike hit a passenger vehicle near the Council of Ministers junction in the Tel al-Hawa neighbourhood of southwest Gaza City.
The Palestinian Red Crescent said its crews transferred five bodies to Al-Shifa Hospital and 13 wounded people to Al-Quds Hospital.
Gaza civil defence spokesman Mahmoud Bassal said the vehicle had been transporting civilians between Gaza City and the central and southern Gaza Strip when it was struck. He put the number of wounded at 20, including women and children.
Earlier on Wednesday, an Israeli airstrike on a home on Al-Wahda Street in Gaza City killed a woman identified as Iman Abdul Aal and critically wounded her husband.
The Israeli military said the strike targeted a Hamas member whom it accused of planning attacks against its forces. It did not publicly identify the alleged target.
In the southern Gaza Strip, Palestinian journalist and imam Mohammed Abdul Aziz al-Najjar, 38, was killed in an Israeli drone strike in the Mawasi al-Qarara area northwest of Khan Younis.
Al-Najjar, who worked as a producer and presenter of religious programmes for Quran Radio, was preparing a report about Quran memorisation when he was struck, according to the Gaza Ministry of Endowments.
He had been displaced from Khuza'a, east of Khan Younis, where he served as imam of the Ibad al-Rahman Mosque.
His body was taken to the Nasser Medical Complex, while another person wounded in the attack was reported to be in moderate condition.
Later on Wednesday, an Israeli drone strike killed 33-year-old Bilal al-Sumairi near the Al-Matahin junction on Salah al-Din Street in Qarara, north of Khan Younis.
At least two other Palestinians were wounded in the attack, including a girl, according to Palestinian reports.
The attacks come despite a US-brokered ceasefire that took effect in October last year.
Israeli attacks have killed at least 1,400 Palestinians in Gaza since the ceasefire, according to health officials in the territory.
More than 74,000 Palestinians have been killed since Israel launched its assault on Gaza, with hundreds of thousands injured and most of the population displaced.

articles.title: Pentagon Does Not Invite Britain, France or Baltic States to NATO Future Talks
articles.body:
The United States plans to hold a meeting in Poland on the future of NATO without the participation of several European allies, including the United Kingdom, France, and the Baltic states.
Politico reports this, citing six diplomats familiar with the planning of the meeting.
The meeting is being organized by the Pentagon, with the initiative being pushed by Elbridge Colby, the U.S. Defense Department’s top policy official.
The meeting is expected to focus on the future of NATO and possible changes to how the alliance operates.
Norway, Sweden, Finland, Poland, Germany, and the Netherlands have been invited to the meeting.
Meanwhile, the lack of invitations for the United Kingdom, France, and the Baltic states has raised questions among diplomats.
These countries have significant defense budgets and play an important role in NATO. One representative of an uninvited country said that his government was trying to understand the criteria used to select participants for the meeting.
The emergence of this format comes amid demands from U.S. President Donald Trump’s administration for allies to increase defense spending and support U.S. policy.
In June, following the first meeting in Bergen, Colby said that the format included allies that were quickly implementing agreements on defense spending, had sufficient military capabilities, and were ready to move on to practical work.
In June 2025, NATO countries agreed to increase defense spending and security-related expenditures to 5% of GDP by 2035.
Of this, at least 3.5% is to be allocated directly to defense needs, while up to 1.5% will be spent on infrastructure, cybersecurity, civilian resilience, and other related areas.
Militarnyi previously reported that Finnish Defense Minister Antti Häkkänen called on NATO member states to increase defense spending.

articles.title: Navalny-founded Anti-Corruption Foundation proposes sanctions relief for repeal of Russian laws used to prosecute anti-war speech and criticism of the military
articles.body:
Navalny-founded Anti-Corruption Foundation proposes sanctions relief for repeal of Russian laws used to prosecute anti-war speech and criticism of the military
The Anti-Corruption Foundation has proposed easing sanctions on Russia in return for Russian authorities repealing repressive laws and dropping politically motivated criminal cases.
The proposal came in response to reports that the U.S. administration is considering easing restrictions on Russia in exchange for the release of political prisoners.
The foundation said “such negotiations should not be limited to lists of individual names” because not all politically motivated cases become public. A complete list of political prisoners in Russia is impossible to compile, and Russian authorities could open new politically motivated criminal investigations after releasing some prisoners.
We therefore propose a different approach: sanctions relief should be tied not only to the release of individual prisoners, but also to the repeal of repressive provisions in Russian law and the termination of entire categories of politically motivated criminal cases.
Decriminalizing Articles 207.3 and 280.3 of the Russian Criminal Code, commonly known as the laws on “military fakes” and “discrediting the army,” would mean releasing those convicted under these provisions, terminating ongoing proceedings, and preventing any new cases from being brought on these grounds. The same principle should apply to politically motivated prosecutions under laws on “extremism,” “financing extremism,” “justifying terrorism,” and similar provisions when peaceful political activity, donations, speech, and beliefs are treated as criminal offenses.
The Atlantic recently reported that John Coale, a special envoy for the U.S. president, proposed easing sanctions on Russia in exchange for the release of political prisoners. He previously secured the release of about 500 political prisoners in Belarus in exchange for sanctions relief. According to the magazine, U.S. President Donald Trump approved the idea of doing the same in Russia.
The Kremlin, however, said the idea “had not been discussed and could not have been discussed” between Moscow and Washington. “We categorically deny that there are any political prisoners and consider it completely inappropriate to frame the issue this way,” Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said.
The list of Russian political prisoners maintained by the human rights organization “Political Prisoner Support. Memorial” currently includes 1,368 names.

articles.title: Could settler violence, Al-Aqsa incursions spark a new intifada?
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Could settler violence, Al-Aqsa incursions spark a new intifada?
Twenty-six years after the Second Intifada, escalating Israeli military raids, settler violence and incursions into the Al-Aqsa Mosque compound have raised concerns about another Palestinian uprising.
The anniversary comes amid Israel's ongoing war on Gaza, mounting violence in the occupied West Bank and growing incitement against Palestinians ahead of Israel's general election on 27 October.
On Wednesday, 2,474 Israeli settlers entered the Al-Aqsa Mosque compound under police protection during the Jewish holiday of Sukkot, according to the Jerusalem Governorate. It said 52,277 settlers had entered the compound since the beginning of 2026.
Israeli forces also carried out raids across the occupied West Bank, arresting Palestinians, searching homes and turning residential buildings into military positions. Meanwhile, settlers attacked Palestinian communities, damaged property and targeted agricultural land.
The developments have revived memories of the uprising that erupted in September 2000 following a visit by then Israeli opposition leader Ariel Sharon to Al-Aqsa, accompanied by a large security presence.
In the first days of October, Israeli police killed 13 Palestinian citizens of Israel while suppressing demonstrations.
For the families of those killed, the anniversary is a reminder of both their loss and the failure to secure justice.
The victims of the Second Intifada
Among those killed was Ahmad Siam, from the village of Muawiya, whose parents were returning from Jordan when they began receiving calls about their son.
"My wife, Ahmad's mother, and I were returning from a visit to Jordan when we were flooded with calls on the way. We felt that something involving us had happened. Then my brother told me that Ahmad had been injured and was lying in hospital," his father, Ibrahim Siam, told The New Arab.
"But when his mother placed her hand on his chest in the intensive care unit, she realised that he had been killed. She addressed him, saying, 'Congratulations on your martyrdom, Ahmad.'"
Ahmad had been deeply affected by the killing of Palestinian child Muhammad al-Durra in Gaza shortly before his own death. He had also participated in demonstrations defending Palestinian land and was among those protesting in support of Jerusalem and Al-Aqsa when he was killed.
His family has preserved his room and belongings for the past 26 years.
An Israeli commission of inquiry, known as the Or Commission, was subsequently established to investigate the October 2000 killings. Although it issued recommendations, no officers were ultimately prosecuted over the deaths.
"We realised that they were not interested in bringing the criminals to justice, so we withdrew from the court. This was even though they knew who the killers were, and we also had indications of their identities," Siam said.
Israel's shift to the right
Palestinian historian Professor Mahmoud Yazbek believes the events of October 2000 marked a turning point in Israel's treatment of Palestinian citizens.
"What many people believed were sudden events reflected the beginning of a new phase in Israeli society's attitudes and Israeli policies towards our community," he told The New Arab.
Yazbek argued that Israeli society has shifted further to the right since then, with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu increasingly dependent on figures such as Itamar Ben-Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich.
He also accused Israeli institutions of attempting to weaken ties between Palestinian citizens of Israel and Palestinians in the occupied West Bank and Gaza.
The struggle over land remains another major source of tension. Yazbek pointed to recent attempts by settlers to establish a presence on land belonging to the Palestinian village of Majd al-Krum in the Galilee.
"It seems that we will witness another chapter of events starting from this period, concerning land, geography and demographics. But we will not leave for anywhere," he said.
Could another uprising erupt?
Lawyer Fouad Sultani, who helped organise legal assistance for Palestinians arrested during the Second Intifada, warned that growing incitement and the arming of settlers and sections of Israeli society could lead to another violent confrontation.
"The scenes from the beginning of the second intifada affected us deeply. The Arab public was ready to protest, and young people were prepared to rise against the injustice inflicted on us as Palestinians," Sultani said. "But perhaps we did not expect protesters to be shot."
Sultani said the events had exposed the vulnerability of Palestinian citizens of Israel despite their formal citizenship.
"We realised that Israeli institutions do not distinguish between a Palestinian inside Israel and a Palestinian in the West Bank, for example, and treat us in the same way," he said.
He also described increasing pressure on Palestinian lawyers and activists, including disciplinary proceedings against him over social media posts.
"More broadly, all of us inside Israel are being targeted. As lawyers, we no longer know the boundaries of the red lines they have drawn for us," he said.
Sultani warned that the ease with which Israeli police opened fire on Palestinian protesters in October 2000 could be repeated, particularly amid continued incitement and the proliferation of weapons.

articles.title: Flydubai copilot transferred to UAE; Israeli official says he likely acted alone
articles.body:
The investigation is still underway, but despite U.S. President Donald Trump saying he had heard that the Omani co-pilot who attacked the captain of the Flydubai flight was linked to Iran, a senior Israeli official said Thursday that investigators have so far ruled out an apparent connection to the Islamic Republic.
Meanwhile, the co-pilot suspected of trying to crash the Flydubai flight was transferred Thursday from Saudi Arabia to the United Arab Emirates. Indian captain Smit Machchhar, whom he attacked in the cockpit, was also transferred to the UAE for further treatment.
The UAE has meanwhile conveyed angry messages to Israel over what Emirati officials viewed as an overly definitive Israeli conclusion that the co-pilot acted out of terrorist motives aimed at undermining the Abraham Accords before the investigation had been completed.
According to an Israeli official, the word “terror” is particularly sensitive for the Emiratis because it can suggest a lack of control. Abu Dhabi therefore prefers not to get ahead of the investigation and is for now taking a cautious approach to determining the Omani pilot’s motive.
A senior Israeli official said the pilot most likely acted alone. After Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu told Fox News that “we know that the attacker pilot underwent Islamist radical indoctrination,” the official said Israel was examining the suspect’s social media activity.
At the same time, the assessment in Israel is strengthening that the motive was nationalist and religious rather than an attempted suicide unrelated to terrorism.
Israel asked to be involved as an observer in the investigation of the pilot in Saudi Arabia and the UAE, but according to the Hebrew report, Riyadh did not agree. “The Saudis are doing everything possible not to involve Israel in the investigation,” an Israeli official said.
Now that the co-pilot has been transferred to the UAE, Israeli officials are relying on close ties and cooperation with Abu Dhabi in hopes of becoming as involved as possible in the investigation, even if only in an observer capacity.
Indian captain Smit Machchhar, who fought the co-pilot after being attacked and stabbed in the cockpit before Israeli passengers intervened, was transferred to the UAE after being hospitalized in Saudi Arabia.
According to the Israeli report, he was apparently stabbed with an emergency axe kept in the cockpit. The Gujarat government announced that it would honor Machchhar with the Vishisht Gujarat Garima Award. Gujarat Chief Minister Bhupendra Patel praised his courage, saying his actions had saved the passengers’ lives.
Netanyahu: There was a ‘loophole’
In an interview with Fox News, Netanyahu acknowledged that the Omani co-pilot had apparently exploited a loophole in rules governing flights to Israel.
Netanyahu said restrictions exist barring pilots from countries without diplomatic relations with Israel from operating such flights, but that the Omani co-pilot had apparently managed to get around them.
“The first thing is you want a background check on pilots,” Netanyahu said. “Even if you have metal detectors, they’re usually for the passengers, and it’s quite possible that pilots just don’t go through that. So obviously, that’s a loophole that has to be corrected.”
Netanyahu also said Israel was receiving “full cooperation” from the UAE government and that both sides wanted to ensure such an incident did not happen again.
He warned that further attempts could occur, saying Israel had indications that Iran and its proxies were seeking to carry out attacks against Israel and Israelis during the election period, and urged Israelis to remain especially vigilant.
Hours later, Trump was asked at the White House whether the pilot had any connection to Iran.
“I would say the answer, based on what I’m hearing, is yes, but we’re working on it right now,” Trump said.
Asked whether the United States would retaliate if Iran were found responsible, Trump replied: “Oh they’ll be hit, very hard, don’t worry.”
For now, however, the senior Israeli official said investigators had ruled out a suspected Iranian connection.
‘I never dreamed Trump would talk about me’
Yaniv Hayun, who helped stabilize the Flydubai aircraft and was later praised by Trump, said he was still processing the drama aboard the flight and his unexpected status as one of its heroes.
“We should celebrate a birthday on this day. All the passengers said, ‘We were born again,’” Hayun said Thursday at his home in Ness Ziona after learning that he would receive a municipal heroism award for his actions.
Later Thursday, Hayun met Netanyahu for a second time. The prime minister hosted several other passengers involved in stopping the attack, including Dr. Shota Musaev, his wife Sigalit and Or Fardilov.
“The whole world sees Israeli heroism,” Netanyahu told them. He also announced that they would light a torch honoring civilian heroism at Israel’s next Independence Day ceremony, although the event is still about six months away.
During the meeting, the passengers gave additional details about the moments inside the aircraft.
Musayev, who treated the badly wounded captain, said: “I saw that the terrorist was injured. On the floor, I saw a lot of blood. It was the pilot’s blood. We don’t know, maybe he was also injured, the terrorist, but not like the pilot. Everything was cut, everything, his hands, his head. Really deep wounds.”
Musayev said he then focused mainly on stopping the bleeding and continuously checking the captain’s pulse and condition.
The passengers said the most dramatic moments lasted only seconds.
“In the end, I came up with the idea of tying him with the headphone cord, and we tied him because we had no other choice,” Musayev said. “Only afterward did they bring us zip ties. That was the only thing in my head, somehow tie him up so he wouldn’t start going wild.”
Hayun said the Omani co-pilot declared that “he had failed in his mission and preferred to die,” while Fardilov said he and the others focused on “holding the situation” under control.
Hayun also responded to Trump’s colorful description of him as “an Israeli plumber who had never flown a plane” but managed to help save the aircraft.
“I’m an upgraded plumber,” Hayun said. “He wasn’t wrong. I don’t work at NASA and I don’t deal with space. I deal with stinking pipes, and he was right. It didn’t offend me.”
Hayun said all he wanted now was to return to normal life. “In my dreams I never thought Trump would talk about me and refer to what I did, and I actually like his humor,” he said. “It was amusing how he described it. I’m not exactly Bruce Lee. I did manage to overpower the terrorist with several other Israelis, pull him backward in a chokehold, and that’s the most important thing.”
Presidential Medal for the flight heroes
President Isaac Herzog spoke Thursday with Hayun and three other Israelis who displayed exceptional bravery aboard the flight, Tzvika Mans, Assaf Rajuan and Dr. Shota Musayev, and told them he intended to recommend all four for the Presidential Medal for Civilian Valor.
The President’s Residence said the Israelis “acted quickly and decisively,” alongside the Indian captain who fought the co-pilot and managed to open the cockpit door.
“At a moment when the lives of so many people were in danger, you acted without hesitation, with courage, resourcefulness and extraordinary mutual responsibility,” Herzog told them. “You risked yourselves to save others and prevented a grave disaster.”
“The entire world saw the beautiful and courageous face of Israeli society,” he added. “I am proud of you and thank you on behalf of the State of Israel. I intend to bring the story of your heroism before the advisory committee for the Presidential Medal for Civilian Valor and recommend that you receive the award.” Tali Mans, Tzvika Mans’ wife, was later also recommended by Herzog for the medal.
According to the President’s Residence, testimony showed that Tali played a significant role in confronting the incident and saving passengers. After hearing violence and commotion from the cockpit, she was the first to alert other passengers and call for help, prompting those who eventually intervened and subdued the attacker.
Even after he had been restrained, the statement said, she continued to act calmly, calling pilots who were in the rear section of the aircraft to come forward and help restore control of the plane.

articles.title: UK rolls out a slew of fresh sanctions against Russia
articles.body:
The British government has announced a package of 31 new sanctions against Russia as the UK steps up economic pressure ahead of the winter.
In a statement on Thursday, the country’s foreign office said the 31 new measures include sanctioning "LNG shadow fleet vessels, Kremlin disinformation networks and perpetrators of civilian torture and child indoctrination."
"Action comes as Russia fired over 3,100 jet-powered drones into Ukraine in September, outstripping its grim wartime record from August," it noted.
The sanctions include eight people involved in the "arbitrary detention, torture and ill-treatment" of Ukrainian civilians, according to the statement.
It added that a further seven individuals are being targeted for their role in the "indoctrination and militarisation" of Ukrainian children, including those deported by the Russian authorities.
"We are targeting both the revenues that help sustain Russia’s aggression and perpetrators of horrendous crimes against Ukrainian civilians, including children. The UK will not flinch in our support for Ukraine," Minister for Europe Lord Wood of Anfield said in the statement.
The UK government said the new measures show the country's determination, alongside partners, to hold those responsible for "Russian state aggression" against Ukraine to account, constrain the revenues sustaining its war, and defend the security of Ukraine, the UK, and Europe.
"While the UK does not seek confrontation with Russia, until (President Vladimir) Putin chooses to end his senseless and barbaric war, the UK’s support for Ukraine will remain unshakeable," added the statement.

articles.title: Rubio orders Iran UNGA delegation to leave United States following stalled negotiations - report
articles.body:
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio ordered Iran's delegation to the UN General Assembly to leave the United States immediately on Monday after negotiations between Washington and Tehran stalled, Axios reported Thursday.
The delegation included Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi, Rubio's Iranian counterpart, who had been involved in indirect negotiations with the United States during his stay in New York.
Although the Iranian officials were expected to leave the United States soon regardless, Rubio's decision constituted an unusual diplomatic rebuke as efforts to negotiate an end to the US-Iran war failed to produce a breakthrough, according to Axios.
"Secretary Rubio kicked out the Iranian delegation who had overstayed their welcome. The UN General Assembly was over, so it was time for them to go," a US official told Axios.
Qatari mediators had been attempting to bridge gaps between Washington and Tehran, but neither side was willing to make the concessions necessary for an agreement, according to the report.
White House concludes Iran negotiations at stalemate
The White House believed on Monday morning that progress might still be possible later in the day, Axios reported. By late afternoon, however, US officials concluded that the negotiations had reached a stalemate.
On Monday evening, acting on Rubio's instructions, the US mission to the UN informed Iran's mission that Araghchi and the delegation had to leave New York immediately, according to the US official cited by Axios.
Araghchi and other members of the delegation left for the airport several hours later and boarded a flight from New York to Doha at 1:20 a.m. on Tuesday.
A second source familiar with the matter told Axios that the US had demanded the delegation's departure, but noted that Araghchi was already scheduled to travel back to Tehran on Monday night.

articles.title: Soviet Union’s collapse is tragedy for tens of millions — Putin
articles.body:
MOSCOW, October 1. /TASS/. The collapse of the Soviet Union was a real tragedy for tens of millions of people who suddenly woke up finding themselves living under foreign realities, Russian President Vladimir Putin said on Thursday.
"Russia has been through a complicated path of fundamental transformations and this process is ongoing," Putin said at the 23nd annual session of the Valdai International Discussion Club.
"We witnessed the collapse of the state system 35 years ago and it was a real tragedy for tens of millions of people who, overnight, found themselves waking up in another country, and it changed their fate, the fate of their children," the Russian president added.
President Putin is taking part in a plenary session of the 23rd annual meeting of the Valdai Discussion Club, titled "Responsibility for the Future: Limits of the Possible or Possibilities Without Limits?".
The club’s flagship conference brings together 120 participants from 40 countries, including Algeria, Brazil, China, Egypt, France, Germany, India, Indonesia, Iran, Japan, Pakistan, South Africa, the United Kingdom, and the United States.
Putin has been taking part in the club’s meetings since its establishment in 2004. The first conference was held in Veliky Novgorod, near Lake Valdai, which gave its name to the event. Since 2014, the club’s meetings had been held in the Black Sea resort city of Sochi, but this year the Valdai session has been relocated to the Moscow Region as it is more convenient for most of its participants to get to Moscow.

articles.title: Airborne T-7 Links Up with Simulators in Air Force First
articles.body:
Three T-7A Red Hawks flew together at Joint Base San Antonio-Randolph, Texas, on Sept. 16—but only one was a real aircraft in the air. The other two jets were virtual, controlled from simulators on the ground. All three shared a single, common operating picture.
The demo marked the first time Air Education and Training Command has demonstrated live, virtual, and constructive simulation with its future jet trainer, the T-7 from Boeing. The demo inserted physical and digital assets into one synthetic environment, in which all three could communicate and work together.
“Think of it as a gaming area,” said Steven “Stein” Dobrinski, a Boeing flight simulator design engineer, in a January interview with Air & Space Forces Magazine. “If I’ve got everything programmed and I’m in the data link, now I’m able to have all the entities, the sims and the airplanes, that are all talking to each other in the same gaming area.”
Using LVC, the simulators and jets can fly as if equipped with missiles, bombs, or pods attached, and when employed by a pilot, others will “see” the effects play out on their displays. The simulators can also “inject” adversary aircraft or threats into a scenario, with threats appearing on everyone’s displays.
The Sept. 16 flight aimed to test and validate the “foundational digital architecture” for LVC to work with the T-7, according to a release from AETC.
The real T-7A was crewed by Col. Michael Trott and Lt. Col. Phillip Bourquin of the 99th Flying Training Squadron, while the simulators were controlled by civilian instructors with the 12th Training Squadron: Robb Erickson, a retired Air Force colonel, and Ryan Sparkman, a retired Air Force lieutenant colonel.
“Through secure, high-bandwidth tactical data links, ground-based flight simulators communicated directly with the airborne T-7A maneuvering across local military training airspace,” according to the release.
Boeing and the Air Force refer to the T-7 simulator as the Ground-Based Training System and see it as integral with the new trainer aircraft. The ability to pair simulators with real planes and inject virtual opponents into a scenario opens up a whole range of trainin capability that legacy T-38 Talon trainers could not support.
Officials envision future fighter pilots collaborating with manned and unmanned systems, along with automation, to manage enormous information streams, as they face off against high-level threats that will be difficult if not impossible to simulate in the physical world.
The most advanced versions of the T-7 GBTS simulator resemble an egg shell, with a 360-degree field of view, cockpit controls that mirror the real T-7 exactly, a seat that moves based on users’ inputs, and even an associated G-suit.
Trott, commander of the 99th and one of the first Airmen to be qualified as an instructor pilot on the T-7, praised the simulator to Air & Space Forces Magazine, calling it far more realistic than existing systems for the T-38 and F-15E, both of which he has used in the past.
The Sept. 16 flight is not the first time the T-7’s LVC capabilities have been tested—Dobrinski told Air & Space Forces Magazine in January that Boeing tried it out in a series of test flights last year. As one of the jets flew to Eglin Air Force Base, Fla., for climate testing, Boeing officials paired it with a simulator in St. Louis and inserted constructive entities.
“It worked like a champ on the way out,” Dobrinski said. “When it came back, we intercepted it again, and I was in one of [the simulators]. We had a four-ship, so we had four pilots in the sims, and we rejoined on the live aircraft and flew with them until they got sick of us, because we were talking on the radio. And we locked them with the radars, and that worked really, really well.”
More test flights followed, expanding up to a six-ship flight, Dobrinski said.
Training officials say live, virtual and constructive training is the future, not only for the T-7 but for other new aircraft, as well. The F-35 is starting to add elements of LVC through its highly advanced Joint Simulation Environment and new F-35 Emulated Non-Operational Flight Program Interoperability Experience, or FENIX, simulators. Air Force aviators used FENIX during Exercise Valiant Shield this summer to connect crews across the Pacific, according to a service release.

articles.title: Lviv court sentences Viacheslav Zinchenko to life for murder of former Ukrainian lawmaker Iryna Farion
articles.body:
Lviv court sentences Viacheslav Zinchenko to life for murder of former Ukrainian lawmaker Iryna Farion
Lviv’s Shevchenkivskyi District Court sentenced Dnipro resident Viacheslav Zinchenko to life in prison for murdering politician Iryna Farion.
Zinchenko was charged with premeditated murder and illegal weapons possession. He denied the charges.
Prosecutors alleged that Zinchenko killed Farion “in connection with the victim’s performance of her civic duty and motivated by national intolerance.” They said he believed there was “discrimination on the basis of nationality against Ukrainian citizens who speak Russian.” Zinchenko viewed Farion, who was known for defending Ukrainian language and culture, as someone who had supposedly “divided the nation.”
As the verdict was read, demonstrators outside the courthouse demanded a life sentence for Zinchenko.
On the evening of July 19, 2024, Farion was shot in the head in an assassination attempt in the courtyard of her home in Lviv. She was a linguist and had served in Ukraine’s parliament, the Verkhovna Rada, during its seventh session. Farion died in the hospital. The shooter fled the scene. Zinchenko was detained in Dnipro on July 25 on suspicion of murdering the former lawmaker. The next day, a court ordered him held in pretrial detention.
